and the accused pl eads that the registration of th e geographical indication is invalid, the followi ng
procedure shall be followed:—
(a) if the court is satisfied that such defenc e is prima facie tenable, it shall not proceed with the
charge but shall adjourn the proceeding for three months from the date on which the plea of the
accused is recorded to enable the accused to file an application before the High Court under this
Act, for the rectification of the register on the ground that the registration is invalid;
(b) if the accused proves to the court that he has made such application within the time so limited
or within such further time as the court may for sufficient cause al low, the further proceedings in the
prosecution shall stand stayed till the disposal of such application for rectification;
(c) if within a period of three months or within such extended time as may be allowed by the court
the accused fails to apply to the High Court for rectification of the register, the court shall proceed
with the case as if the registration were valid.

(2) Where two or more applications in the name of the same applicant are accompanied by provisional specifications in respect of inventions which are cognate or of which one is a modification of another and the Controller is of opinion that the whole of such inventions are such as to constitute a single invention and may properly be included in one patent, he may allow one complete specification to be filed in respect of all such provisional specifications:

(1) Any person may, within four months from the date of the advertisement or re -advertisement of an application for registration, give notice in writing in the prescribed manner and on payment of such fee as may be prescribed, to the Registrar, of opposition to the registration.
(2) The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice on the applicant for registration and, within two months from the receipt by the applicant of such copy of the notice of opposition, the applicant shall send to the Registrar in the prescribed manner a counterstatement of the grounds on which he relies for his application, and if he does not do so he shall be deemed to have abandoned his application.
(3) If the applicant sends such counter -statement, the Registrar shall serve a copy thereof on the person giving notice of opposition.
(4) Any evidence upon which the opponent and the applicant may rely shall be submitted in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time to the Registrar, and the Registrar shall give an opportunity to them to be heard, if they so desire.

Any person who knowingly makes use on a computer of an infringing copy of a computer programme shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven days but which may extend to three years and with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand ru pees but which may extend to two lakh rupees: Provided that where the computer programme has not been used for gain or in the course of trade or business, the Court may, for adequate and special reasons to be mentioned in the judgment, not impose any sentence of imprisonment and may impose a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees.

(2A) The Registrar of Copyright shall, within fourteen days from the publication of the notice in the Official Gazette, post the notice on the official website of the Copyright Office so as to remain in the public domain for a period of not less than three years. An advertisement application registration relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be assigned by the applicant subject to the provisions herein. Such assignment shall require execution of a written instrument specifying the assignor and assignee, and detailing the specific rights being transferred, whether exclusive or non-exclusive. The Registrar may request further documentation substantiating the legal capacity of both parties involved in any such assignment. Where an application has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed to possess all the rights and privileges which the applicant possessed prior to the assignment. Any subsequent assignments must also adhere to these requirements, ensuring a clear chain of title is maintained within the register. The Registrar may refuse registration of an assignment if it appears incomplete or otherwise not in compliance with this Act.

A person shall not engage in the business of representing others before the Controller relating to applications for patents or matters arising thereunder without being duly authorized by a certificate of practice issued under this Act. For the purposes of this section, a “practise patent agent” means any individual who, either solely or jointly with another person, undertakes activities such as preparing, filing, and prosecuting patent applications, or providing advice concerning patentability or infringement. A foreign national may apply for a certificate of practice provided that they possess qualifications substantially equivalent to those prescribed herein for Indian applicants and satisfy the Controller regarding their good character and professional competence.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licences under the patent and such licence shall be irrevocable unless expressly stated otherwise in the terms of the agreement. Where a patent has been assigned or an exclusive licence granted, subsequent assignments or further grants of exclusive licences relating to the same invention shall be void, provided that the assignee or exclusive licensee provides written notice to any prospective assignees or licensees within thirty days of the initial assignment or grant. The right to assign a pending application for patent extension under this Act remains with the original applicant unless otherwise agreed upon in writing and registered with the Controller. Furthermore, an entity receiving a licence pursuant to the Budapest Treaty shall be deemed to hold such rights subject to any existing encumbrances on record.

The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any rights prior existing. An application for registration may be assigned or transmitted by way of mortgage, pledge or otherwise, provided that such assignment or transmission does not affect the validity of the registration itself. Where a trade mark has been used continuously by the previous proprietor and the subsequent assignee or transferee ceases such use within the period specified under this Act, the right to use the trade mark may revert to the original registered proprietor. A transmissible case arises when an application for registration is assigned before its acceptance, and the assignor retains a continuing interest in the outcome of that application.

A collective mark shall be registered only upon an application by a society or association formed under law, representing persons engaged in trade or commerce, and having regard to the objects of the society or association as stated in its memorandum. The Registrar may require such proof as he deems necessary to establish that the applicant qualifies as a society or association within the meaning of this Act. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a collective mark may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, demonstrating prejudice arising from the mark’s use and asserting a right to relief including an injunction preventing its unauthorized application. Further, any proprietor of a registered trade mark who demonstrates that the use of a collective mark is creating unfair competition or dilution of their distinctive character may apply for rectification under this Act.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be accompanied by a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed under this Act and including particulars regarding its origin, method of derivation, expression of traits, and stability data. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation demonstrating genetic uniformity and distinctiveness, particularly where the variety is claimed as essentially derived from an existing variety. For the purposes section 41, evidence relating to farmers' rights concerning traditional knowledge associated with the plant variety shall be considered during examination. Provided that such evidence is verifiable through recognized institutions or community protocols. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the information provided is insufficient or misleading regarding the aforementioned aspects of the plant variety’s characteristics and lineage.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file a request for examination within one year from the date of receipt of the acknowledgment stipulated under this Act. Where an objection is taken against a proposed trademark during examination, the applicant may submit a reply addressing the grounds of the objection and supported by relevant documentation demonstrating distinctiveness or acquired reputation. The Registrar shall consider such replies and may either proceed with registration or direct further inquiry. A *trade mark registered* under this Act confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior conflicting rights as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or revoking its registration, the Appellate Board may confirm, vary, or reverse such decision, substituting if necessary any decision which it considers appropriate. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order, and the High Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine such appeals subject to the provisions of the relevant Code of Civil Procedure. The determination of the High Court shall be final. It is provided that any suit for infringement or for passing off referred to in section 66 may be filed notwithstanding any appeal pending before the Appellate Board or the High Court.

For the purpose of this Act, "filed registry fee" means the sum prescribed under this Act as being due upon the presentation of an application for registration of a trade mark and which remains outstanding pending examination or adjudication thereof; such fee shall be deemed to accrue to the credit of the Trade Marks Fund. The amount constituting the filed registry fee may vary depending on the class of goods or services specified in the application, and the form of representation employed. Where an applicant submits a layout design consisting of distinctive graphical elements alongside their trade mark application, a supplementary filing fee proportionate to the complexity of said layout design shall also be payable as provided herein.

The proprietor of any proprietor trade mark may grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensee, provided that prior written consent of the proprietor is obtained, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, a proprietor may enter into agreements whereby another party undertakes to use the trade mark under defined circumstances, including but not limited to distribution or manufacturing arrangements; these undertakings are also considered assignable with the proprietor’s approval. Any assignment or license granted in contravention of this provision shall be void and unenforceable against third parties claiming rights under this Act. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the reputation and goodwill associated with their proprietor trade marks, even when licensed to others.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a trade mark shall be deemed accepted for registration upon publication thereof in the Official Gazette. Acceptance is conditional; specifically, such acceptance remains provisional until the expiry of three months from the date of such publication. During this period, any person may, under this Act, file a notice of opposition to the proposed registration. The Registrar shall consider all oppositions filed within that timeframe and determine their validity according to established procedures as provided herein. Failure to adhere to gazette subject conditions renders the acceptance liable for revocation.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is known to the applicant, a map of the area from which the goods originate, and a statement of the land, terroirs or other natural factors that contribute to the qualities or characteristics of the goods. The Registering Authority may require further information demonstrating the conformity of the goods with established standards, including production methods and quality control measures, as provided herein. Any person claiming rights in respect of a geographical indication may file an objection under this Act within three months from the date of publication of the application for registration. Such objections shall be considered by the Authority, ensuring due regard to the principles of geographical indication respect and fair trade practices.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the applicant shall have the right to file a reply within the time specified by the Registrar. Should the Registrar consider the reply unsatisfactory or fail to adequately address all grounds of opposition, he may direct the applicant to amend the application or withdraw it entirely. Further, if an appeal is preferred against a decision declining registration, and the appellate authority remands the matter for reconsideration, the registrar shall afford the appellant another opportunity to submit evidence. Registration ought effected expeditiously where no substantial opposition exists; however, delays attributable to procedural irregularities by the applicant will not be grounds for automatic approval. The Registrar may, at any time, require further particulars or clarification from any party involved in proceedings before him.

An application for registration of a design may be filed by any person claiming to be the owner of the design or by any manufacturer authorized by the claimant. Where an application is presented by a person other than the true and first inventor, he shall provide satisfactory evidence to substantiate his claim under this Act. The Controller shall, upon receiving such an application, initiate proceedings prosecution in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Upon successful completion of these proceedings and satisfaction that the design is registrable, the registration proprietor shall be entered into the Register of Designs. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board under this Act if a Controller, acting upon an application for inclusion of an invention in the omission register, determines that such invention was not disclosed as prior art during examination proceedings. The applicant may challenge this determination, demonstrating with reasonable certainty that the cited document did not reasonably inform the skilled person regarding the claimed subject matter. Provided that, where the omitted information relates to a design registered under the Design Act 2000 and concerns ornamental features, the Board shall consider whether such omission prejudiced the patentability assessment of the invention. The Controller’s decision is final unless it appears to the Appellate Board that there was an error apparent on the face of the record or that the Controller acted without due consideration of relevant evidence presented during opposition proceedings.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that use of the proposed indication is likely to mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods concerned. The applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the distinctiveness and reputation associated with the claimed geographical territory. Where an existing registered geographical indication is falsified through the application of a mark or sign, creating a false association with the genuine product, the aggrieved proprietor may apply for rectification under this Act. Such rectification proceedings are subject to provisions regarding evidence and hearings as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider whether the use constitutes a *geographical indication falsified* and infringes upon the exclusive rights granted to the registered proprietor.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. An appeal under this Act shall lie only on a question of fact or law arising out of the said order and not otherwise. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall admit appeals only if it is satisfied that the appellant has made out a sufficient case for the appeal to be admitted. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, the Tribunal may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the order appealed against or substituting it with an appropriate order. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further prefer a proceeding appellate to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where a patent has been granted, any interested person may file a notice of opposition to the patent within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to novelty, inventive step, and undue anticipation. The Controller may require the opponent to furnish such further particulars as he deems necessary to enable the patentee to file a counterstatement. A counterstatement filed by the patentee shall address each ground of opposition raised in the notice. The Controller shall give both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence, either orally or in writing, subject to procedural guidelines issued by the Patents Office. Decisions regarding the validity of the patent following opposition proceedings are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

An application for a patent of addition may be filed by any person who is entitled to apply for and obtain a patent under this Act, provided that the subject matter of such additional patent relates to the invention claimed in the patent already granted. The applicant shall disclose in his application the particulars of the patent already granted and clearly define the relationship between the inventions claimed in the two patents. Upon receiving an application for a patent of addition, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the connection between the original invention and the subject matter of the additional patent. The grant of a patent of addition shall not extend to any matter which was disclosed or described in the specification of the parent patent. Any opposition proceedings relating to the patent of addition shall be conducted as provided herein, with due consideration given to the prior art pertaining to both inventions.

Any person making an application for registration of a mark claiming priority under Article 15 of the Paris Convention shall be deemed to have made such claim from the date appearing on the prior application, provided that the applicant furnishes satisfactory evidence thereof within three months from the date of filing the application in India. Failure to submit this documentary proof as required herein will render the claimed priority invalid and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any misleading or fraudulent representation regarding the date claim made in an application registration mark shall be deemed a cognizable offence under this Act, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with a fine.

The right to institute proceedings under this Act relating to any registered trade mark shall vest with the assignee or transferee where such assignment or transmission has been duly recorded. Provided that, in cases involving conflicting claims regarding the ownership of a transmissible case arising from an alleged fraudulent transfer, the Registrar may require both claimants to submit evidence substantiating their respective rights. Further, if it appears to the Registrar that the purported transfer was intended to circumvent any order made under this Act or to prejudice the interests of any other party, he shall notify all concerned and reserve the right to adjudicate on the validity of the transfer before determining the rightful claimant. Any decision taken by the Registrar concerning such a transmissible case is subject to appeal to the relevant appellate authority.

A user party proceeding may be instituted by any person claiming rights in respect of an alleged infringement of a registered trade mark, provided that such person has given notice to the proprietor of the trade mark and to all other known users of the mark. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such application, determine whether the applicant is indeed a person with a substantial interest in the matter. Further, any party affected by the outcome of a user party proceeding may appeal against an order made by the Registrar under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be the duty of the appellant to demonstrate prejudice arising from the decision being appealed. The Registrar may require such parties to furnish security for costs as deemed appropriate.

An application for rectification of register may be made by any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Designs Register. Such application shall be in Form D and accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds upon which the applicant relies, supported by all relevant documents and evidence. The application must be presented to the Controller within six months from the date of the publication of the design in the Designs Journal, subject to an extension granted by the Controller for reasons deemed sufficient.

The Controller shall serve notice of the application on the registered proprietor, affording them a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-statement. Proceedings relating to rectification shall be conducted as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure followed in suits before ordinary courts of law. The Controller’s decision regarding the rectification register is final and binding, provided that an appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark alleges that any other person is making use or proposing to make use of a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to his registered trade mark, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, he may apply to the relevant High Court for relief. The application shall specify the acts of infringement complained of, and the remedies sought, including but not limited to injunctions restraining the infringing activities and damages sustained by reason thereof. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall take into account any benefit accruing to the defendant or loss suffered by the plaintiff due to the alleged infringement. The proprietor shall be entitled to apply for discovery of documents relevant to establishing the extent of such use and associated profits. These regulations governing applications for relief are subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Where an application for registration is refused under this Act based on objection from any person claiming proprietary rights in respect of identical or similar marks used in connection with patented articles, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may only be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order and must specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged. The Registrar shall provide a reasoned statement outlining the basis for the objection and the evidence considered in reaching the determination. Failure by the appellant to demonstrate, through admissible documentary or testimonial evidence, that the claimed proprietary rights are invalid or do not extend to the goods or services specified in the application will result in dismissal of the appeal as provided herein.

Where the patentee of a patent granted under this Act desires to grant an exclusive license to work a patented invention within the invention territory india, such license may be assigned or surrendered subject to the provisions herein. The terms and conditions of any such assignment shall be recorded in the prescribed manner with the Controller, including details regarding royalty rates payable by the assignee to the licensor, which royalty rate shall not be less than two percent of net sales realized from the working of the invention. Provided that if the license is granted to a person resident outside india, the Central Government may require security to be furnished as deemed appropriate to safeguard national interests and ensure compulsory licensing provisions are adhered to. The patentee shall provide all necessary documentation relating to such assignments upon request by the Controller or any authorized officer.

A person shall be deemed a Member for the purposes of this Act if that person is registered as an entity engaged in the design, fabrication, testing, or marketing of semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs and has maintained continuous compliance with all applicable regulatory filings under this Act. A Member’s status may be suspended by the Controller if it is determined that the Member has failed to submit required annual reports detailing their activities related to semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs, or if a finding of substantial infringement of another party's registered layout design rights has been made against them following due process as provided herein. Any individual holding a significant managerial position within such an entity shall be considered responsible for ensuring adherence to these requirements and may be held liable under this Act in cases of non-compliance.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to rectification, revocation or infringement of a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the appellant and respondent, hear arguments and examine evidence relevant to the appeal, subject to such procedures as it deems fit. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Further, any party found to have instituted frivolous or vexatious proceedings act before the Appellate Board may be liable to pay costs, including compensation for loss of time and expenses incurred by the other parties involved in the litigation.

Where a patent relating to a computer programme is granted and subsequently subject to a request for early publication, such request may be entertained only if accompanied by an affidavit affirming that no prior public disclosure of the invention occurred before the date of filing. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the requesting party liable for costs incurred by the Controller in investigating potential anticipatory disclosures. Any challenge to the validity of the patent based on alleged prior publication must specifically detail the nature and extent of said publication, and demonstrate its impact on novelty or inventive step. The determination of whether a disclosure constitutes ‘published expiry’ requires consideration of all available evidence; an appeal against such determination lies to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal.

Where an objection is raised against a patent grant alleging non-compliance with the provisions relating to inventiveness, the Controller may require the applicant to submit documentary evidence substantiating the inventive step claimed. Failure by the applicant to provide such documentation within the time specified shall be deemed conclusive proof of absence of novelty or inventive step, and the application may proceed for rejection. Any certificate purporting to have been issued by a duly constituted expert appointed under this Act, verifying the technical soundness of the invention or confirming its compliance with prescribed standards, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding relating to the patent’s validity. Such certificates are subject to challenge based on demonstrable bias or lack of expertise, provided that such challenges are brought within six months of the certificate's issuance.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person infringing their rights conferred by registration, seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity, damages proportionate to the loss sustained by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, and the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. Where an infringement involves the use of identical or deceptively similar offices trade marks in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including account of profits made by the infringer. Provided that a proprietor seeking remedies under this Act shall demonstrate reasonable diligence in the exercise of their trademark rights. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the appellate body as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall be deemed to be a geographically defined area under this Act if the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of goods originates from that place. For the purposes of registration as a geographical indication authorised, the name of the geographical indication must accurately identify the originating area and not contain any descriptive terms which are misleading regarding such characteristics. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and the originating area; this evidence may include documentation relating to traditional production methods or integrated circuits layout designs employed in their manufacture. Goods bearing a registered geographical indication shall be identifiable as such, subject to provisions concerning fair use.

Where a person institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of layout-design rights under this Act, the remedies available shall be those prescribed herein and may include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, and delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. The Court determining such infringement shall have regard to any measures taken by the registered proprietor to maintain the confidentiality of the layout-design prior to registration. For civil court purposes, a finding of infringement constitutes prima facie evidence of the validity of the registered layout-design. Provided that, in assessing damages, the Court may consider any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity, even if those profits are not directly related to the sale or use of the infringing integrated circuit.

The registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of its initial registration, subject to renewal as provided herein. An application for renewal may be filed within one year preceding the expiry of the said period. However, the registration registered under this Act may be cancelled by the Controller if it is established that the layout-design was not originally valid or infringed upon existing rights prior to the date of application. Such cancellation may also occur if the applicant fails to pay the prescribed renewal fees within the stipulated timeframe, or demonstrates a lack of diligent prosecution of the registration. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for the registrant to be heard before issuing any order for cancelling registration registered.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall be constituted of a CIAL Member or a Technical Member of the Appellate Board and such other persons as the Central Government deems necessary for the proper disposal of the matter, ensuring expertise in semiconductor technology and intellectual property law. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during an investigation may result in penalties not exceeding five lakhs of rupees; repeated violations shall attract enhanced fines and potential criminal prosecution under relevant provisions. The Appellate Board’s decision is final, subject to judicial review only on grounds limited to the exercise of jurisdiction. A gene fund sub will be established for supporting research into novel semiconductor materials.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears, on the face thereof, to be erroneous or defective, any person aggrieved shall have the right to apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for its rectification. Such application shall specify the nature of the error or defect and the relief sought, which may include the addition, deletion, or modification of particulars relating to the patentee, invention, priority date, or claims. The Board shall serve notice upon the patentee named in the Register, affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard, including presenting evidence and arguments against the proposed rectification. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of such order. The Board’s decision concerning the rectification register notice shall be final pending any appeal under this Act.

Any action for damages arising from the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of works protected under this Act shall be brought before a civil court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the cause of action arose. The plaintiff must provide evidence demonstrating reasonable belief that the defendant has engaged in acts contrary to the provisions herein relating to copyright ownership. Failure to do so may result in dismissal of the suit with costs. Where marks registered accordance with the Trade Marks Act, 1999 are demonstrably utilized to create confusion regarding the origin or authenticity of copyrighted works, such actions shall be considered aggravated infringements subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein. The court shall have power to issue injunctions and award compensatory damages reflecting the commercial harm suffered by the copyright owner.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, who is conducting business in India, shall file an application with the Registrar specifying the trade mark sought to be registered, the class or classes of goods or services associated therewith, and the address for service in India. The application must include a clear representation of the trade mark and a list of names and addresses of all persons interested in the applicant’s business. Where the applicant utilizes a descriptive term as part of the trade mark, they shall provide an affidavit demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and advertising, establishing that the public associates the term with the applicant's goods or services. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify the accuracy of information provided concerning the business india applicant’s activities and the proposed trade description.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, direct that the shape of specified goods be considered as part of the distinctive character of such trade mark. Such direction shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates, through evidence presented during proceedings under this Act, that the shape in question signifies a substantial and unique association with the goods and has acquired distinctiveness through reputation or recognition earned by the proprietor’s use thereof. The application must include detailed technical specifications delineating the precise trade marks shape, including dimensions and material composition where relevant. Any party may object to the direction being granted, submitting counter-evidence demonstrating that the shape is primarily functional or descriptive of the goods, thereby precluding its registration as a trade mark shape.

Any geographical indication signifying goods originating from within the territorial limits of the State of Kerala, and claiming association with the traditional weaving practices employed in the houses parliament of Alappuzha district, shall be eligible for registration as provided herein. An application for such registration must specify the quality, reputation or other characteristic wholly attributable to its origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued adherence to established production methods and a geographical boundary consistent with historical usage. Upon successful registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall published expiry of the registered indication after a period of ten years from the date of such publication, subject to renewal applications filed in accordance with regulations framed under this Act.

An aggrieved party may prefer an appeal against any determination made by the Patent Examining Officer relating to the grant of a patent, subject to the provisions regarding maintainability under this Act. Provided that such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against; and failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The appellate authority may, upon hearing both sides, confirm, vary or reverse the decision of the Examining Officer. Further, an appeal section shall not preclude the Controller from entertaining any application for review if it is demonstrated that a substantial question of law has arisen during the proceedings and was not previously considered.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed trade mark shall submit all required documentation in the registrar prescribed manner, including but not limited to, a clear representation of the mark, a list of goods or services with which it is intended to be associated, and details of prior use, if any. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage of the examination process, and failure to provide such information within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Any representation submitted electronically must conform precisely to the technical specifications published by the registrar periodically on the official website. Where a trade mark is deemed descriptive of the goods or services, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through evidence of extensive use and consumer recognition, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act may grant licences for the use of their registered trade mark, specifying the geographical area and the goods or services in relation to which such use is permitted. Such licences shall be in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Further, the proprietor may assign the entire interest in a registered trade mark, including all rights and privileges pertaining thereto, to any person, provided that such assignment is made in accordance with the prescribed formalities and duly recorded. Any subsequent licensee of a registered trade mark shall hold only those rights expressly conferred upon them within the terms of their licence agreement, and shall be bound by the conditions stipulated therein. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the use of their registered trade mark notwithstanding any licensing arrangement.

An application filed with the Registrar for registration of a trademark incorporating a design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall be deemed invalid if it is shown that an identical or confusingly similar design has previously been registered under this Act, or is currently subject to a pending registrar application. The applicant may appeal against such determination within sixty days from the date of notification of the Registrar's decision. Provided that, the appellate authority shall consider whether the similarity between the designs constitutes a likelihood of confusion on the part of consumers, taking into account the overall impression created by the marks and the nature of the goods or services with which they are associated. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may further appeal to the relevant High Court.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark, hereinafter referred to as the “licensor,” desires to grant a license relating to goods wholly or partly manufactured, processed, or assembled in India using imported raw materials, such license shall be assignable subject to conditions stipulated by the licensor. The assignment may include rights pertaining to the use of distinctive signs and associated goodwill derived from the original registration. Provided that any sub-licensee operating under this arrangement shall clearly indicate on all goods bearing the trade mark, a statement confirming they are “imported India produced” items, as determined by the Registrar. Further, the licensor may stipulate limitations regarding geographical scope or specific product categories covered within the license agreement. Any alteration to these conditions requires prior written consent from both parties and notification to the Trade Marks Registry.

For the purposes of this Act, a musical work shall be defined as a composition consisting of melody and harmony, irrespective of whether it is reduced to notation or embodied in phonograms. A musical work includes lyrics which form an integral part of the work, but does not extend to mere words or phrases forming part of such lyrics if they are common literary expressions. Where a musical work is accompanied by artistic elements, such as illustrations or cover art, copyright therein shall subsist separately under this Act in respect of those artistic works, subject to any agreement between the author of the music and the artist creating said accompanying elements.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and offered for sale or distributed without authorization under this Act, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief. Such proceedings shall be brought before a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The court may, upon being satisfied that an infringing copy exists and has been made in violation of the provisions herein, grant temporary injunctions restraining the defendant from further acts of reproduction, distribution, or sale. It is provided that any party seeking such relief shall furnish security to compensate the other party for losses incurred as a result of the injunction. The court may also order the destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation, subject to due process considerations. Further, evidence presented demonstrating commercial exploitation of the infringing copy will be given significant weight during proceedings.

An application for rectification of entries relating to registered trademarks, including claims of dilution or unfair competition, shall be heard and determined by an Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act. The term "Adjudicating Officer Period" refers to the duration during which an Adjudicating Officer holds office, which shall not exceed five years from the date on which they assume charge, subject to earlier termination upon resignation or removal as provided herein. Any order passed by the Adjudicating Officer may be appealed against before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such order. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines for the conduct of proceedings and the assessment of costs.

Where any individual is alleged to have committed an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark, such individual shall be deemed to have engaged in unfair trade practices and may be subjected to civil penalties as provided herein. The investigating officer, upon receiving a complaint regarding a commission alleged offence, shall immediately record statements from all relevant parties including the complainant, the accused, and any witnesses. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act concerning the cessation of infringing activities will result in enhanced fines and potential imprisonment for those found responsible. Further, damages may be awarded to the registered proprietor to compensate for losses incurred due to the infringement.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, alongside corresponding information regarding their classes of goods or services. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from inaccuracies or omissions within the registrar index may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification; such petitions must specify the nature of the error and its detrimental impact on the petitioner’s legal interests. The Board shall have the power to direct the Registrar to amend the registrar index accordingly, provided that any amendment does not adversely affect existing rights holders without due process. Further, a person aggrieved by a refusal to grant access to information contained within the registrar index may appeal such decision to the Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstration of legitimate need for said information.

An international application form filed pursuant to this Act shall be deemed a representation of the applicant’s exclusive claim to the specified goods or services within the territories designated therein, subject to any conflicting prior rights established under the laws of those jurisdictions. Any party disputing the validity of such an international registration may initiate proceedings before the relevant intellectual property authority demonstrating a likelihood of confusion arising from the earlier use of an identical or similar mark for identical or similar goods or services. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving that the designation of territories in the international application form was made in good faith and without intent to deceive or mislead any potential consumer, provided that evidence of reasonable inquiry into existing registrations is presented.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a verified statement attesting to the exclusive use of the proposed trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, provided that such verification is supported by documentary evidence acceptable to the Registrar. The Registrar may, at any time and without assigning reasons, require the applicant to provide further documentation substantiating the claim of exclusive use, including but not limited to affidavits from distributors, sales records, and advertising materials. Failure to comply with such a requirement within the period specified by the Registrar shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The India registrar require adherence to these evidentiary standards to ensure transparency in trade mark registration proceedings.

The registered proprietor of a layout-design in the design registry shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring rights to use the protected layout-design. Such licenses may be granted subject to terms and conditions as agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee, provided that any such agreement explicitly states the scope of permitted acts including reproduction and commercial exploitation. Assignment of a registered layout-design or any interest therein shall require execution of a formal instrument witnessed by at least two witnesses and duly stamped according to prevailing law. The assignee shall be deemed the new registered proprietor under this Act, with all rights and obligations attaching thereto. Any license granted prior to assignment shall remain valid unless expressly terminated in writing by both parties. Further, the Central Government may issue guidelines regarding royalty rates for compulsory licenses as provided herein.

An international registration designating India shall be deemed to constitute an application for registration of the marks specified therein in respect of the goods or services for which such designation was made, subject to compliance with all requirements under this Act applicable to applications filed on or after the date of such designation. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the international registration, including details of earlier trade mark registrations or pending applications relied upon in support thereof. Any representation appearing on the register resulting from an india international registration shall be subject to the same rights and limitations as if it were a trade mark registered directly under this Act.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trademark that is identical or confusingly similar to a registration trade mark shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Further, the court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, as well as any materials used in their manufacture or packaging. Where damages are proven, the aggrieved proprietor shall be entitled to recover from the infringer such sum not exceeding one crore rupees as the court deems reasonable, representing compensation for loss suffered by reason of the infringement. This provision applies irrespective of whether registration trade mark is actively being used.

Where an act constituting infringement of copyright is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of commission offence notwithstanding that they were not directly involved in the physical reproduction or dissemination of the copyrighted work. An appeal against any conviction or order made under this provision may be filed within sixty days from the date of such conviction or order before the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the offence was committed, and shall be governed by the provisions relating to appeals as provided herein. The appellate authority may, after hearing all parties involved, confirm, vary, or set aside any such order; however, the finding of guilt established at trial shall stand unless affirmatively challenged and substantiated on appeal.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods manufactured outside India, the proprietor shall, subject to any conditions specified therein, provide a written notification to the Trade Marks Registry within ninety days of the commencement of such manufacture. This notification must detail the country of origin and the manufacturing process employed. Failure to comply with this requirement does not, however, render the registration void but may be raised as a ground for revocation under this Act by any interested party. An appeal against an order requiring such goods manufactured notification lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; provided that the Board shall consider whether the non-compliance constitutes substantial deception or misrepresentation to consumers.

Any person found to be using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark without due license or consent shall cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees. Where such use is determined by the Controller to constitute an act of unfair competition impacting demonstrable industrial application of the mark’s proprietor's goods or services, the penalty shall be doubled. Further, any director, manager, secretary, or other officer in default of this Act, being responsible for the offence, shall also be deemed guilty and liable to punishment as if he were the person actually committing such act. Recovery of damages may be pursued under provisions relating to civil remedies.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is demonstrably calculated to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, an interested party may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such petitions shall be entertained only if the petitioner establishes, through documentary evidence including but not limited to market surveys and consumer perception studies, that the infringing use has resulted in demonstrable financial detriment. The Board shall consider whether the continued registration is consistent with the public interest under this Act. Further, any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning section 36e ixd shall be subject to appeal before the relevant High Court.

An applicant seeking registration of a design affidavit registered relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit Form D along with the requisite fee as prescribed. The application must contain a true and complete representation of the layout-design, including all relevant technical specifications and supporting documentation demonstrating originality. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any deficiencies or provide further clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Failure to comply with such directions within the stipulated period shall render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained by the Office. Objections, if any, may be filed within two months from the date of publication as provided herein. The applicant shall have an opportunity to respond to such objections before the Registrar proceeds with examination.

For the purposes of this Act, “fees surcharge” means any additional amount levied on prescribed fees relating to the registration of layout-designs, or for extensions of protection under this Act, and shall be determined by notification published in the Official Gazette. The Central Government may prescribe different rates of fees surcharge based on factors including, but not limited to, the complexity of the layout-design, the applicant’s status as a small enterprise, and the time taken for processing an application. Any fees surcharge collected shall be credited to the Fund established under this Act and utilized exclusively for promoting innovation in integrated circuit design.

Where a recording means a person engaged in the creation of an audio-visual work, such person shall be deemed to possess all rights pertaining to authorship under this Act, subject to any agreement executed prior to the commencement of the recording process. Provided that, if such recording is undertaken on behalf of and at the express direction of a registered user party, the terms of engagement between the recording means person and the said registered user party shall govern the allocation of royalties and other benefits arising from the commercial exploitation of the work. Any assignment of copyright in respect of the recorded work must be executed in writing and duly notarized to be valid under this Act. Further, a recording means person may elect to retain ownership of their copyright, licensing usage rights to others as they deem fit, provided that such licenses are transparently documented.

Where any individual is charged with an accused offence involving the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark, such individual shall be entitled to present evidence demonstrating honest, contemporaneous belief regarding the absence of infringement. This evidentiary burden extends to establishing that the alleged infringing use occurred within a reasonable understanding of fair dealing principles as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon review of submitted documentation and hearing arguments from both parties, determine whether this belief negates the elements constituting the accused offence. Any such determination shall be subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority, with provisions for costs awarded at its discretion based on the merits of the dispute.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall publish a registration notice in such manner as may be prescribed, including electronic dissemination through the Trade Marks Registry website. Any proprietor of an existing trade mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered mark may, within three months of the publication of the registration notice, file with the Registrar a request for rectification seeking invalidation of the registration. Such requests shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and provide supporting documentation as required by regulations framed under this Act. Furthermore, any collective management organization acting as a registration copyright society administering rights in literary or artistic works incorporated within goods bearing the registered trade mark may apply to the Registrar for assignment of sub-licensing powers relating to those copyrighted elements, subject to conditions prescribed herein.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent under this Act based on a convention application shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating compliance with all applicable laws of the convention country. Failure to do so may result in rejection of the patent application or, if a patent has already been granted, revocation thereof. The Controller is empowered to demand further documentation and clarification from the applicant concerning the validity of the convention claim, and any attempt at fraudulent misrepresentation shall render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of a patent based on a convention application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. The burden of proof relating to the date of priority under the convention application rests solely upon the applicant.

The holder of a design affidavit registered under this Act may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use, reproduction, and exploitation of the layout-design. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Any assignment of ownership or a substantial portion of the rights associated with a design affidavit registered herein requires prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the terms of transfer and identifying all parties involved. The assignee shall be deemed subject to any existing licenses granted under the original registration, provided that the terms of such licenses do not conflict with the assignment agreement. Further, the Registrar may require an undertaking from the assignee ensuring continued compliance with obligations as provided herein relating to security measures protecting the layout-design.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant exclusive licences in respect of any goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, and such licence may be granted for a term not exceeding the remaining period of protection of the registration. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or of the benefit of any registered trade mark, shall include all rights relating to use of the effect registered trade mark, unless the assignment expressly provides otherwise. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensee shall be deemed to be the proprietor for the purposes of suing for infringement only with respect to the goods or services specified in the licence agreement. The Registrar may require evidence of such licences and assignments to be filed, as provided herein, and may refuse registration if the terms are considered unduly restrictive.

Any agreement whereby the entire copyright or exclusive rights pertaining thereto in respect of any cinematograph film are assigned to another party shall be deemed an assignment copyright under this Act, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. Such assignments may encompass the right to reproduce the work, include its adaptation, distribute prints, and exhibit publicly, as mutually agreed upon by the assignor and assignee through a written contract. Provided that, where the assignment relates to a work jointly authored, all co-owners of the copyright shall execute the agreement or their duly authorised representatives do so on their behalf. The duration of any such assignment shall not exceed seventy years from the year following the date of creation of the cinematograph film, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the written instrument. Further, an assignee may sub-license rights as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark shall furnish all information required by the Registrar under this Act and shall be deemed to have made a false statement if such information is subsequently found to be untrue. Any person making a misstatement in a registrar application shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may also face criminal prosecution for offences cognizable by a Magistrate first class. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to submit further documentation substantiating the distinctiveness of the mark or its use in commerce; failure to comply within the stipulated period shall render the registrar application liable for rejection. Repeated non-compliance with these provisions will result in disqualification from filing future trademark applications for a period determined by the Registrar.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring rights to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the consideration for granting a licence shall be determined by contract. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include any existing licences attached thereto unless explicitly excluded in writing by both parties involved. The rules carry provisions regarding the recording of such assignments and licences with the Trade Marks Registry, ensuring transparency and priority among claimants. Further, where a licensee defaults on the terms of their licence agreement, the proprietor may seek redress through appropriate legal channels as provided herein.

Where an owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another person is engaging in activities likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or nature of goods or services, and such activities constitute a court suit infringement under this Act, the owner may institute legal proceedings seeking equitable relief. Such relief shall include, but not be limited to, an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark or confusingly similar marks, as well as damages sustained by the trademark owner due to the infringement. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, the court shall consider any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activities and any losses suffered by the plaintiff directly resulting from such infringement. The court may also order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Appellate Board. The Board shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating prima facie novelty and inventive step, notwithstanding any prior publication or use disclosed during examination. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of that order. It is provided that the register patents shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein unless proven otherwise through documented legal challenge, and any attempt to register shall brought before the Controller for initial assessment.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a registered proprietor of a layout-design may grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the protected layout-design for specific purposes, including but not limited to manufacture, import, and sale. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of a layout-design right, whether partial or complete, also requires execution via a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignee and registered with the Controller General. The terms of any assignment shall clearly define the scope of rights transferred, including geographical limitations and duration. Further, where an assignment includes pre-existing contractual obligations relating to the layout-design, those obligations remain binding upon both assignor and assignee as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer of such assignment is subject to similar registration requirements.

The assignment of copyright in works generated by artificial intelligence systems shall be governed as follows: where a work is created with substantial input from an AI system, and such input is licensed under terms permitting commercial exploitation, the assignor’s rights are limited to those expressly granted within the original license agreement. Any subsequent assignment of copyright must clearly delineate the scope of permitted uses derived from the licensed AI contribution, ensuring transparency for potential licensees. Failure to do so shall render the assignment voidable at the option of a third party adversely affected. The jurisdiction for any dispute arising under this provision relating to such assignments shall be subject to the provisions of civil procedure 1908, and the aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief to prevent unauthorized exploitation. Provided that, rights pertaining to original artistic expression remain with the human creator, even where AI tools are employed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a musical work shall vest in the author of the work. Where the composer and lyricist are distinct persons, copyright shall subsist separately in respect of the music and the words. Any person claiming to be the owner of copyright in any musical work may, within thirty days from the date on which such claim is asserted, serve notice thereof upon the Registrar of Copyrights specifying particulars of the work and the grounds for the claim. The Registrar shall publish a notification regarding such claims in the Official Gazette. Upon receiving objections to the claimed ownership under this Act, the Registrar shall provide all parties with an opportunity for hearing before determining the matter. Decisions made by the Registrar are appealable to the relevant High Court as provided herein.

Where a registered layout design is infringed, the owner shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. The injured party may institute civil proceedings for damages, which shall include compensation for loss of profits and any measure of the damage suffered by the owner attributable to the infringement. Further, subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts to mitigate losses, exemplary damages may be awarded at the discretion of the court. A request for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement is also permissible under this Act. The procedure for determining the extent of damages shall follow principles of fairness and proportionality, considering factors such as the duration of the infringing activity and the willful nature thereof. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding remedies may appeal to the relevant appellate forum as prescribed.

Subject to appeal to the High Court, any determination made by a civil court purposes relating to infringement of layout-design rights under this Act shall be final until modified or reversed in appeal. Provided that an aggrieved party may challenge such determination on grounds including but not limited to errors of law apparent on the face of the record, misdirection in assessing substantial similarity, or failure to consider relevant evidence presented during the original proceedings. The High Court may, while hearing an appeal, require further discovery or examination of witnesses as it deems necessary for just resolution. Further, any order passed by a civil court concerning interim injunctions or other conservatory measures shall be subject to similar appellate review and scrutiny under this Act.

Where, in proceedings relating to revocation or validity of a patent, a substantial question of scientific or technical complexity arises, the Controller may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, direct the appointment of an independent scientific adviser. The costs associated with such an adviser shall be borne by the petitioner or respondent as determined by the Controller. Failure to comply with directions issued by the appointed independent scientific adviser, including providing requested documentation or appearing for examination, shall constitute contempt of court and render the party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any person found to have misrepresented their qualifications in order to serve as an independent scientific adviser is subject to prosecution under relevant provisions concerning false evidence.

Where any work is registered under this Act in the name of a company, and it is subsequently established that an infringement of copyright relating to such work has occurred, the determination of liability shall proceed as follows. If the company proved offence was committed by its agents or employees acting within the scope of their authority, the Registrar may issue notices requiring the company to demonstrate due diligence in preventing such infringements. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of preventative measures, including employee training and internal compliance protocols, may result in the imposition of penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider the nature of the work, the extent of the infringement, and the company’s overall copyright management system when assessing culpability.

Where an application is filed for registration of a mark under this Act, the application date shall be deemed to be the date on which the specification filed proceeded through the prescribed formalities. Provided that, if the applicant has previously filed an identical or similar mark relating to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the current application, the Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence demonstrating prior use and reputation, and the application date shall then be adjusted accordingly. Further, where a request for amendment of the specification is made after the initial filing, such amendment must not substantially alter the character of the mark; otherwise, a fresh application date shall be assigned to the amended document as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout design" means the three dimensional representation of an integrated circuit upon a mask used in the manufacture of semiconductors; provided that such representation includes distinctive topological features which define the arrangement of elements comprising the integrated circuit. A “registered layout design” is one accepted for registration under this Act and entered into the Register of Layout-Designs, as provided herein. An application for registration of a layout design shall disclose whether it incorporates any previously registered layout design, and if so, specify such prior registrations. The term "layout design" excludes features solely attributable to achieving technical effects or producing manufacturing results.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the patentability of an *article patented*, specifically relating to novelty or inventive step, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars demonstrating compliance with the provisions herein. Such a requirement shall not be deemed to invalidate the application unless the applicant fails to respond within the time stipulated by the Controller and such failure is substantiated before a High Court on appeal. Further, if it is alleged that the claimed invention infringes upon existing rights or utilizes a gene fund shall be considered as prior art, the burden of proof lies with the party making such allegation; provided that the Controller may, at his discretion, order an inquiry into the veracity of said claim.

Where a Board of Appeal finds that an invention does not fulfil the requirements of novelty or inventive step under this Act, the applicant may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Board of Appeal. The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Board of Appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. An appeal shall only be on grounds of law and not on matters of fact already decided by the Appellate Tribunal unless those facts have been determined in accordance with principles of natural justice. The High Court may, while hearing an appeal, dismiss it or entertain it subject to just conditions.

An international application filed under this Act shall be processed in accordance with the Convention on Patents and the Paris Convention. The Controller General may, upon receipt of a certified copy of the priority document accompanying the international application, direct that the application be treated as if it were originally filed in India, subject to any modifications or clarifications deemed necessary by the Controller. Where an applicant has previously sought protection for an article through registration on the design registry, such prior action shall not prejudice the examination of the patent application relating thereto. The prescribed fees for processing an international application shall be remitted electronically, as provided herein. Any request for extension of time under this Act concerning an international application must be accompanied by a duly verified affidavit explaining the reasons for delay and supported by relevant documentation. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application.

The Register of Registered Designs maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person found to wilfully alter or deface entries within the register shall be liable to prosecution and may face imprisonment extending to two years, or a fine, or both, as determined by the relevant court. The Controller shall ensure that the register is maintained with meticulous accuracy; any demonstrable negligence in maintaining this record will render the Controller subject to disciplinary action and potential civil penalties. A comprehensive index shall accompany the register, regularly updated to facilitate efficient searches. Furthermore, the register shall kept secure from unauthorized access or tampering at all times.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any patentee or registered proprietor desiring to grant a license in respect of the patented invention or assigned right may execute an instrument of assignment or licensing agreement. Such instrument shall clearly specify the scope of the rights granted, including but not limited to field of use, duration, and royalty rates, as agreed upon between the parties. Where any dispute arises concerning the validity or interpretation of such license or assignment, an appeal section shall be available under this Act, allowing aggrieved parties to seek redressal before a designated authority. The Controller may, after hearing all concerned parties, issue orders relating to the enforcement of these rights and conditions precedent for their continued operation. Further, any modification to the terms of a licensed right requires prior consent from the patentee or assignee.

Where a patentee elects to grant a license relating to any patented invention under this Act, such license shall be assignable in the prescribed manner, subject to the terms and conditions agreed upon between the parties, and recorded with the Controller as per rules framed for that purpose.
