Provided that where the licensed party subsequently seeks to assign the said license to a third party, prior written consent of the original patentee shall be obtained and documented. The assignment shall not affect any existing trade mark exists associated with the invention unless explicitly stated otherwise in the agreement between the parties. Any attempt to transfer or pledge such a license without adhering to this prescribed manner will render the transaction voidable at the option of the patentee, who may seek injunctive relief as provided herein.

The registered mark, “Evergreen Spices,” shall be deemed a valuable asset subject to assignment and licensing as provided herein. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license for use of the said mark upon any product other than those specifically detailed in their specification claim relating to culinary herbs and related seasonings must submit an application to the Controller detailing the scope of such permitted usage, including geographical territories and duration. The Controller may approve or reject such applications based on considerations of consumer protection and potential dilution of the Evergreen Spices brand identity. Marks indications serve to identify goods; therefore, any sublicensee shall adhere strictly to the terms stipulated in the primary license agreement and as further defined by the Controller’s approval. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the sublicense liable for damages and revocation of their usage rights under this Act.

An application for a patent shall disclose the matter claimed in clear terms and sufficiently support the claims made therein. The invention described must meet all requirements under this Act relating to novelty and inventive step; failure to do so will render the claims invalid. Where an applicant seeks protection for a method of use, such claims shall be restricted to the scope permissible as provided herein, ensuring that any associated product claims are appropriately linked to said method. Claims incorporating elements derived from prior art disclosed in the application itself shall only be allowable if those elements are essential to achieving the claimed inventive step. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the interpretation of ambiguous claims during examination.

An application for a patent may include a specification patent addition, detailing an invention which is not an essential feature of the primary invention claimed in the original patent application. Such additions shall be clearly identified within the amended specification as a “patent addition” and must demonstrate a nexus to the subject matter originally disclosed. The Controller General may require further clarification regarding the relationship between the main invention and the patent addition, particularly concerning novelty and inventive step. A patent of addition granted under this Act shall have an expiry date calculated from the original filing date of the primary patent application, provided that the amended specification adequately describes both inventions as a single unified disclosure. The applicant shall furnish all necessary drawings and claims to accurately reflect the scope of the patent addition.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the registered owner of a layout design may grant licenses conferring rights to use or reproduce the said design, either in whole or in part, for specific purposes or territories. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be assigned freely, provided that any assignment is notified to the Controller within thirty days of its execution. Where an application for a license involves a layout design subject to a prior registered layout design, consent from the original proprietor must be obtained unless such use falls under fair dealing provisions as defined herein. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or enforceability of a license agreement relating to a layout design shall be referred to a Layout Design Appellate Board for determination, and its decision shall be binding on all parties involved.

Where an objection is raised alleging that a proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, the Registrar shall consider all relevant factors including the similarity of the marks, the identity or relatedness of the goods or services, and the likelyhood of confusion on the part of the public or damage to the proprietor of the earlier mark. The Appellate Board may, upon appeal, substitute its own assessment for that of the Registrar regarding whether the similarities between the trade marks warrant a finding of deceptive similarity, provided that such substitution is based on demonstrable errors in law or fact. Further, evidence presented by either party shall be weighed fairly and impartially, subject to admissibility under established principles of jurisprudence.

Where, subsequent to registration of a patent under this Act, particulars relating thereto are found to be incorrect, ambiguous or omitted, any person aggrieved may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application shall specify the errors sought to be corrected and state the relief claimed. The Controller shall serve notice upon the patentee and other interested parties as provided herein, affording them a reasonable opportunity to file their objections or counter-claims. Upon consideration of all materials presented, including any expert testimony deemed relevant, the Controller may order such rectification as appears just and equitable. It is further provided that notice rectification shall be effected within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt of the application, unless circumstances warrant an extension granted by the Controller.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the mark and may specify, where the mark comprises a device, the colours intended to be used therein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information relating to the mark as he deems necessary for the purposes of examination under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark that is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark in relation to identical goods or services, the application shall be refused, subject to any provisions regarding use and reputation. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, consider allowing registration notwithstanding such refusal. A trade mark relation exists between an applicant and the intellectual property rights conferred by successful registration.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall include detailed documentation substantiating the unique qualities and characteristics attributable solely to the specified geographical area. Such documentation must be verified by an authorized consortium representing growers within the defined region; failure to provide such verification will render the application ineligible for consideration under this Act. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating continued adherence to traditional production methods, provided that any alterations to these methods are disclosed and assessed for their impact on the geographical indication's distinctiveness. A ‘registration referred fact’ concerning a prior use of the name shall be considered only if it is accompanied by affidavits from at least three producers actively engaged in cultivation within the relevant territory.

Where an application for the registration of a mark includes a reference to any other mark already registered under this Act, or which is pending registration, and such marks are owned by the applicant, the Registrar may direct that the two marks shall be treated as *marks registered associated* for the purposes of examination and subsequent enforcement. Such direction shall be recorded in the register of trade marks. The proprietor of any mark so directed to be treated as associated shall be entitled to use both marks jointly or separately, subject to compliance with all relevant provisions regarding permissible usage. Further, any opposition filed against one of such *marks registered associated* shall be deemed to extend to the other mark, provided that notice is given to the proprietor accordingly and the grounds for opposition are applicable to both.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an applicant aggrieved by any decision relating to the refusal or acceptance of registration of a work shall have the right to appeal to the appellate authority constituted under this Act. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the order is challenged. The appellate authority, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the Controller, shall pass a reasoned order confirming, reversing or modifying the decision appealed against. Any further dispute arising from the order of the appellate authority may be subject to judicial review under principles of natural justice, provided that such review does not extend to questioning the merits of the original registration determination.

An application for a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file the requisite documentary evidence as prescribed by the Regulations within six months from the date of request made by the Trade Marks Registry, or where such failure continues for a further period of three months following a second request. Any person aggrieved by an order directing abandonment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order; provided that the Appellant shall deposit with the Board a sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the prescribed fee for late filing, or such higher amount as the Board deems just under this Act. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Trade Marks Registry may, at any time, initiate prosecution proceedings against an applicant found to have made false statements in their trade mark application.

Where an appeal arises under this Act from any decision or order of a Registrar, and the appellant alleges demonstrable prejudice resulting from an error apparent on the face of the record pertaining to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a trade mark, the Register Court shall give priority consideration to such appeal. Provided that, if the respondent disputes the existence of said prejudice, the Register Court may direct the production of further evidence by either party. The Register Court shall not be bound by any prior determination made by the Registrar regarding the similarity of marks or the descriptiveness thereof, subject to a finding that the Registrar’s decision was manifestly unjust. Any order issued by the Register Court concerning such appeals is final, save for an appeal to the Supreme Court under established procedures.

Where a trade mark is registered in the name of a company, and any element thereof is also registered *mark separately registered*, the proprietor may, subject to an agreement in writing, grant a license to use the entire trade mark or any particular goods or services associated with that mark. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that the assignee complies with all conditions precedent to the original registration and subsequent licensing agreements. Further, a company may, through board resolution duly recorded in its minutes, irrevocably assign the right to use a *mark separately registered* element of its composite trade mark to another entity, including an individual or partnership, as it deems fit. Any such assignment shall be notified to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days and shall become effective upon registration thereof.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant patent or revocation thereof under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear appeals arising under this Act and may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the original decision and substituting its own. Failure to comply with any order made by the Appellate Board shall render the defaulting party liable for a penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, wilful infringement of an order of the Appellate Board constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to license the use of that trade mark for purposes identifying goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements may grant non-exclusive rights allowing multiple licensees to utilize the mark concurrently within defined geographical territories or product categories. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include all associated licenses previously granted, unless expressly excluded by written consent from both the assignor and assignee. Where a licensee utilizes a trade mark in a manner inconsistent with the terms of their license, or engages in activities that demonstrably dilute the distinctiveness of the mark, the proprietor may initiate proceedings under this Act to have such use deemed falsify trade and seek injunctive relief.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have constructively consented to the introduction of alterations to their submitted representation, provided that such alteration does not fundamentally alter the distinctive character claimed for the mark and is consistent with the goods or services specified in the application. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, refuse an amendment if it determines that the proposed change introduces a new trade mark or substantially departs from the original specification. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar permitting or refusing an application permit amendment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of such determination, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the Registry’s action.

Where a registered layout design is found to contain inadvertent discrepancies attributable to clerical errors during registration proceedings, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, permit correction of such errors without requiring fresh application and payment of prescribed fees. Provided that any proposed correction shall not substantively alter the original layout design as recorded in the Register of Layout Designs, nor introduce new matter not disclosed therein; and further provided that a notice of objection regarding the proposed correction may be filed by any interested party within thirty days from the date of publication of such proposal under this Act. The Tribunal’s decision on an appeal against an order permitting or refusing correction shall be final.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that it designates India and subject to any modifications required by this Act. Where an international registration designating India is opposed under this Act, the opposition proceedings shall be conducted as if the application for registration were made under section 9 and the International Bureau shall furnish such information as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar may require the deposit of security with any applicant or registered proprietor in connection with an international registration, provided that such requirement is proportionate to the potential damages arising from infringement. Further, remedies for passing off shall be available notwithstanding any registration under this Act relating to a mark included in an international registration.

The owner of a zb trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon in writing. Any license granted under this Act may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the licensor may impose restrictions on the licensed territory or duration of the license. Assignment of a zb trade mark, including any associated goodwill, requires registration with the prescribed authority and shall operate from the date of such registration. Provided that, where an assignment includes a continuing right to receive royalties, the agreement must clearly define the royalty calculation method and reporting frequency. Further, any sub-license granted by a licensee shall require prior written consent from the original owner of the zb trade mark, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appellant shall specify the order appealed against and the grounds upon which such appeal is based, and shall serve a copy of the appeal on the Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in the dismissal of the appeal.

The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, after affording the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Registrar shall be bound by the decisions of both the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal and the High Court in relation to the trade mark application.

Any person who, having knowledge of registered offices trade marks used in relation to any goods or services, uses a mark which is identical or deceptively similar to that registered office trademark in connection with goods or services identical or closely resembling those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at such amount as may be determined by the court, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered offices trade marks and any benefit gained by the infringing party. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, issue an injunction restraining the use of the infringing mark, provided that it is satisfied that the infringement causes or is likely to cause damage to the reputation or goodwill of the registered trademark.

Any person found to have knowingly and willfully infringed upon the rights of a registered plant variety, including unauthorized commercialization or distribution thereof, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Where such infringement is demonstrated to have been facilitated through misleading representations concerning the origin or characteristics of the harvested material, the penalty may be enhanced up to three times the assessed damages. A farmer utilizing propagating material of a registered plant variety obtained in contravention of this Act shall be subject to remedial action including mandatory reporting and potential forfeiture of subsequent harvests. The Controller may issue directives for the cessation of infringing activities and order compensation payable to the right holder, taking into account the scale and duration of the offense.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the owner of a board use layout may grant licenses conferring the right to utilize, reproduce, or commercially exploit said layout for specific purposes. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Assignment of rights pertaining to a board use layout is permissible, provided that such assignment includes all rights granted under this Act concerning the layout’s utilization and reproduction. Any transfer of ownership or licensing agreement relating to a board use layout shall require registration with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, as prescribed herein. Failure to register an assignment may render it unenforceable against subsequent transferees. The licensor retains the right to terminate any license if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the integrity of the registered layout design.

Where an objection is raised under this Act to the registration of a proposed mark registered trade, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit written representations addressing the grounds for such objection. The objecting party may then file a counter-statement responding to the applicant’s submissions. Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Registrar's decision on whether to proceed with registration shall be final until challenged through that process. Provided that any representation or counter-statement contains material misstatements of fact, either party may apply to the Appellate Board for an order setting aside the Registrar’s determination and directing a reconsideration of the matter. The burden of proving such misrepresentation rests entirely upon the applicant.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced, distributed, or publicly displayed any copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. Such damages may include actual loss suffered by the copyright owner and a sum not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, awarded at the discretion of the Court. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. The institution of proceedings under this Act shall be exclusively within the jurisdiction of a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the presiding officer, subject to principles of natural justice.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement thereof against any person using or proposing to use a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in relation to goods or services. Such remedies may include an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and damages sustained by the plaintiff as a consequence of the infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the damage suffered, the profits made by the infringer, and the need to deter similar infringements in the future. Further, where an infringing use is found to have resulted in dilution of distinctiveness of the registered trade mark, enhanced damages may be awarded. The rights respect registration conferred under this Act are paramount and shall be vigorously defended against any unauthorized exploitation.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order adjudicating officer passed under this Act relating to the determination of infringement or validity of a registered layout-design, or concerning any other matter provided for under this Act. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the concerned party is served with notice of the order. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, at its discretion, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. An applicant aggrieved by any decision or direction issued by the Tribunal in a proceeding appellate may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The Tribunal shall give notice to all parties concerned and provide them an opportunity to be heard before passing any order.

Where a registered trademark is assigned or transmitted, the assignee or transferee may, subject to any terms specified in the instrument effecting such assignment or transmission, grant further licenses relating to the use of the mark within the territory covered by the registration. Such sub-licenses shall be deemed assignments for the purposes of this Act and are subject to the same requirements regarding notification to the Registrar as an initial assignment. The proprietor of a registered trademark shall retain the right to revoke any license or sub-license granted, provided that adequate compensation is offered to the licensee in accordance with principles of fairness and equity. Further, any subsequent assignment transmission rights relating to the mark are contingent upon adherence to these licensing conditions unless expressly waived by the original proprietor through a written agreement filed with the Registrar.

An application for the registration of a layout-design shall be made to the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, containing particulars verifying ownership and detailing the nature of the integrated circuit. Where an applicant seeks recognition as a proprietor registered layout, they must demonstrate exclusive right over the design under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical specifications and schematics supporting the application, and shall provide the applicant an opportunity to rectify any deficiencies identified during examination. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to registration or rejection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout-designs, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees and conditions.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall, in the application, clearly indicate whether the trade mark is being used in relation to any goods or services. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark indicating that they *carry business india* in connection with specified goods, they must provide documentary evidence demonstrating continuous use of the mark within India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of such usage if deemed necessary. Failure to adequately substantiate this claim shall render the application liable for rejection. Any alteration to the goods or services associated with a registered trade mark requires notification to the Registrar, subject to prescribed fees.

Applications for registration of literary works, including computer programs and databases, shall be processed by the Registrar in accordance with the prescribed procedures. An applicant aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, or concerning objections raised under this Act, may appeal to the appellate board. The appellate board shall consider such appeals within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt thereof and shall pass orders in writing accompanied by reasons for the decision. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the appellate board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to just cause shown. The Registrar may require such additional information or documentation as deemed necessary during processing.

The completeness of a patent specification shall be determined with reference to its enabling disclosure and best mode provisions, and where an objection is raised regarding inadequacy of description or lack of clarity in relation to the claimed invention, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating compliance under this Act. The Controller may, upon review of such objections and considering expert testimony presented by either party, direct a revision of the patent specification; however, any alteration made pursuant to such direction shall not substantively broaden the scope of protection initially sought, subject to appeal before an appellate authority. It is provided that the determination of whether a specification discloses the best mode remains within the exclusive purview of the Controller and is amenable to judicial review only on grounds of perversity.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding rights in a new variety may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the commercial exploitation thereof, including but not limited to rights for propagation, sale, distribution, or research purposes. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area and duration for which they are valid, and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of rights in a new variety is permissible with prior notification to the Authority, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the protected material. The Authority may impose conditions on such assignments to ensure continued benefit to farmers and preservation of genetic resources. Further, any license granted or assignment made shall be recorded within one month with the designated registering authority, as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act against any person using, without due cause or consent, a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to their index registered trademark. Such use may constitute infringement, and the proprietor may apply for an injunction restraining the infringing activity, as provided herein. Where the alleged infringer has, in the course of trade, employed language or designs that are descriptive but do not directly incorporate the index registered trademark, a court shall consider whether such usage creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. An invention far claimed within an advertising campaign utilizing the infringing mark may be considered as aggravating circumstances when determining damages. The Registrar may also order the erasure of any registration obtained through fraudulent means related to this infringement.

Application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the design and confirming that the applicant is the rightful owner or authorized agent thereof. Where an application is made by a person other than the creator of the layout-design, such as a proposed registered proprietor acting on behalf of the original designer, the declaration must explicitly state the basis for their claim to ownership, including details of any contractual agreements relating to rights in the design. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim before proceeding with examination. Any alteration to the declared ownership information after the application’s filing is subject to approval by the Registrar and may necessitate a fresh declaration.

Where any patent has been granted in respect of an invention, and it is subsequently determined under this Act that the invention was not novel or obvious at the date of filing of the patent application, or that the invention does not fall within the definition of “invention” as provided herein, the Controller may order for the revocation of such patent. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the validity of a patent may appeal against such decision to the Appellate Board. Subject to this, any party seeking to challenge the subsistence of a patent shall be required to demonstrate that they have suffered material loss or damage as a direct consequence of the continued operation of the patent. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for all interested parties to present their case before making any order concerning the revocation of a register patents referred to in section sixty-seven.

Where a patent has been granted in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and an objection is filed against said grant by any person aggrieved under this Act, such person may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the patent, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum indicating the grounds upon which it is based, and the prescribed fee. Provided that if the appellant failed to comply with procedural requirements during the examination stage, the Appellate Board may dismiss the appeal summarily. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may file an appeal from such order; however, a section appeal shall only be entertained where substantial questions of law are involved and the requisite fee is duly paid.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a *fee payable notice* to the applicant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the refusal is based and state the amount of the prescribed fee that may be paid within the time specified therein, being not less than thirty days from the date of publication of the trade mark journal containing the notice. The applicant shall, if desiring to pursue the application notwithstanding the refusal, remit the stated fee within the stipulated period. Failure to do so will render the application deemed abandoned. Any person may, subject to any conditions prescribed herein, file a representation against the acceptance of the trade mark following payment of the fee and publication of such acceptance. The Registrar shall consider all representations received before determining whether or not to proceed with registration.

Where a literary work is comprised substantially of elements originally derived from traditional cultural expressions belonging to indigenous communities, and such derivation occurs without prior informed consent as provided herein, the author shall be deemed to hold copyright subject to conditions. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ascertaining the provenance of said elements before registration of copyright is granted. Further, any commercial exploitation of the literary work utilizing these traditional cultural expressions requires a prominent acknowledgement of the source community and a declaration detailing measures undertaken to ensure equitable benefit-sharing with that community. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the copyright liable to revocation under this Act.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed invalid under this Act if it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Controller that the claimed subject matter was previously disclosed in a publicly accessible publication originating outside India, provided that such disclosure did not constitute prior teaching as understood within established principles of inventive step. The burden of proving such previous disclosure and its impact on novelty shall rest upon the applicant challenging the validity of the patent. Further, any appeal against an order determining invalidity based on this provision may only be entertained if the appellant establishes a clear nexus between the disclosed information and the specific elements comprising the invention as claimed; otherwise, the appeal shall stand dismissed.

Where the transmission of a registered trade mark occurs through operation of law, such as by way of inheritance or dissolution of a partnership, the successor in title shall be deemed to have acquired the exclusive right to use the trade mark subject to any prior registrations or applications. Any person utilizing the trade mark without express written consent from the assignee following such transmission shall be liable for damages and account of profits made through the infringing activity. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized use after transmission, issue an injunction restraining further infringement. Failure to comply with this restraint constitutes a civil offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

A collective mark shall be deemed to exclusively identify goods or services offered by members of an association of producers, manufacturers, merchants, service providers, or users, and shall represent a common characteristic attributable to the collectivity. Such characteristic may relate to the quality, origin, mode of production, or other distinguishing features of those goods or services. The registration of a collective mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified therein, subject to any conditions as provided herein relating to authorized users and their adherence to standards maintained by the association.

Applications for registration of copyrights shall be made to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office may request further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the nature of the work, its authorship, and any prior assignments or licenses relating thereto. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements under this Act. Where a decision regarding registration is contested, an appeal lies to the copyrights appellate tribunal constituted for this purpose. Such appeals shall be heard expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice, and the tribunal’s determination shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision of the Constitution.

The Controller may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating substantial investment in the development or adaptation of a protected integrated circuit layout design, grant a non-exclusive license to utilize such design for purposes directly related to national defense or critical infrastructure security. Such licenses shall be subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government, including limitations on sub-licensing and requirements for periodic reporting regarding usage patterns. The Controller may permit correction of minor technical errors in the licensed layout design, provided that such corrections do not substantially alter the original inventive concept and are approved prior to implementation. Any assignment or transfer of rights under a license granted as provided herein shall require prior notification to and approval from the Central Government, considering the interest of the security of India and ensuring continued compliance with stipulated conditions.

Where an applicant for a patent, prior to grant, has entered into a contractual agreement assigning rights in the invention to another party, such assignment shall be recorded with the Patents Office within three months of the execution of the agreement. The application sub section (2) provides that any subsequent assignee may also record their interest upon providing satisfactory proof of title and payment of prescribed fees. Further, where an application has been made jointly by two or more applicants, and a license is granted to a third party relating to the invention claimed in the patent, such licensee shall be deemed to hold assignable rights subject to the terms of the license agreement as provided herein. The Controller may require submission of the complete licensing agreement for verification purposes. This provision does not preclude any applicant from retaining ownership or exercising rights pertaining to the patented invention.

The owner of copyright in film sound, being the producer of the cinematographic work, shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to reproduce the said film sound in any medium, including but not limited to audio recordings and musical scores. Such licenses may specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses of the reproduced film sound, subject to reasonable royalty payments as determined under this Act. Assignment of copyright in film sound is permissible by way of a registered agreement, clearly identifying the assignor and assignee and detailing the extent of rights transferred. Provided that any license granted prior to assignment shall remain valid and enforceable against the assignee. Further, where a license has been exclusively assigned, the original producer retains the right to audit royalty accounts for a period of three years following the termination of the agreement. The grant or assignment is deemed invalid if it contravenes provisions relating to fair dealing.

An application for registration of a biological material shall be accompanied by a detailed inventory specifying the source, method of acquisition, and any modifications undertaken. The Controller may require submission of documentation demonstrating compliance with relevant bio-safety guidelines as provided herein. Where the applicant seeks to claim protection based on an invention utilizing a microorganism, such organism must be deposited in an internationally recognized depository authority, adhering to the procedures outlined under this Act. For applications referencing international agreements, “treaty means Budapest” and any amendments or protocols thereto shall be deemed incorporated for the purpose of interpreting registration requirements concerning microbial deposits and access conditions.

Any person who, without due cause or reasonable excuse, represents that goods or services are affiliated with or endorsed by a trade marks proprietor shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or both. Provisions act shall ensure that such representations are deemed false if they create a likelihood of confusion amongst the public regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services. Further, any trade marks proprietor aggrieved by such misrepresentation may institute civil proceedings seeking damages and an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing the deceptive practice. The Court may also order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing representation as it deems fit.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable ground for the omission to pay the fee. The Controller may, subject to satisfaction that the applicant has diligently pursued the invention and that no prejudice accrues to other parties, grant a certificate restoring the patent as if it had not lapsed. However, any claim in respect of an invention disclosed in the restored patent shall be deemed invalid if such claims were previously challenged under this Act during the original term of the patent. The Controller may require payment of all overdue renewal fees and a penalty for late payment before granting restoration.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the identity of the applicant and confirming their entitlement to seek protection under this Act. Where the applicant is a body corporate, the declaration must be signed by a duly authorized officer thereof. In cases where an individual engages a legal practitioner or other agent to file the application on their behalf, such practitioner shall provide particulars of their professional qualifications and registration details in a prescribed form annexed to the application. A person claiming to be a practitioner person may also submit evidence demonstrating continuous engagement in providing intellectual property advisory services for at least three years preceding the date of application, as deemed necessary by the Registrar.

The assignment of a trade mark, or any right accruing thereunder, shall require execution of a formal instrument witnessed as per prevailing practice and registered with the Registrar within thirty days of such assignment. Where an application for registration is assigned prior to its acceptance by the Registrar, the assignee may, subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, apply to have the benefit of the said application transferred to them, providing evidence of the assignment. The Registrar shall decide upon applications for transfer of assignments based on the validity and completeness of the documentation presented. Any license granted in respect of a registered trade mark shall be recorded with the Registrar, detailing the scope and duration of such rights conferred upon the licensee. Provided that any subsequent assignment or further licensing agreement relating to the same trade mark must also be duly recorded as per these provisions.

For civil court purposes relating to infringement actions under this Act, “layout-design” means a three-dimensional representation of the integrated circuit’s structure, expressed in terms of the arrangement of layers and interconnections as deposited on or within a semiconductor material; provided that such representation does not include features which are necessary to achieve mechanical functionality. The term "integrated circuit" shall have the meaning assigned thereto under this Act. A layout-design is deemed to be infringed if any person, without authorization, makes a layout-design that infringes the exclusive right of the registered proprietor as provided herein. Such determination shall be made irrespective of whether the infringing layout-design incorporates all elements of the original design.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model shall furnish with the application details pertaining to any prior publication relating to the invention. Such publications, whether in India or abroad, will be assessed for their impact on novelty and inventive step. Where an earlier publication discloses all elements essential to the claimed invention, the application may be rejected under this Act. However, if the disclosure was made incidentally during the course of an authorized exhibition or demonstration, a grace period shall apply. This grace period allows for consideration of the utility model’s patentability even after the published expiry period of such incidental disclosures, provided that the applicant demonstrates diligent efforts to secure protection following the public display.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall contain particulars verifying ownership and detailing the nature of the design sought to be protected under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to rectify any deficiencies or ambiguities therein before proceeding with examination. Where the applicant demonstrates satisfactory compliance with prescribed formalities, the layout-design shall be deemed eligible for preliminary scrutiny. Upon successful completion of that process, a certificate of registration confirming the existence of a registered layout is issued, specifying the date of entry and other relevant details pertaining to the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license for use of the trade mark under this Act, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the grantor, provided that any assignment without such consent shall be deemed void. The grantor may stipulate conditions within the license agreement regarding quality control measures relating to goods or services bearing the *trade mark used* and may reserve the right to terminate the license in instances of non-compliance with these stipulated standards. Further, a licensee seeking to assign their rights under a trade mark license shall provide the grantor with detailed information pertaining to the proposed assignee, including their business activities and reputation. The grantor shall have thirty days from receipt of this notification to either consent or withhold consent to the assignment, providing written justification for any refusal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a person shall be deemed to have reproduced a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design if that person has created a record embodying it by any means whatsoever. Such reproduction is permissible only with prior authorization from the registered proprietor, provided that such authorization may be granted subject to conditions relating to royalty payments and duration of use as determined by the Controller. The Controller shall ensure compliance with these conditions and may issue directions for their enforcement. Further, where a layout-design incorporates elements previously disclosed, the reproduction shall not infringe any existing right unless the reproduction constitutes an unauthorized adaptation or alteration of the original semiconductor design. Any person contravening this provision shall be liable to penalties as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered design shall furnish such reports and documentation as may be prescribed by the Controller relating to the manufacturing process employed in the production of articles incorporating said design. Such information need not be disclosed if it pertains directly to techniques deemed essential for maintaining necessary security india, or where compliance would compromise national strategic interests as determined by the Central Government. Provided that, any request for disclosure shall include a detailed justification outlining the specific governmental concern necessitating access and specifying the measures taken to safeguard confidential commercial data during review. The Controller may, after consultation with relevant government agencies, issue directives regarding the level of detail required in these reports, subject to ensuring fairness and proportionality between national security concerns and proprietary rights.

An application for registration as a Geographical Indication shall include detailed particulars regarding the production methods employed within the defined territory. The applicant must demonstrate that the name proposed as a Geographical Indication is not descriptive of the goods in relation to their kind, quality or other characteristic and does not conform to established trade practices. Furthermore, evidence establishing consumer recognition of the connection between the goods and the geographical origin shall be submitted. Any alteration to production techniques which materially affects the distinctive qualities of the goods shall apply geographical indications only if approved by a committee constituted under this Act. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed Geographical Indication would likely deceive or cause confusion among consumers.

Any proprietor instituting a case proceeding against an infringer shall file with the relevant jurisdictional authority a sworn affidavit detailing the initial date claim for use of the impugned mark within India. Failure to provide such documentation, or providing information demonstrably false under oath, renders the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may prejudice their right to seek injunctive relief as provided herein. The Registrar shall have the power to issue summons requiring further clarification regarding the veracity of any date claim presented. Further, where an infringer demonstrates prior honest concurrent use predating the proprietor’s asserted date claim, the Court may dismiss the case proceeding with costs against the plaintiff.

For the purposes of this Act, “payable notice” means a notice served under this Act which satisfies the requirements of being delivered in a form specified by regulations made by the Registrar, containing all information prescribed therein, and dispatched to the intended recipient at the address registered with the Registrar or otherwise notified as their principal place of business. A payable notice shall be deemed to have been duly served when it is received by the addressee, or if sent by post, upon proof of dispatch in accordance with postal regulations. Failure to comply with these requirements renders a notice not a payable notice and may preclude reliance on its contents under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to a geographical indication means any person who cultivates, harvests, processes, manufactures, prepares, grows, produces, extracts, handles, or otherwise deals with goods which are claimed to originate from the specified geographical territory and if such goods are agricultural goods, produces the goods and has control over their quality and characteristics as they emerge from that origin. A producer shall be deemed to have control over the quality and characteristics of goods if they adhere to the standards and practices defined in the registered specification for the relevant geographical indication. Any entity engaging in activities described herein may apply for registration under this Act, subject to fulfilling all prescribed conditions.

The Register may, upon receipt of a duly completed application for registration of a geographical indication and after verification of all particulars as provided herein, issue an acknowledgement to the applicant specifying the provisional date of filing. Any subsequent alteration to the proposed name or emblem of the geographical indication shall be deemed a fresh application subject to payment of the prescribed fee paid fee. The Registrar may, at any time, require the proprietor of a registered geographical indication to furnish such further information as the Registrar deems necessary for verification of authenticity and continued protection under this Act. A transmissible use layout depicting the territorial boundaries associated with the geographical indication shall be submitted alongside the application, and any subsequent modifications must be approved by the Registrar. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in suspension or revocation of registration.

Any registered Geographical Indication, hereafter referred to as an “GI,” may be assigned or licensed subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar and recorded in the Register of GIs. Such assignments shall require consent from the registered proprietor and must specify the duration and geographical extent of the rights transferred. A licensee shall be deemed a practitioner within the meaning of this Act, possessing limited rights as defined in the license agreement. The Registrar may impose restrictions on licenses to prevent dilution or misuse of the GI’s reputation. Further, any transfer or licensing arrangement involving a GI relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or wine, must explicitly state provisions for maintaining quality standards consistent with those historically associated with the houses parliament year of origin. Failure to adhere to these conditions renders the assignment or license voidable at the Registrar's discretion.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to submit a request for amendment of their application, provided such request is made within six months from the date of publication under this Act. The Registrar may entertain an application permit amendment if satisfied that the proposed alteration does not substantially affect the identity of goods or services for which the trade mark is sought and does not mislead consumers as to the nature, quality or origin of those goods or services. Any such request shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a clear statement detailing the existing representation and the intended modification. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant before determining whether to grant the application permit amendment. Decisions regarding amendments are subject to appeal under procedures as provided herein.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act may institute proceedings relating to the infringement of their registered trade mark notwithstanding that such proprietor has assigned the entire interest in the trade mark to another party. Provided that, where an assignment has taken place, the assignee shall be deemed to be the sole person entitled to maintain any action or other proceeding for damages or for injunctions relating to the infringement thereof. Further, a party proceeding notwithstanding any prior notice of such assignment shall be subject to the same limitations and conditions as if they were the original registered proprietor. This provision applies irrespective of whether the assignee has notified third parties of their ownership.

An advertisement application registration shall be deemed invalid if it contains any representation which is false or misleading concerning the layout design’s originality or its conformity with applicable technical standards. Any person aggrieved by a registered layout design may, subject to conditions as provided herein, file an objection within ninety days from the date of publication of the advertisement application in the Official Gazette. The Registrar shall serve notice on the applicant and the objector, affording them opportunities for argument and submission of evidence. Further, the applicant may submit counter-evidence within thirty days after service of the notice. If the layout design incorporates elements already registered under this Act, the registration may be revoked upon a finding of substantial similarity.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association, cooperative society, producer group, or individual interested in the collective protection and promotion of goods originating from a particular territory. The Registrar shall consider an area shall considered geographical if the applicant demonstrates that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to its origin within the defined geographical limits. Further, the application must include detailed maps delineating the boundaries of the geographical unit. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration may appeal under this Act. Failure to comply with prescribed procedural requirements during the registration process shall liable penalty as determined by the Registrar and notified in the Official Gazette.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any cinematograph film for public exhibition through broadcast shall obtain a license from the Controller under this Act. Such license shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates that adequate measures have been implemented to prevent unauthorised reproduction or distribution of the said cinematograph film, including but not limited to technological protection measures and contractual safeguards with all involved parties. The broadcasting organisation shall furthermore ensure that any accompanying commentary or adaptation does not distort the original artistic intent as embodied within the cinematograph film. Provided that a written agreement exists between the broadcasting organisation and the copyright owner of the cinematograph film, outlining royalty payments and usage terms, the Controller may waive certain procedural requirements as provided herein.

Where a person alleging infringement of a layout design has suffered damage as a result thereof, such person may institute legal proceedings for redressal under this Act. The measure of damages shall be determined with due regard to the loss of profits reasonably attributable to the infringing activity, taking into account any profit made by the infringer as a consequence of that infringement. It is provided that in determining damages, the court shall consider evidence relating to the extent of the market affected and the prevailing price for similar layout designs. The determination of a *layout design relation* between the original work and the alleged infringing copy shall be a key factor in assessing both liability and the appropriate quantum of compensation. Further, any order restraining the infringer from continuing the infringing activity may include an assessment of costs incurred by the claimant.

Applications for the registration of registry trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. Every application shall state an address for service in India, and if the applicant is not residing or carrying on business in India, he shall appoint a person resident in India as his agent for the purpose of receiving communications under this Act. The Registrar may require any further information to ascertain whether the proposed trade mark is distinctive in its class and refuse registration if the application does not comply with these requirements. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall furnish a copy thereof to the applicant and publish it in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may, within the time specified therein, file a notice of opposition under this Act. The registrar shall consider any such opposition and determine whether registration should proceed as provided herein.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is presented alleging non-use, the Registrar shall direct the proprietor of the trade mark to show cause why the registration should not be expunged. Such direction shall specify the period during which the trade mark has not been used and require the proprietor to provide evidence demonstrating continued honest intent to use the mark. The Registrar may consider factors including advertising expenditure, sales figures, and licensing agreements in assessing such intent. If, after considering all submissions, the Registrar finds that the trademark has not been genuinely used, or there was no intention to use it, then register sufficient cause exists for expungement under this Act; provided that a period of six months may be allowed for remedial action as determined by the Registrar.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark shall submit a request in the form specified by the Trade Marks Rules, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must clearly identify the mark proposed for registration and state the goods or services with which it is associated. Where the mark incorporates a geographical indication as defined under this Act, the applicant shall furnish an affidavit confirming their entitlement to use the said indication and detailing measures taken to prevent its misuse. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the distinctiveness of the trademark and its potential impact on existing registered marks. Any representation or statement made in the application is subject to verification during examination.

A proprietor registered layout may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to acts restricted under this Act, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation of the registered layout-design. The proprietor retains full ownership of the intellectual property unless explicitly transferred through a written assignment executed as per prescribed procedures. Any assignment of a proprietor registered layout must disclose all prior licenses granted and their material terms. Further, any licensee may sub-license rights within the scope permitted by the original license agreement, provided that such sub-licensing is expressly authorized therein. The proprietor shall maintain records of all licenses and assignments and make them available for inspection upon request by the Controller.

Applications for registration as a Copyright Society shall be submitted to the Copyright Societies Registrar in the prescribed Form VII, accompanied by certified copies of the society’s memorandum and articles of association, detailing its objectives relating to the collection and distribution of royalties. The applicant shall furnish proof of representation of not less than seven copyright owners or authors, demonstrating their consent to the society's formation and activities as provided herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may call for such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain compliance with the requirements under this Act. Registration shall be granted if the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed society fulfills all stipulated conditions and operates in the public interest; otherwise, rejection notices will be issued detailing reasons for non-compliance.

An application for a patent relating to an invention shall contain a statement specifying the claims sought to be protected by the patent; and such claims shall define the scope of protection unequivocally. The Controller General may, upon receiving an objection from any person regarding the validity of a claim or the propriety of its inclusion in the patent specification, direct the applicant to clarify or amend the said claim. For the purpose of determining novelty and inventive step under this Act, the date claim is deemed to be the earlier of either the date of filing of the complete specification or the date claimed as the priority date by the applicant, provided that such priority date has been duly recorded in the prescribed manner. The applicant shall furnish all necessary documentation substantiating the priority claim within the timeframe stipulated herein.

A collective mark shall be registered only where the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the adaptation and usage standards governing its display and application. Any member utilizing a registered collective mark who contravenes these prescribed standards, or engages in conduct detrimental to the reputation of the mark, shall be liable for damages as determined by the appropriate civil court. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party or acting suo moto, initiate proceedings against such offending member and, following due process, may order suspension or revocation of their membership privileges within the collective body. Furthermore, wilful infringement resulting in substantial financial loss to other members shall attract penalties as provided herein, including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term up to three years.

Where a proprietor establishes that another has employed deceptive practices in connection with registered trademarks, and such practices involve the use of a sign substantially identical to the trademark in relation to dissimilar goods, creating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods, the aggrieved party may petition the relevant intellectual property tribunal for injunctive relief. This right shall be subject to the respondent demonstrating that their use constitutes fair dealing under this Act and does not amount to used falsifying trade. Provided that any finding of used falsifying trade requires clear and convincing evidence establishing intent to deceive or capitalize on the reputation associated with the registered trademark, appeals may be made to the appellate forum within sixty days of such a determination.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that their copyright has been infringed through unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or public performance of a literary work, they may institute legal proceedings to seek redress under this Act. Subject to provisions regarding limitation periods, any such action must be commenced within three years from the date the infringement is reasonably ascertainable. The plaintiff shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a direct result of the infringing activity, or where actual damage is difficult to quantify, a sum not exceeding ten per cent of the reasonable cost of production and sale of the work. Furthermore, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, provided that such relief is demonstrably necessary to prevent irreparable harm. Any suit arising under this Act shall be brought before a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the cause of action arose.

Where an invention has been granted patent protection under this Act, the patentee shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of the invention, specifying the field of application, territory, and duration of such license. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the patentee. Assignment of rights pertaining to the use invention is permissible, subject to registration with the Controller, and such assignment shall include all rights and obligations arising under this Act related to the patented process or product. The Controller may require disclosure of royalty rates in any license agreement presented for registration, ensuring equitable access to technology. Furthermore, a patentee intending to assign or license an invention relating to pharmaceuticals must provide notification to the government detailing proposed terms, provided that such terms do not unduly restrict competition within the pharmaceutical sector.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without due cause, and such use constitutes an unfair appropriation of reputation or goodwill associated with the said trade mark, the aggrieved proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief under this Act. Such injunction may restrain not only the infringing party but also any person deriving benefit from the infringement, provided that the court is satisfied that the continued use would likely cause further damage to the registered trade mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. The court shall consider all relevant circumstances when determining whether a compelled court say by an expert witness regarding consumer perception is necessary for just adjudication of the matter; however, such compulsion will be limited to clarifying technical aspects directly impacting assessment of likelihood of confusion.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, an applicant for a patent may grant a non-exclusive license in respect of the invention claimed in the allow application patent to any person, provided that such grant is made prior to the sealing of the patent. The terms and conditions of such license shall be recorded in writing and filed with the Controller within thirty days of the grant, detailing the royalty rate and duration of the license. Further, a patentee may assign their entire interest in the allow application patent, including any licenses granted therein, to another party by way of an instrument in writing, duly executed. Such assignment shall be recorded with the Controller as provided herein, and shall become effective only upon such recording. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding the proposed licensee’s capacity to exploit the invention commercially.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall accompany a certified copy of the appointment notification pertaining to any member appointed bench constituted under this Act to hear appeals against decisions concerning the validity of the layout-design. Provided that, where such notification is not readily available, an affidavit from the applicant confirming the existence and composition of the relevant member appointed bench may be submitted in lieu thereof. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of the submission. Any alteration or modification to a registered layout-design shall necessitate a fresh application subject to the same requirements concerning notification verification as provided herein, ensuring continued compliance with the provisions relating to registration and protection under this Act.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional dwellings, including but not limited to structures commonly known as placed houses parliament, shall require submission of detailed architectural plans demonstrating adherence to established regional construction techniques and materials. Such applications must further include documented evidence confirming continuous use of the indicated methods within the defined geographical area for a minimum period of thirty years preceding the date of application. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed geographical indication lacks distinctiveness or falsely suggests a connection with the identified traditional dwelling practices. Any alteration to the architectural design or construction methodology, subsequent to registration, shall be subject to approval by the Geographical Indications Registry and may invalidate the registered status as provided herein.

A registered user party, as defined herein, is a person duly registered under this Act as having exclusive right to use a trade mark in relation to particular goods or services for which the proprietor of the trade mark is also registered. Such registration may occur with the consent of the proprietor and subject to any conditions specified therein. A registered user party shall be entitled to institute proceedings relating to infringement of the trade mark, provided that such proceedings are brought on behalf of and for the benefit of the proprietor. The rights conferred upon a registered user party extend only to the goods or services as defined in their registration certificate and do not encompass any other aspect of the proprietor's trade mark ownership.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, makes use of that indication in connection with goods or services specified in the registration, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed based on the extent of dilution caused to the distinctiveness and reputation of the protected geographical indication. The registered proprietor geographical may institute civil proceedings against any such infringer seeking an injunction restraining further infringing activity and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing said action. Further, where infringement is proven, goods bearing the unauthorized indication are liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein. Any false or misleading representation concerning the origin of goods shall be deemed a violation subject to penalties under this Act.

Where a patentee elects to license the manufacture or use of a patented article, such license shall be assignable in accordance with the provisions under this Act relating to assignment of patents, subject to the conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. Any subsequent assignee of such a license shall be deemed to hold the rights and obligations as if they were the initial licensor, provided that the patentee retains the right to revoke the license upon demonstrating substantial breach of contract by either the licensee or any assignee. The patentee may grant multiple licenses relating to the same patented article, but where such licenses are non-exclusive, priority shall be determined according to the date of execution of each respective agreement. A requirement exists that all assignments and sub-licenses concerning a requires patented article must be registered with the Controller within three months of their creation.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without the consent of the proprietor, and such use creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public as to the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services, an action may be brought under this Act. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating that the continued uses trade mark in question are detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered mark. Provided that, if the defendant can demonstrate prior honest and contemporaneous use of a similar sign before the date of registration, such use may not constitute infringement subject to conditions as provided herein regarding validity registration trade. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages in respect of any such unauthorized use.

Where a registered trademark is used exclusively for the export of goods, the owner shall, upon filing an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form and furnishing such evidence as the Registrar deems appropriate to demonstrate continued exclusive use for export purposes, be entitled to maintain registration under this Act. The Registrar may require periodic submissions from the manner registered proprietor demonstrating ongoing compliance with these conditions; failure to provide such documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall render the trademark liable for review and potential removal from the register of trademarks. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the continued registration of an export-only trademark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions herein relating to timelines and procedural requirements for appeals. The Registrar’s determination on whether exclusive use has been maintained is final, barring such appeal.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Varieties Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or by any condition imposed during registration, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals and pass orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding natural justice. Further, if a registered variety is found to be infringing upon the rights of a traditional farmer or indigenous community, demonstrated through documented evidence of prior use and cultivation, the Authority may order revocation of registration and award compensation for damages suffered. The remedies available under this Act shall include injunctions preventing unauthorized exploitation of protected varieties, as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product containing a layout design consisting of elements substantially similar to a registered layout design without the authorization of the owner thereof shall be liable for damages.
