Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalties which the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license under this Act. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts, subject to ensuring that such restraint does not unduly impede legitimate commercial activities. The owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to seek recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark, or requiring amendment thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is received. The appellant shall deposit with the Registry such sum as may be prescribed, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. It shall also dispose th appeal expeditiously, considering the balance between public interest and commercial considerations; provided that any subsequent application relating to the same trade mark may be taken into consideration during proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, "copy" with respect to any work shall include the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes, whether such process is undertaken for commercial gain or otherwise. A copy so made shall be deemed an infringing reproduction if it reproduces substantial portions of the original work. The right to control the making of such copies vests in the owner of copyright under this Act. Provided that, where a registered breeder of plant varieties has secured intellectual property rights relating to a particular botanical illustration depicting said variety, permission for photocopying or similar reproduction must be obtained from the breeder prior to dissemination.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent under this Act shall, if the invention is also claimed by a patent granted or applied for in a convention country, be required to disclose within the application particulars of such prior applications. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the patent liable for revocation by the Controller upon petition from any interested party demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the non-disclosure. Where an applicant has filed a 73 convention application relating to an invention already patented in India, the subsequent patent shall be deemed invalid if it does not substantially differ from the earlier granted patent and incorporates elements disclosed therein without proper acknowledgement or justification. Penalties for wilful misrepresentation regarding prior applications extend to fines exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and potential imprisonment of up to three years.

A trade mark application is deemed to be filed when it is delivered at the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed under this Act. For the purposes of processing a trade mark application, the applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is sought, as are required for classification under the International Classification of Goods and Services. An application may be refused if it contains any matter that is likely to deceive the public concerning the nature, quality or geographical origin of the goods or services. The Registrar shall record all particulars of a trade mark application in the prescribed manner.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to registration under this Act, an applicant claiming a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment” in India shall furnish documentation demonstrating continuous operation at a specific physical location for a minimum period of twelve months preceding the date of application. Such documentation must include utility bills bearing the applicant’s name and address, lease agreements or property ownership records, and evidence of ongoing business activity as determined by relevant governmental authorities. Provided that, where an applicant operates through a franchise agreement, proof of such agreement and authorization from the franchisor shall be submitted. The Registrar may require further verification to ascertain the genuineness of the establishment, and failure to comply with these requirements will render the application liable for rejection.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to the provisions of international treaties and conventions, be treated as applications for the purposes of claiming priority from an application made in a contracting state. Where an applicant has filed a provisional or complete application relating to an invention in India, and subsequently files a Patent Cooperation Treaty application designating India, the date of filing the earlier Indian application shall be taken into account in determining the right to claim priority. The Controller General may, as provided herein, require applicants seeking benefits under the Patent Cooperation Treaty to furnish certified copies of relevant documents pertaining to the international stage. Such documents shall be deemed part of the record for examination purposes and are subject to scrutiny under this Act.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated, through evidence presented before the Controller, that the claimed invention was previously described in a publication accessible to the public, notwithstanding any assertion by the applicant regarding independent conception. The burden of proving prior publication and its impact on novelty rests upon the petitioner challenging the validity of the patent. Provided that, such challenge may be successfully sustained only if it is established that a person skilled in the relevant art would have been motivated to reproduce the invention based on said publication. Further, any appeal against an order determining lack of inventive step shall require demonstration of manifest error in the Controller's assessment of obviousness, subject to prevailing case law.

Where the copyright in a literary work is vested in an organization registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1960, and such organization has entered into an agreement with its members for the purpose of exploiting that copyright, the organization shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein. Provided that any member who contributed substantially towards the creation of the literary work may, subject to the terms of the aforementioned agreement, apply to a judicial proceeding seeking recognition of their individual rights in respect of such contribution. The organization may grant licenses or assign the entire copyright or portions thereof relating to the literary work to third parties as it deems fit, provided that such assignment includes provisions ensuring equitable remuneration for contributing members, proportionate to their involvement in its creation.

The Authority shall maintain a Register of Plant Varieties for each class of varieties and upon receipt of an application for registration, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish details regarding the source material utilized in the development of the variety. Any sums received by the Authority as registration fees, benefit-sharing amounts from commercialized varieties, or penalties imposed under this Act shall be credited into a dedicated account maintained with the Reserve Bank of India. This account shall constitute fund for the purposes of supporting research and development activities related to plant breeding, conservation of genetic resources, and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in seed production. The Authority may also invest portions of this fund as deemed prudent by its governing board, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Any person found to have knowingly made a false statement in a design affidavit registered under this Act shall be liable for a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred and fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, such person shall also be subject to proceedings for recovery of costs incurred by the Controller in rectifying the erroneous registration or investigating allegations of falsity. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information regarding discrepancies between the registered design and actual goods, initiate an inquiry into the veracity of the design affidavit. Where it is established that the layout-design incorporates elements infringing on existing intellectual property rights relating to j) “goods”, the Controller shall have power to order cancellation of the registration and impose additional penalties as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings alleging an infringement of his rights under this Act, he shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and also to claim damages sustained by him as a direct consequence of such infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the loss suffered by the proprietor, the profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity, and any other factor deemed just and equitable by the adjudicating authority. Subject to appeal to a higher judicial forum, decisions regarding damages are final. Common Regulations governing trade mark disputes shall apply uniformly across all jurisdictions within the Union, ensuring consistent application of remedies for infringement. Provided that, in cases involving wilful infringement, enhanced damages may be awarded.

An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings and documentation pertaining to the fabrication process, detailing all layers and masking techniques employed. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the technical specifications if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Any prior publication or commercial exploitation of the integrated circuit design outside India shall be disclosed in the application, subject to provisions relating to grace periods as provided herein. An applicant seeking registration shall affirm that they are the rightful owner of the layout-design and possess exclusive rights over its reproduction and use. The Registrar may reject an application if it finds that the submitted documentation is incomplete or fails to adequately describe the integrated circuit.

Subject to the conditions outlined herein, a copyright owner desiring to grant a license in respect of their work shall execute a written instrument specifying the scope of such license, including but not limited to the geographical territory, duration, and permitted acts. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive at the discretion of the copyright owner, provided that any assignment of copyright under this Act must also be evidenced by a written instrument. Further, where a work is jointly authored, the provisions sub section (1) relating to licensing shall apply with modification to reflect the rights and obligations of each co-owner. Any party receiving a license or assignment shall be bound by the terms stipulated therein, and any unauthorized use beyond the scope of such agreement constitutes infringement. The copyright owner retains the right to terminate a license upon written notice if material breaches occur.

An eligible good qualifies for registration as a registered geographical indication where its qualities, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its origin within a defined area. Such an area shall be determined by the Geographical Indications Registry based on documented evidence demonstrating a continuous link between the product and that geographic territory. Provided that any person seeking to apply patent protection relating to a process used in the production of goods conforming to the standards specified for a registered geographical indication must disclose such use within the application, subject to review under this Act. The Registrar may require further verification concerning the authenticity of claims regarding origin and quality before granting registration, ensuring compliance with established protocols as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication, or any condition imposed on the use thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the appellant and the respondent, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Where a registered geographical indication relates to goods that are not produced in the territory it identifies, any proprietor of a prior trademark for those goods shall be entitled to apply to have the registration revoked, subject to demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the continued use of the geographical indication. Remedies available under this Act include injunctions preventing unauthorized use and damages recoverable by proprietors of registered geographical indications.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent application or a granted patent, by way of assignment, license, or otherwise, shall furnish to the patent office a certified copy of the instrument evidencing such claim. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the transfer was absolute or conditional. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the validity and scope of any license agreement presented for registration. Where an assignment is made subsequent to the initial filing of a patent application, the previous assignor shall be deemed to retain no rights under this Act unless expressly released in writing by the assignee, duly registered with the patent office central. Any alteration or modification to a previously registered license must also be reported and approved as provided herein before it becomes effective against third parties.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a mark if it consists exclusively of the marks shape goods, provided that such shape is dictated solely by factors relating to the characteristics of the product itself. Where a proprietor seeks to register a three-dimensional configuration as a trade mark representing the marks shape goods, they shall demonstrate that the said shape signifies distinctiveness in relation to the specified goods or services. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act concerning the registrability of a mark based on its shape may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and injunctions against use.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention, it shall be incumbent upon them to demonstrate with reasonable certainty that the claimed subject matter was not previously disclosed under this Act or any other law. The Controller may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating the asserted priority claim, and failure to provide such satisfactory proof within the prescribed time period will render the application liable for rejection. It is provided that an appeal against such a decision of the Controller shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions regarding timelines and maintainability under this Act. A patent shall not be granted unless the priority date claim is definitively resolved and found to be valid.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied therewith, he may prefer an appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall lie only on a question of law and not otherwise, subject to the proviso that where the findings of fact affect a substantial question of law, the appellate authority may examine such findings notwithstanding their nature as findings of fact. The Controller may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller in exercise of his powers under this Act relating to an *order appellate* may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall contain particulars specifying the name of the goods, the territory from which the goods originate, and the prior use, if any, of the name of the Geographical Indication. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin; failing this demonstration, registration shall be denied. Further, the proposed indication must not describe any ingredient or component of the goods but instead signify a specific locality. Any alteration to the registered Geographical Indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such alteration does not substantially affect the distinctiveness of the *indication*.

Subject to the provisions of this Patents Act, 1970, any person claiming title to an invention which is the subject matter of a patent application may grant licenses under that application to other parties, either wholly or partially, and such license agreement shall be in writing and specify the scope of rights granted. Assignment of patent rights, including all or any part of the patent, the benefit of the application, or the patent itself, may also be effected by written instrument, and registration of such assignment with the Controller is mandatory for it to be deemed valid against third parties. Further, where a license or assignment includes provisions relating to royalties or other considerations, these shall be clearly articulated within the agreement. The Central Government may, under this Act, prescribe conditions governing the transfer of patent rights to ensure equitable access and prevent anti-competitive practices related to patented technologies.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any integrated circuit layout design infringing a registered layout design shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to five times the actual losses suffered by the owner of the registered layout design. Such losses shall include lost profits and reasonable royalty fees. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registrant, issue an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender liable for imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or both. Applications for rectification of entries in the design registry are subject to penalties for false statements.

Where any person considers that another person has infringed a patent granted under this Act, such person may institute proceedings for relief against the infringement in the manner provided herein. Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement shall be granted if it is established that the patented invention was being used without authorization. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized use or manufacture of a patented article, direct any person aggrieved by such action to submit evidence substantiating the claim. Any patent filed designating India and subsequently found invalid due to prior publication or use shall be liable for damages payable to those prejudiced by the grant. The amount of compensation shall be determined based on the extent of commercial detriment suffered.

Any applicant aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of his application for registration shall have the right to appeal to the Controller within three months from the date of communication of such decision. The Controller may, after giving the appellant an opportunity of being heard and after considering the evidence submitted, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed against. Where an appeal is preferred under this Act, the applicant shall be deemed to have waived any objection which he could have raised but for the provisions of section 105. The Controller’s order on such appeal shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided herein. Any person whose interests are adversely affected by an entry in the register may apply to the Appellate Board for redressal of his grievances.

For the purposes of adjudicating disputes under this Act relating to infringement or validity of registered layout-designs, there shall be constituted a member appointed bench known as the Layout-Design Adjudication Tribunal. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish such number of Benches as it deems necessary for expeditious disposal of cases. Each Bench shall comprise at least one Judicial Member and two Technical Members, all possessing expertise in semiconductor technology or intellectual property law, as provided herein. Decisions of a member appointed bench shall be final subject to appeal under the provisions relating to appeals against orders of the Controller.

An appeal, as provided herein, shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark. For the purposes of this Act, “th appeal specified” means that where an appeal is admitted against an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, and subsequently challenged before the High Court, the time limit for preferring such further appeal shall be calculated from the date on which the judgment or order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board is communicated to the appellant. Subject to any procedural requirements under this Act, a party may seek clarification regarding the scope of an order made in relation to a trade mark application.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, where an application for patent relating to an inventive step discloses that it has been derived from a prior disclosure made by another party, the Controller shall require the applicant to demonstrate, through documentary evidence and testimony, that they are indeed the true and first inventor of the subject matter claimed. Such demonstration must establish that the applicant conceived of the invention independently or contributed significantly to its development beyond merely implementing the earlier disclosure. The burden of proving this lies entirely upon the applicant. Provided that, if the Controller is satisfied that the prior disclosure was made without the knowledge or consent of the applicant, and that the applicant has diligently pursued the inventive step, registration may proceed subject to such conditions as the Controller deems appropriate.

Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry against the acceptance of an application for registration, asserting that the proposed trade marks, when used in relation to the goods services description specified in the application, would likely cause confusion amongst the public, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit a written response addressing such objections. The Registrar may require the applicant to attend an oral hearing to further clarify their position. Following consideration of the objection and any submissions made by the applicant, the Registrar’s decision shall be communicated in writing. Any party aggrieved by this decision may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The appeal period is deemed to commence from the day following the date of such communication.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration, amendment, revocation or refusal of registration of a geographical indication institutes an appeal under this Act, the Appellate Board shall hear and dispose of such appeals within six months from the date of receipt of the appeal. The central government shall, upon receiving representations concerning alleged misuse of a registered geographical indication, direct the Registrar to investigate whether any unfair competition or deceptive practices are being employed that infringe upon the rights conferred by registration. Provided that, if the Registrar finds merit in such allegations and determines that infringement has occurred, he may issue directions for rectification of trade practices as deemed necessary; however, any party disputing these findings may appeal to the Appellate Board within thirty days.

The Registrar shall maintain an entry register variety for each plant variety recorded under this Act, detailing essential characteristics and geographical provenance as declared by the applicant. Any person aggrieved by an entry made, or omitted to be made, in the entry register variety may within sixty days from the date such entry is published, file an appeal before the Appellate Board. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted by both the appellant and the Registrar, including expert testimony regarding varietal stability and distinctiveness. Provided that, the burden of demonstrating error or material misrepresentation in the entry register variety shall lie with the appellant. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeal under the appropriate provisions relating to judicial review.

Where an action is brought before a competent authority alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, the defendant shall be required to demonstrate, as provided herein, compliance with all applicable conditions precedent. Specifically, the defendant must satisfy the court that their use of the indication does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services in question and that such use is consistent with established trade practices within the relevant sector. Further, if the defendant contends good faith reliance on a prior registration or usage, they shall submit documentary evidence substantiating this claim, including but not limited to marketing materials and sales records. The authority may require further submissions as deemed necessary for assessment of the infringement defendant satisfies these conditions.

Where a person, knowing that another’s registered trademark is connected in the minds of the public with particular goods or services, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar thereto in relation to dissimilar goods or services with the intention to mislead consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, such use shall constitute used falsifying trade. The owner of the registered trademark may institute legal proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of the said used falsifying trade, including loss of profits and any damage to reputation caused thereby. Further, a court may grant an injunction restraining the person from continuing such infringing conduct. It is provided that the right to claim damages shall not arise unless the owner proves actual financial detriment attributable to the misleading use.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted under this Act, or intends to assign the entire interest in such patent, the licensing agreement or assignment deed shall explicitly detail all aspects of the filing specification matter pertaining to the claimed invention. Such disclosure must include, but not be limited to, descriptions of the inventive concept, detailed methodologies employed in its creation, and any supporting data presented within the original application documents. The Controller may require further clarification regarding this specification matter if deemed necessary for public understanding and transparency. Provided that the patentee ensures accuracy and completeness in these disclosures, such licenses or assignments shall be considered valid and enforceable as provided herein. Failure to adequately address the filing specification matter may render the license or assignment voidable at the discretion of the Controller.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing to accept an application for registration of a trade mark, the Appellate Board may, subject to any conditions it deems fit to impose, direct that the matter be remitted to the Registrar for reconsideration. Such direction shall specify the grounds upon which the original decision was deemed erroneous. The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the right to institute proceedings in the High Court against any person infringing their rights under this Act, notwithstanding any prior communication or warning given. Provided that, if the infringement is alleged to be unintentional, the Court may, as provided herein, order rectification of the error rather than award damages.

Where a patentee desires to assign their interest in a granted patent, or to grant an exclusive license under that patent, such assignment or license shall be recorded with the Controller. The instrument effecting the transfer must specify the full name and address of both the assignor and assignee, or licensor and licensee, as applicable, and clearly define the scope of the rights being transferred. To substantiate the claims made in the assignment or license agreement, a duly sworn affidavit from the patentee, or their authorized representative, shall be submitted to the Controller. This affidavit must attest to the authenticity of the document and confirm that the transfer is executed freely and without coercion. Failure to provide a satisfactory evidence affidavit may render the recorded assignment or license voidable under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit a duly completed form petition in the prescribed format, obtainable from the designated office or its website. The form petition must clearly specify the title of the layout-design, the name and address of the claimant, and details pertaining to the first marketing date outside India, if any. Provided that, where the applicant is an entity incorporated outside India, they shall furnish a certified copy of their incorporation certificate as supporting documentation. Any alteration or erasure made on the form petition after its submission renders it invalid, requiring resubmission. The Registrar may reject a form petition deemed incomplete or containing false particulars under this Act.

Where any person alleges that another has contravened a provision relating to layout-design rights, such person may file a complaint with the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority. The complaint shall be accompanied by detailed particulars as prescribed under this Act, including but not limited to, evidence demonstrating unauthorized reproduction or importation of the allegedly infringing integrated circuit layout design. Failure to provide complete and accurate petition particulars contained within the complaint will render it liable for dismissal without further notice. The Authority may, subject to due process, impose penalties commensurate with the severity of the infringement, including monetary damages and injunctive relief. Any appeal against an order issued by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority shall be made within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, “registration common regulations” shall mean the procedures and conditions governing the acceptance and processing of applications for registration of trademarks by multiple applicants seeking identical or deceptively similar marks in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. Such regulations are established to ensure equitable consideration under this Act and prevent undue delay caused by conflicting claims. An application may be held pending if it is determined that another application, filed prior thereto, raises a substantial conflict; provided that the Registrar shall provide both applicants with written notice of such pendency and an opportunity to submit representations.

Any action seeking damages or injunctive relief pertaining to allegations of unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation of cinematograph films shall be filed exclusively within the civil courts. The determination of territorial jurisdiction under this Act shall be governed by the principles established under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as amended. Provided that, where a copyright owner demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe that an infringement extends beyond the geographical limits of a single district, they may elect to initiate proceedings in any district court having jurisdiction over at least one location where such infringement occurred or is reasonably believed to have occurred. The plaintiff shall be required to submit an affidavit detailing the basis for asserting jurisdiction across multiple districts. Failure to do so may result in dismissal of the action without prejudice.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed renewed upon payment of the prescribed renewal fee within the time limit specified under this Act. For the purposes of this section, “renewal” means the continuation of protection conferred by the registered trade mark for a further period of ten years from the expiry of the initial or previous term of registration. The Registrar may entertain an application for renewal even if it is filed after the due date, provided that any additional fee prescribed in this behalf is remitted along with the renewal application. Any alteration to the representation of the trade mark shall be treated as a new application and not as part of the forms application renewal process.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor" shall mean any material capable of conducting electricity under specific conditions and exhibiting semiconductive properties, including but not limited to silicon, germanium, gallium arsenide, and related compounds. A “layout-design” in relation to a semiconductor integrated circuit includes the three-dimensional arrangement of layers, interconnections, metallic areas, doping, and other elements which define its electrical functioning. The term "integrated circuit" shall mean a product having an interconnected or embedded semiconducting structure; provided that such structure is designed as a whole for performing a specific function. Any modification to a layout-design, subject to the provisions herein, shall be deemed a derivative work.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “literary work” shall be deemed to include unpublished manuscripts submitted for evaluation by publishing houses, provided that such submission is accompanied by a declaration from the author affirming their intention to publish the work within a period not exceeding five years from the date of application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claim of authorship and the nature of the manuscript’s submission process. Where an applicant seeks registration for a literary work jointly authored, all co-authors shall be required to consent in writing to the application and share equally in the copyright accruing under this Act, subject to any contractual agreements between them duly filed with the Registrar. The refusal of registration may be appealed before the designated appellate authority as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application filed outside India, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the earlier application as evidence. Such certification shall be obtained under the procedures prescribed by the relevant national authority or, where applicable, pursuant to the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits for Industrial Designs. The applicant shall provide this documentation within the time specified in the notice issued by the Controller; failure to do so may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of such certified copies may appeal under this Act, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Costs incurred in relation to these proceedings shall be determined by the Appellate Board and are liable costs unless the appellant demonstrates reasonable grounds for the appeal were absent.

For the purposes of this Act, an “independent scientific adviser” means a person possessing demonstrable expertise in a field relevant to the invention claimed in a patent application or relating to the alleged infringement thereof, who is not employed by, nor has any significant financial interest in, either the applicant or the accused infringer. Such an adviser shall be appointed under this Act where the Controller deems that technical complexities necessitate external assistance for informed decision-making. Recognition trade marks, if presented as evidence concerning prior use or public familiarity with a technology, may be considered by the Controller during proceedings involving an independent scientific adviser’s assessment.

An applicant seeking to amend an application for patent may do so only with the prior written consent of the Controller and after providing a copy of the proposed amendment to all other parties involved in related proceedings under this Act. Such amendment shall be permissible solely if it does not substantially alter the scope of protection initially sought, as determined by the Controller’s assessment at the time of the original application's filing date. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements renders the amended application void ab initio. Any party aggrieved by a decision allowing or refusing an application amend may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, and notice rectification shall be afforded to all concerned during the appellate process.

For the purposes of this Act, "trade mark" shall mean any sign, symbol, device, lettering, numerals, shapes, configurations, colours or any combination thereof adopted to distinguish goods or services of one enterprise from those of others and shall include any element that may constitute a trade mark as provided herein. A trade mark may be registered in respect of goods or services, or both, by way of use or intention to use. The registration of a trade mark does not confer upon the proprietor any right to prevent the use of the same sign or symbol by others unless such use is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin of the goods or services.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to have been filed for a period exceeding twelve months where the applicant, following the initial publication or public disclosure of any matter constituting the invention, but prior to the date of filing the patent application as provided herein, undertakes activities that would reasonably indicate an intention to commercially exploit said invention within the territory of India. Such activities include, but are not limited to, offering for sale, distributing, or demonstrating the invention publicly. The determination of whether india filed months constitutes a bar to patentability shall be assessed on a case-by-case basis considering all relevant circumstances.

Where an owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another person is using a sign detrimentally affecting the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered mark, such owner may institute a suit infringement registered under this Act. Provided that, prior to initiating legal proceedings, the owner shall furnish a written representation to the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the suspected infringement and affording them a period of thirty days for response and remediation. Further, if the infringing use is demonstrably unintentional and arises from honest, non-commercial activity, the Court may, subject to considerations of public interest and equitable principles, grant relief proportionate to the harm caused, without necessarily requiring cessation of the activity. The owner shall bear the burden of proving both ownership of the registered mark and the existence of infringement as provided herein.

The owner of copyright in any work, whether registered or not, may grant an exclusive license authorizing the doing of specified acts relating to that work, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the licensor and licensee; provided that such license shall clearly define the scope of the permitted acts, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation. The registrar copyrights shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all assignments and licenses granted under this Act, detailing the parties involved, the work subject to the assignment or license, and the duration thereof. Any subsequent assignee or licensee may record their interest in the Copyright Office for evidentiary purposes. Failure to accurately reflect the terms of an agreement within the recorded document shall render such recording voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence, satisfactory to the Registrar, establishing the origin of the goods and their association with a particular geographical area. Where the name of the Geographical Indication includes an expression indicating quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods, the application shall specify the characteristics which give rise to that quality, reputation or other characteristic. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness and protectability of the proposed Geographical Indication. Any person claiming to be an interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of a notice under this Act, file objections relating to the registration of the Geographical Indication.

Where an applicant seeks to amend a pending application permitted amended under this Act, such amendment shall not alter the fundamental character of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Any alteration intended to circumvent existing registrations or create confusion amongst consumers will be deemed a falsifying trade mark and shall be rejected outright. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant seeking amendment to submit evidence demonstrating the continued distinctiveness of the amended mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Failure to provide such evidence within the prescribed period shall result in rejection of the application and imposition of a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees; repeated offences will attract enhanced penalties and potential prosecution under relevant provisions relating to trade malpractices.

For the purpose of this Act, a ‘layout design’ includes features relating to the arrangement or interconnection of elements which define an integrated circuit. The term 'element' shall encompass any circuitry, semiconductor material, or other component incorporated within the layout design. Where an application for registration is received, and the Controller determines that the layout design incorporates original features not previously disclosed, the registry shall place the application on record pending examination as to novelty and inventive step. Provided that such placement does not constitute a grant of exclusive rights under this Act, and subject to any objections raised by third parties within the prescribed period.

Where an application is filed seeking to amend a registered trade mark, such application shall specify with particularity the alterations proposed to be made to the representation of the trade mark, including but not limited to changes in colour, device, or wordings. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of the proposed amendments. An application to *amend register* shall be refused if the alteration sought would substantially affect the distinctive character of the registered trade mark as it was originally accepted for registration, subject to any prior use established under this Act. Any such refusal shall state the reasons therefor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any producer of a film sound recording shall be entitled to grant licenses for the reproduction, distribution, and public exhibition of such recordings. Such licenses may be granted in whole or in part, and may specify conditions regarding territory, duration, and manner of use. Assignment of rights relating to a film sound recording is permissible only through a registered agreement executed before the Registrar of Copyrights, containing details of both assignor and assignee, including their addresses for service of notices. Where a license is granted under this Act, the producer shall provide reasonable information regarding the terms and conditions thereof to any person seeking access to such information, provided that such request does not compromise trade secrets or confidential business practices. Any subsequent transfer of rights relating to a film sound recording requires similar registration as an assignment.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as to the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory from which it originates, the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable to its origin, and the manner in which the geographical indication is used. Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application under this Act, the applicant may submit their response within a period specified by the Registrar. The Registrar shall consider such objections and responses and may either accept or reject the application. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to registration or refusal thereof may appeal to the Appellate Board. This provision applies equally where action is taken for infringement or for passing off referred to in section 66.

Any reproduction of a substantial portion of a copyrighted work, whether published or unpublished, without authorization from the copyright holder constitutes infringement copyright work. Such unauthorized acts include, but are not limited to, photocopying, digital scanning, and distribution in any medium. Where an infringing copy is made for commercial gain, the offender shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a percentage of the potential lost revenue reasonably attributable to the infringement, as determined by the relevant civil court. Further, where the infringement is proven to have been willful, aggravated damages may be awarded up to three times the amount of actual damages. The owner of copyright may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “proposed registered proprietor” means an individual or body corporate to whom application for registration of a trade mark has been made and who is reasonably expected to become the registered proprietor upon completion of the examination process and any subsequent appeals. Such expectation shall be determined by the Registrar based on compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act relating to distinctiveness, deceptiveness, and prior rights. The Registrar may require further documentation from an applicant identified as a proposed registered proprietor to ascertain their eligibility and intention to utilize the trade mark in accordance with prescribed guidelines, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act claiming priority from an earlier application made in a country outside India, the date of filing such foreign application shall be deemed to be the date of filing the Indian application for the purposes of determining seniority and any other right arising under this Act. Provided that, if the Registrar has reason to believe that the claimed priority is not genuine or that the applicant does not possess the necessary legal standing in relation to the earlier application, he may require the applicant to submit such evidence as he deems appropriate to substantiate the claim. The Registrar shall record the deemed date registration prominently on the register of trade marks and provide notice thereof to any party who has previously filed an opposition against the mark. Any subsequent amendment to the trade mark shall not affect the deemed date registration unless approved by the Registrar, subject to such conditions as he may specify.

Where an application for patent includes drawings depicting objects or processes, such drawings shall be construed as representations intended solely to illustrate aspects of the invention claimed. The Controller may, at any stage of examination, direct the applicant to provide further clarification regarding any element depicted within said drawings, provided that such direction is accompanied by a reasoned explanation outlining the ambiguity necessitating additional detail. Any reference made under this Act to “the drawing” shall encompass all sheets submitted as part of the application’s technical documentation, irrespective of their sequential order or labeling. The interpretation of claims referencing specific features shown in the drawings shall be governed by principles of form references act, ensuring consistency between textual descriptions and visual representations. Failure to comply with a direction under this provision may result in rejection of the patent application.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that indication on goods conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act. Such licenses may include provisions concerning quality control and packaging requirements, provided that the terms do not unduly restrict competition or innovation. Assignment of a registered geographical indication, including any associated patent rights obtained for processes integral to its production, shall require prior approval from the Central Government. The assignee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations applicable to the assignor under this Act. Any license granted without adherence to these provisions may be revoked as provided herein. Further, sub-licensing is permitted subject to the terms of the original license agreement and with notification to the Geographical Indications Registry.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance is filed, the Controller shall require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices as prescribed under regulations issued by the Central Government. Such evidence must be current and verifiable through independent audits conducted within the preceding three years. Provided that, if the invention relates to a process for producing such a substance, documentation pertaining to quality control measures implemented throughout the production chain shall also be submitted. Further, where an applicant seeks patent protection under this Act in relation to biological material deposited pursuant to the Budapest Treaty means budapest, the deposition must adhere strictly to the requirements outlined therein and remain accessible for inspection as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark, or concerning any matter arising under this Act where no other right of appeal is specifically provided, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The appellant shall deposit such fees as are prescribed for appeals before the Tribunal. Provided that, if the aggrieved party can demonstrate reasonable cause for delay, the Tribunal may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the lapse of the stipulated period, subject to its satisfaction regarding the justification for the delay. Further, the Tribunal shall consider any counter-claims filed by other interested parties in relation to the trade mark concerned.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety contributing to the National Gene Fund shall be eligible to license those rights for research purposes relating to traits deemed beneficial for food security or rural livelihoods. Such licenses may be granted on non-exclusive terms, provided that the licensee undertakes to share resultant data and findings with the Central Government within a stipulated timeframe. Assignment of rights related to varieties contributing to the National Gene Fund shall require prior approval from the Authority, ensuring equitable distribution of benefits derived from commercialization. The Authority may stipulate conditions regarding royalty rates and geographical limitations in such assignments. Further, any transfer of technology involving plant genetic resources linked to contributions made to the National Gene Fund must include provisions for benefit-sharing with local communities involved in conservation efforts.

The producer relation cinematograph film shall be deemed the owner of copyright therein, subject to any agreement entered into prior to the commencement of principal photography. Any license granted by the producer relating to reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of the work may specify a limited duration and geographical territory as determined within the terms of such license. Further, assignment of copyright in the cinematograph film, whether partial or complete, requires execution of a written agreement specifying the scope of rights transferred and the consideration paid. The exclusive rights conferred upon the producer under this Act include the right to authorize or prohibit the making of copies, communication to the public, and any other acts restricted by law. Provided that, where a performer’s contribution is demonstrably integral to the film's artistic merit, they may negotiate for a share in royalties derived from exploitation of those rights as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark has been assigned or licensed, and any dispute arises concerning the validity of that assignment or license, or relating to infringement claims predicated upon the use of the mark, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum. Such proceedings shall be deemed to include appeals against decisions made by the Registrar regarding revocation or rectification applications affecting the registered trade mark. The appeal specified period for challenging a decision under this Act concerning such assignments or licenses is sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that an extension of time may be granted in circumstances where demonstrable hardship would result from strict adherence to the prescribed timeframe. Any party seeking such an extension must file a written application justifying the delay within thirty days of the expiry of the initial appeal specified period.

An application for registration of a utility model shall include with it a detailed set of amendment specification documents pertaining to any modifications made to the originally submitted design. These documents must clearly delineate each alteration from the initial submission and provide justification for such changes, referencing relevant technical data or experimental results where applicable. The Controller may require further clarification or supplementary materials regarding these amendment specification documents if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Any applicant seeking to incorporate revisions through amendment specification documents shall file an affidavit confirming the accuracy of the information presented therein. Failure to adhere to prescribed formats and submission protocols relating to amendment specification documents will render the application liable for rejection.

Where a trade mark has been assigned or licensed, and an application for rectification of that trade mark is made, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the assignor or licensee demonstrating continued use of the mark subsequent to the assignment or license agreement. Such consideration will include assessment of whether the ongoing usage materially impacts the distinctiveness of the mark as originally registered. The Registrar may require further clarification from either the assignee or licensor regarding the scope and duration of their respective rights, particularly where conflicting claims arise concerning permitted uses. Provided that the assignor or licensee can establish a legitimate interest in maintaining the integrity of the trade mark’s reputation, they shall be afforded an opportunity to present arguments against rectification. The Registrar is not bound by any contractual limitations contained within the assignment or license agreement itself.

The Registrar shall not register a trade mark which, when used in relation to food products, is deemed by the relevant authorities under the Food Adulteration Act to be misleadingly descriptive of the product’s composition or quality. This restriction applies irrespective of any prior use or reputation acquired by the applicant for the trade mark. An application may proceed if the Registrar is satisfied that appropriate safeguards are in place to prevent consumer confusion arising from such a depiction, including but not limited to prominent disclaimers and certification marks. Furthermore, where a food product originates from a registered geographical indication, any proposed trade mark shall clearly differentiate itself from the protected name and characteristics associated with said geographical indication, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the design incorporates or comprises any coat of arms, public seal, flag, emblem, name or initials of any sovereign nation or foreign state; provided that the Registrar may entertain an application containing such elements if the applicant demonstrates to his satisfaction that use is authorized by the appropriate government authority. The Controller General shall furnish a certified copy of the design registration to any person applying for it, upon payment of the prescribed fee and subject to verification of identity as per rules framed under this Act. Any individual found to be infringing a registered design may be required to submit detailed documentation pertaining to their manufacturing processes. Designs deemed essential for national security, particularly those relating to defense or critical infrastructure, are considered necessary security india and shall receive heightened protection.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "Appellate Board" means a body established under notification by the Central Government, constituted as provided herein, and vested with exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals arising from orders passed by Copyright Adjudicating Officers. The Appellate Board shall be deemed to be a civil court for certain proceedings only as specified in this Act and subject to its own procedural rules. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final, but are subject to judicial review under law relating to writ petitions. The composition, powers, and functions of the Appellate Board are detailed elsewhere within this legislation.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in accordance with the provisions relating to applications for registration of trademarks, subject to any modifications specified herein. Where an application contains particulars which are incomplete or ambiguous, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification within a prescribed time period. Any such requirement shall be communicated by written notice served on the applicant. Failure to comply with such a notice may result in the rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all communications relating to an application and make it available for inspection as provided herein. A *registrar person* acting under this Act is empowered to issue notices, demand documents, and conduct hearings concerning any matter arising during examination or opposition proceedings.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license relating to the use of an indication registered under this Act shall, prior to such grant, provide notice to the Registrar specifying the geographical area covered by the registration and detailing the terms and conditions of the proposed license agreement. The Registrar may, after affording opportunity for objection to interested parties, issue directions regarding the permissible scope of such licenses, particularly concerning quality control measures applicable to goods bearing the registered indication. Assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication shall require prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not alter the essential characteristics or reputation associated with the registration. Further, any subsequent transfer relating registration geographical boundaries must be notified to the office within three months and is subject to review under this Act.

The owner of a registered certify goods mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to affix such mark upon goods meeting the prescribed standards. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may extend to the use of associated designs incorporated into the packaging or presentation of the certified goods, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Any assignment of a registered certify goods mark shall include all rights pertaining to any existing licenses attached thereto; provided that such assignment is executed in the prescribed manner and duly notified to the Registrar. The Registrar may require disclosure of license terms during examination of an application for registration or upon request from an interested party, ensuring transparency and preventing anti-competitive practices relating to certified goods. Further, sub-licensing shall be permitted only with prior written consent from the original owner under this Act.

Where a patent has been granted, its validity may be challenged before the Controller based on grounds established under this Act, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step. Upon receiving such a challenge, the Controller shall provide the patentee with an opportunity for reasoned response and counter-argument, recorded in writing. If, following due consideration of all evidence presented, the Controller determines that the claimed invention does not meet the statutory requirements, a cessation patent may be declared, revoking the original grant. Any party aggrieved by such declaration or by the refusal to declare a cessation patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, as provided herein, presenting arguments and documentary proof supporting their position before the relevant authority. The Layout Design Registrar shall maintain records of all proceedings related to cessation patents.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein, submit evidence demonstrating adherence to an agreement means madrid protocol concerning the international registration of marks. Such evidence must clearly articulate the designated Contracting Parties included within the scope of the international registration and specify any limitations or disclaimers applied during the application process. The Registrar may request further clarification regarding the applicant’s compliance with the aforementioned agreement, including details pertaining to translation requirements for elements of the mark not originally in English or Hindi. Failure to adequately substantiate adherence to an agreement means madrid will render the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement within such time as may be prescribed. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider all evidence submitted by both the opponent and the applicant and shall record its findings on the distinctiveness of the mark and any likelihood of confusion arising from its use. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or refusal of a trade mark, or concerning rectification proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board shall hear arguments and consider evidence presented before it, subject to such rules as are prescribed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark accordance” exists where a proposed trade mark, when used in relation to specified goods or services, does not directly signify an association with another enterprise engaged in similar activities unless such association is demonstrably authorized through a written agreement. This determination shall consider the overall impression created upon the relevant consumer base and whether the use of the mark creates confusion regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Further, trade mark accordance shall be assessed irrespective of any superficial differences between the marks, focusing instead on their conceptual similarity as perceived by an average consumer exercising reasonable care in purchasing decisions.

Any proprietor registered as having exclusive right to use a geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, may institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act and shall be entitled to seek remedies including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor or authorized user, and disposal of infringing goods. Provided that where an act constituting infringement also constitutes an offence under the Indian Penal Code, the offender shall be liable to prosecution under both this Act and the said penal code. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from any registered proprietor, direct law enforcement agencies to investigate suspected infringements and initiate appropriate action as deemed necessary. Further, costs of litigation relating to infringement proceedings shall be determined by the court considering the nature and extent of the infringement.

Any party aggrieved by the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to provisions regarding time limits as provided herein, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to errors apparent on the face of the record pertaining to the publication of a registration notice. The Registrar shall, within thirty days of receiving such appeal, transmit all relevant documents and records to the Tribunal for consideration. It shall be open to the applicant whose application was affected by the decision under appeal to present counter-arguments and evidence, provided that any such submissions are filed within fifteen days from service of the appellant’s grounds.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the registration of a patent or any other matter arising under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to just consideration of the evidence presented. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where a patent has been granted in contravention of any provision of this Act, the Controller may, sua bonitio, initiate revocation proceedings. The Controller register patents only after due diligence and adherence to procedural safeguards as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the revocation of a patent based on grounds of non-obviousness or lack of inventive step shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Order Appellate Authority. Such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said decision, and shall specify the orders sought for reversal or modification, along with concise reasons supporting the appeal. The Order Appellate Authority may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or set aside the order appealed against. Provided that if any party demonstrates to the satisfaction of the appellate authority that they were unable to file within the stipulated time due to circumstances beyond their control, an extension of time may be granted at the discretion of the Authority.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, publish a preliminary acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal, accompanied by a statement indicating the date on which objection may be lodged. Any person possessing a legitimate interest subject to this Act may, within four weeks from the date of such publication, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, specifying the grounds for opposing registration and providing supporting documentation as prescribed herein. The Registrar shall promptly acknowledge receipt of the notice of opposition and transmit a copy thereof to the applicant for registration. Failure to comply with the stipulated format or payment of the requisite fee renders the registration notice invalid. Further, any subsequent amendment to the grounds stated in the initial notice requires prior consent from the Registrar.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a ‘producer’ shall be deemed to be the individual or legal entity responsible for the creation and initial fixation of an audio-visual work. This determination shall include, but not be limited to, those directly involved in directing, filming, editing, and sound recording processes. An applicant claiming status as producer must submit with their application a sworn affidavit detailing their specific contribution to the production’s genesis and outlining the chain of rights ownership pertaining to the work. Provided that where multiple individuals or entities contribute significantly to the creation process, the Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claimant's designation as producer, ensuring clarity regarding copyright ownership and protection afforded under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a computer programme shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the calendar year of its first publication. Where a computer programme has been published without right or law, the author thereof shall be deemed to be the person who caused the publication to take place, and such person shall be liable for any infringement occurring after such publication. Any party infringing copyright in a computer programme shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner of the copyright, taking into account the benefit accrued to the infringer. Provided that, where an infringement is committed wilfully or for commercial gain, the court may award exemplary damages not exceeding ten times the amount of the actual damage established. The right to claim relief under this Act shall accrue within three years from the date the cause of action arises.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication alleging that such registration was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, may file an application with the Geographical Indications Registry. Such application shall specify the particulars of the alleged fraudulent conduct and provide supporting evidence demonstrating material deception influencing the initial grant. The Registry shall serve notice upon the applicant whose registration is challenged, affording them opportunity to respond under this Act. Should the Registrar find merit in the allegations, rectification may be ordered; however, any party aggrieved by such order or refusal thereof, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days. Such appeal shall be subject to the provisions of the Indian Penal Code relating to false evidence and conspiracy where relevant.

The registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall remain valid subject to its assignment or licensing under conditions as provided herein. Any registered proprietor desiring to grant a license conferring rights in respect of the layout-design may, through an instrument executed in the prescribed form and manner, assign such rights wholly or partially, irrevocably or revocably, to another party. Provided that where a registration is subsequently cancelled, any existing licenses granted prior to the cancellation shall remain enforceable for a period not exceeding three years from the date of the order cancelling registration registered, unless a case proceeding is initiated by the former proprietor seeking their termination. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification of such assignment or licensing agreement, record the details in the Register and issue certificates accordingly. Further, any alteration to the terms of an existing license requires prior approval from the Registrar.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings, plans or other representations depicting the said layout-design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars as are necessary for the proper examination of the application under this Act. Such particulars shall include a detailed description of the functionality and intended use of the integrated circuit. Where an application is deemed deficient in its form petition particulars, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the deficiencies within a prescribed period. Failure to comply with such notice may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein.

Where the Registrar is satisfied, upon review of objections filed under this Act against the registration of a literary work as an original composition, that such work incorporates substantial portions of pre-existing material without transformative alteration, he may direct the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating independent creation. Such evidence shall be deemed insufficient if it consists solely of testimony affirming authorship, and the Registrar shall prescribe guidelines for acceptable demonstrative proof. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of notification of the order. The appellate tribunal’s determination regarding whether a work is prescribed or not shall be final, subject to further judicial review on grounds limited to jurisdictional error.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any disclaimers required under this Act; provided that such refusal shall not prejudice any subsequent application filed by the applicant incorporating the same mark but omitting the disclaimer. Where an application register proprietor seeks to alter the particulars relating to ownership or address appearing in the Register, they shall submit a request in the prescribed form and along with the requisite fee. The Registrar may require verification of the information provided, subject to satisfying themselves that the proposed alteration does not contravene any provisions of this Act or the Marks Act 1999. Any such alteration shall be recorded in the Register and notified as per regulations framed by the Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any individual or entity possessing the exclusive right to a computer programme shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating thereto. Such licenses may encompass, but are not limited to, reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public display of the computer programme, as determined within the license agreement. Assignment of ownership in a computer programme shall require execution of a written instrument, duly attested by at least two witnesses, specifying the scope of transfer and any associated warranties. A licensee may further sub-license rights granted under this Act, provided that such sub-licensing does not contradict or diminish the original terms stipulated within the primary license agreement. Any modification to a computer programme undertaken by a licensee shall remain subject to copyright protections as provided herein, unless explicitly waived in writing by the owner of the intellectual property.

Where a patent invention is, after grant, found to infringe upon prior usage or knowledge existing within India, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date of sealing of the patent and require demonstrable proof of continuous use or public acknowledgement predating the patent application’s filing date. The court may, after affording the patentee an opportunity to be heard, determine whether the alleged prior usage constitutes a valid defense against infringement claims. If infringement is established based on such prior usage, the court shall have the power to grant relief including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the patentee from enforcing their rights and awarding damages proportionate to the losses suffered by the aggrieved party as provided herein.
