An appeal against an order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a layout design may be made to the Layout Design Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The appellant shall, along with the memorandum of appeal, pay such fee as may be prescribed under this Act. Provided that if the Appellant demonstrates satisfactory cause for failing to comply with the time limit specified herein, the Tribunal may entertain the appeal. The Tribunal shall give notice to the Registrar and afford him an opportunity of being heard. Subject to compliance with all applicable regulations regarding procedural fairness, the tribunal’s decision on any such appeal is final. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Layout Design Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to a High Court.

A specification patent shall disclose the matter in respect whereof protection is sought with sufficient particularity to enable the subject matter to be made or used by any person skilled in the art; provided that where the invention relates to varieties registered under this Act, the specification shall clearly identify such registered varieties and detail the characteristics distinguishing them from existing cultivars. The term "specification" as employed herein includes all drawings, claims, and abstract forming part of the patent application. Further, a specification shall not contain any matter which is extraneous to the claimed invention or which would unduly obscure the understanding thereof by a person skilled in the art.

Where an applicant seeks to amend the filing specification matter after the publication of the patent application under this Act, such amendment shall only be permissible if it clarifies or explains the originally claimed invention and does not introduce any new subject matter beyond what is adequately supported by the original disclosure. Any proposed alteration that substantially broadens the scope of protection sought will be deemed to contravene the principles of novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from a third party regarding such amendment, require the applicant to submit an evidence affidavit verifying the consistency between the amended specification and the original disclosure. Failure to satisfy the Controller’s requirements or providing a false statement in the affidavit shall render the application liable for rejection.

The proprietor of a registered copyright design shall be entitled to sue for and recover damages suffered by him by reason of an infringement of his design. Such damages may include loss of profits resulting from the infringing use, as well as any expenditure reasonably incurred by the proprietor in taking action against the infringer. Where an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the design has been granted, the measure of damages shall be such sum as the Court deems just and proportionate to the harm suffered, subject to the principle that the plaintiff must demonstrate a causal link between the infringement and his loss. The Court may also award costs in favour of the prevailing party under this Act. Provided that any claim for damages arising from copyright design infringement must be brought within three years from the date of discovery of the infringement.

A practitioner person registered under this Act shall be deemed to possess specialized knowledge relevant to the assessment of infringement claims pertaining to semiconductor integrated circuit layout designs. Any application for registration as a practitioner person must include detailed particulars regarding their qualifications, experience in intellectual property law, and any prior disciplinary actions taken against them by professional bodies. The Controller may require such applicant to appear before an examining officer at a time and place specified in the notice, and tender evidence substantiating the claims made in the application. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, a practitioner person registered under this Act is obligated to maintain records of all consultations undertaken and make them available for inspection by the Controller upon request. This provision applies without prejudice to any confidentiality agreements entered into independently by the practitioner person.

The Registrar shall prescribe the form and content of applications for registration of service marks relating to financial services. Such applications must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the particulars furnished therein and confirming that the applicant is duly authorised to use the proposed mark in connection with the specified services. The application, once submitted, shall not be processed until all prescribed fees have been remitted through the designated electronic payment gateway or as otherwise directed by notification issued by the Registrar. Any alteration to the service description or class of goods and services indicated in the initial application requires prior approval from the Registrar obtained in the authorised prescribed manner, subject to a further fee being paid. The Registrar may require additional documentation demonstrating ongoing compliance with regulatory requirements applicable to financial institutions.

Applications for patents relating to pharmaceutical products shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding patentability as provided herein. An application concerning a pharmaceutical product may be rejected if it is determined that the invention was not novel or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge. The Controller General may, upon receiving representations from interested parties, including generic drug manufacturers and consumer protection groups, direct the examination branch to undertake a supplementary assessment regarding the inventive step involved in such inventions. Evidence pertaining to clinical trial data and bioequivalence studies shall be considered relevant during this process. Any decision made by the examining officer concerning the patentability of a pharmaceutical product is subject to review by an appellate authority as provided under this Act, ensuring due consideration for public interest concerns.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods attributable to its origin. Where any person believes that the acceptance of an application for registration is erroneous, or that any registered geographical indication is being used in contravention of this Act, such person may, relating plaintiff forthwith to the Geographical Indications Registry, file a representation against the proposed registration or the existing registration. The Registry shall consider such representations and provide an opportunity for all interested parties to be heard under this Act. Any decision made by the Registry regarding a representation is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license to use such mark, and incorporates within the terms thereof provisions relating to quality control measures for goods bearing the mark, any assignment of that license shall be subject to the condition that the assignee undertakes to maintain those same quality control standards as were stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Failure to adhere to these conditions may result in a revocation of the assigned license by the grantor. Furthermore, where an entity knowingly uses a false trade description relating to goods or services offered under a licensed trademark, representing them as originating from, or being approved by, the proprietor without due authorization, such actions shall be deemed a violation under this Act and render the offending party liable for damages. The proprietor may also seek injunctive relief to prevent further misrepresentation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application may be made to the Controller by any person seeking authorization for a compulsory licence export of a patented invention. Such application shall specify the patented product, the intended exporting nation, and the quantity proposed for export, demonstrating reasonable attempts to secure a voluntary license from the patentee. The Controller shall consider whether the patented invention addresses an unmet need in the importing country and if the patentee has not granted a voluntary licence within a reasonable period. A notification of such application shall be served upon the patentee, who may submit objections. The Controller’s decision regarding the compulsory licence export shall be recorded and published as provided herein.

An application constituting a convention application shall be deemed to comply with the requirements of novelty and inventive step only if it satisfies conditions prescribed under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates that the earlier application was filed in a designated convention country. The time period for determining compliance with these requirements shall run from the date of filing the earliest application made by the applicant or any person who was the true and first inventor. Further, where an international preliminary examination is requested under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the determination of inventive step may be deferred pending the outcome of such examination, subject to regulations framed for this purpose. The Controller may require submission of certified copies of prior applications as evidence supporting compliance with these stipulations.

Any aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright under this Act may appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of order, provided that the appellate tribunal shall not be bound by the decisions or findings of any lower authority. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during such an appeal shall render it inadmissible. The Tribunal may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Any person found guilty of wilful infringement shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding ten times the actual damages suffered by the copyright owner, or in default of payment, imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Applications for registration of designs shall be examined by the Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act, who shall verify that the design complies with all requirements pertaining to novelty and originality as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence and specimens as the Adjudicating Officer may deem necessary to ascertain these qualities. Where an objection is raised concerning prior publication or a similar registered design, the Adjudicating Officer shall provide the applicant an opportunity for written response and presentation of counter-evidence. Decisions regarding registrability are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Adjudicating Officer’s determination on matters of fact relating to design features shall be final, barring appeals based solely on legal errors.

Where a patent is granted under this Act and subsequently revoked by order of the Controller, any person aggrieved by that revocation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear such appeals expeditiously and may allow the appeal, substituting its own order for that of the Controller, or dismiss the appeal. If a patent is revoked and the appellant fails to demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing they would have obtained a patent but for an error apparent on the face of the record, they shall be liable to pay costs incurred by the respondent in defending the revocation proceeding. Further, any party who has knowingly made false statements or withheld material information during the patent process is subject to penalties as provided herein and may be ordered to account for profits derived from the infringing activity.

An appeal arising from any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or concerning rectification proceedings, shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear and dispose th appeal upon such evidence as it deems relevant, affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard. Any party intending to challenge a decision made by the Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that decision. A required registrar person shall furnish necessary records to the Tribunal for its consideration in adjudicating any appeal under this Act.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by a detailed report prepared by an authorized institution, specifying the essential characteristics of the variety and demonstrating its stability and reproducibility across multiple generations. The Authority may require further testing or data submission if it deems the initial report insufficient to ascertain these qualities. Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections from any person claiming rights or interest in the variety. Any objection received must be substantiated by documentary evidence and submitted within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. The Authority shall then provide an opportunity for both the applicant and the objector to present their case during a hearing. Following such proceedings, the Authority’s decision regarding registration of the denomination variety shall be final.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association, subject to the provisions relating to acquired distinctiveness. The applicant shall have the right to appeal such refusal under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. Further, where a trade mark is registered following provisions act in relation to prior use, the Registrar may require the registration proprietor to submit evidence establishing continued use of the mark for a period not exceeding five years from the date of registration. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the trade mark vulnerable to expungement upon application by an interested party. The Registrar’s decision on any appeal under this Act is final, provided that it is subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a proposed geographical indication, alleging that the said indication does not relate exclusively to the goods or services with which it is sought to associate it, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to present evidence demonstrating such exclusive relation. The objector may then submit a counter-statement rebutting this evidence. If, after considering all submissions and any expert opinions obtained under this Act, the Registrar remains unconvinced that the geographical indication relates genuinely and exclusively to the specified goods or services, registration shall be refused. Any party aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication, presenting arguments demonstrating compliance with the requirements for registration as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, refusal, modification, or revocation of registration of a registered breeder variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Such an appeal shall lie irrespective of whether the decision concerns the validity of any claim made in respect of novelty, distinctiveness, stability, or uniformity required for registration under this Act. The Appellate Board may, while hearing appeals, direct the Registrar to undertake further examination into any matter relevant to the determination of rights concerning a registered breeder variety. Further, where data pertaining to a registered breeder variety is temporarily stored as transient incidental storage during digital transmission, that storage shall not be deemed an infringement of breeders’ rights as provided herein.

Where a patent has expired by virtue of the effluxion of time as provided herein, any person aggrieved by reason of an infringement of the patent during its term may institute proceedings for damages against the patentee. Such proceedings shall be subject to the limitation period of three years from the date the cause of action arose. The measure of damages recoverable shall reflect the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the patentee lawfully licensed the invention, or the patentee’s profits attributable to the infringement, whichever is the greater amount. Provided that, in determining such profits, due account shall be taken of any expenditure incurred by the patentee which directly relates to the exploitation of the patented invention. The right to claim damages relating to published expiry shall not extend to actions predicated on matters arising after the date of publication.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated to the Controller, through documentary evidence and testimony, that the claimed invention was previously employed in any commercial activity within India, notwithstanding its non-disclosure to the public. Provided that, such demonstration must establish that the use constituted exploitation of the invention and not merely incidental operation. The burden of proving prior use shall rest upon the applicant challenging the patent’s validity. Further, where a registered trademark is affixed to goods manufactured utilizing the challenged process, the evidence presented must also address any deceptive or misleading implications arising from such mark use. Appeals against decisions under this provision may be made to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The author of a computer program shall retain all rights pertaining to authorship under this Act unless such rights have been explicitly assigned or licensed. Where an assignment is made, it may be absolute or subject to limitations as agreed upon between the assignor and assignee. An exclusive licensee, having received a license granting them sole right to exploit certain copyright works, shall be deemed for all purposes relating to enforcement of those rights to be the author in relation to the specific acts licensed. This provision does not prejudice the original author’s ability to grant further licenses concerning non-licensed aspects of their work. Any subsequent assignment or license granted by an exclusive licensee shall require express written consent from the original author, provided that such consent may be withheld only for demonstrable reasons relating to artistic integrity and commercial viability.

For the purposes of this Act, "tea" with reference to a geographical indication means Camellia sinensis (L.) O. Kuntze, or any variety or hybrid thereof, cultivated for its leaves or buds and processed for infusions; and “Darjeeling tea” shall mean tea exclusively produced in specified areas within the Darjeeling district, including but not limited to areas situated at an elevation of not less than two thousand feet above sea level, as notified by the Central Government. The Registrar may register said geographical indication if satisfied that it is used to identify goods originating from such area and possesses qualities or characteristics attributable exclusively to the influence of the environment, including natural factors and human craftsmanship.

Where an invention is subject to a patent granted under this Act and concerns a process for producing a substance intended for use, or produced in, the food industry, the published expiry period shall be calculated from the date of first commercial exploitation of that substance. Provided that, if the patentee fails to provide satisfactory evidence demonstrating such commercial exploitation within six months of an appeal against a pre-grant opposition under this Act being dismissed by the Appellate Board, the Controller may, subject to due process and affording the patentee an opportunity for hearing, deem the invention not commercially exploited and recalculate the published expiry period accordingly. Any party aggrieved by such a determination may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days of notification of the order.

An applicant seeking registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication shall demonstrate, through documented evidence, continuous and verifiable adherence to the quality standards prescribed by the consortium representing the collective interest in the indicated good. Such evidence must detail compliance with production methods, processing techniques, and any other relevant criteria outlined within the product specification document currently maintained by the consortium. The Registrar may require further verification from independent assessors appointed by the consortium to ascertain ongoing conformity. An authorised user’s rights are subject to revocation if they fail to maintain these standards or act in a manner detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication, as determined under this Act and following due process.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Agriculture Commissioner under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising out of orders relating to revocation of registration or opposition proceedings, and any other matter as provided herein concerning plant variety rights. Subject to just cause shown, failure to file an appeal within the stipulated time shall be deemed a waiver of the right to seek redressal. Furthermore, where infringement of registered plant breeder’s rights is established, the Board may order remedies including damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the claimant and account of profits made by the infringer. The layout design registered in connection with the protected variety shall also be afforded protection against unauthorized use.

Where a trade mark is registered in accordance with this Act, the Registrar may, upon application by any interested party and after affording due opportunity for hearing, direct that a manufactured notification specifying the geographical origin of goods bearing the trade mark be affixed to such goods or their packaging. Such direction shall not be issued unless it is demonstrated that use of the trade mark creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the actual place of manufacture. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to a manufactured notification may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein. The Board’s decision shall be final.

For the purposes of this Act, “circumstances application advertised” means the period commencing from the date on which notice of acceptance of an application for registration is first published under this Act and concluding thirty days thereafter. During such circumstances application advertised, any person claiming by use as a prior right shall be entitled to file a notice of opposition. The Registrar may, subject to prescribed conditions, extend the duration of the circumstances application advertised where satisfied that representations concerning the trade mark have been made to the public before the date of publication of acceptance. Such extensions shall not exceed sixty days in aggregate.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from any order passed by the court registrar refusing registration of an indication or revoking a registered geographical indication, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar may entertain an application for rectification of a register on grounds including newly discovered facts demonstrating consumer confusion arising from use of a similar sign, but such applications are subject to review by the court registrar before being referred to the Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by an interlocutory order passed by the court registrar in proceedings relating to registration or revocation may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within thirty days, and the appellate authority shall determine whether the order was demonstrably erroneous.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the class or classes to which the invention relates and a full description of the invention, including all drawings necessary to understand it. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the nature and scope of the claimed invention, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign an official filing date and record the details in the prescribed register. Any person claiming inventorship under this Act must provide documentation substantiating their contribution to the conception of the act patent. The Controller may reject an application if it is found to be deficient in clarity or completeness as per guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Any person who uses, without due cause and after notice from the Register of Geographical Indications, a sign that is identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication for goods of the same class shall be deemed to have committed an infringement. Such use includes, but is not limited to, applying the sign to goods, offering or exposing them for sale, using them in advertising, and importing or exporting them. Provided that, where the alleged infringing activity constitutes fair use under established principles of trade practice, as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority, no action shall be taken under this Act. The Register may, upon receiving a complaint regarding potential infringement registered geographical indications, issue directions to cease such activities subject to compliance with due process.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association, cooperative society, producer group, or individual engaged in the production, processing, and/or supply of goods claiming such protection. The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application, issue a public notice inviting objections from interested parties within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit their response within one month thereafter. Following consideration of all submissions, if the Registrar is satisfied that the indication is distinctive and conforms to the requirements as provided herein, he or she shall proceed with registration. Upon registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall record particulars including the registered proprietor, which may be an assignee where ownership has been transferred in accordance with applicable law. The geographical indicati registered shall then be deemed protected under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rectification of a registered trade mark, entertain an action for removal of entries on the register if it is demonstrated that the *mark registered manner* has become non-distinctive through reason of subsequent use by other parties. Such applications shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the alleged loss of distinctiveness, including consumer surveys and market analysis reports submitted in triplicate. The Registrar shall provide a copy of such application and supporting documentation to the proprietor of the trade mark for comment within thirty days of receipt. Any response from the proprietor may include counter-evidence refuting the claim of non-distinctivity. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall issue an order either rectifying the register or dismissing the application, providing detailed reasons for the decision. Appeals against such orders are permitted to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

The use of a certification trade mark shall be permitted only by bodies duly recognized under this Act and possessing demonstrable expertise within their respective fields. Any entity utilizing a certification trade mark without such recognition, or employing it to falsely represent conformity to specified standards, shall be liable for damages proportionate to the misrepresentation caused and subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to a certification trade mark requires prior approval from the relevant recognizing authority; failure to obtain this approval renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Authority. The Registrar may, sua bonâ fide, initiate proceedings against any body found in violation of these provisions and impose fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered Geographical Indication owner may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication in connection with goods for which it is registered, provided that such license shall be documented in writing and specify the territory and duration of the granted rights. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication, including by way of mortgage or pledge, shall also be recorded as per the prescribed manner. Further, any licensee or assignee may sub-license or assign their respective rights subject to the terms stipulated in the original license or assignment agreement. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing all licenses and assignments granted relating to registered Geographical Indications, including particulars of the parties involved and the scope of such authorizations; patent means patent as defined under the Patents Act, 1970, will be considered in assessing potential conflicts.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication has been filed, and the Registrar deems it necessary to ascertain the views of interested parties regarding the distinctiveness of the goods or services associated with the proposed indication, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the Official Gazette. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the application, including the name of the notice applicant and a description of the geographical area sought to be protected. Any person having a lawful interest may, within the period specified in the notice, submit objections or representations to the Registrar. The defendant geographical indication holder shall be deemed to have a lawful interest for the purposes of this provision. Objections received shall be considered by the Registrar and an opportunity afforded to both the applicant and objector to present their case under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "infringement" shall include the use of a registered trademark in relation to goods or services identical or metamerically similar to those for which the mark is registered, without authorization from the proprietor. Such use shall be deemed an act of infringement irrespective of any demonstrable intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers, provided that where such use occurs due to honest and reasonable belief in a right to do so, the offender may be subject to innocently punishable imprisonment not exceeding three months. Nothing herein shall prevent a court from considering whether a patent shall be granted for an invention incorporating elements of a registered trademark.

An application for registration of a design relating to an article shall be deemed invalid under this Act if it incorporates elements derived from a pre-existing invention, irrespective of whether such invention is currently protected by patent. The Controller may require the applicant to demonstrate that any incorporated element constitutes a novel and non-obvious modification of the original inventive concept, sufficient to warrant separate design protection. This requirement shall apply particularly where the application claims novelty based on aesthetic variations of a functionally defined article. For the purposes of determining such validity, the assessment of whether an element represents a genuine clause invention will consider its contribution to the overall character and appearance of the registered design.

Where an application for patents contains claims relating to a method or process, and it is demonstrated to the Controller that the claimed invention incorporates a novel clause invention which, if implemented, would result in the production of a substance already known to be used as a pharmaceutical ingredient, the patent may be granted subject to the inclusion of measures reasonably designed to prevent abuse of the exclusive rights conferred. Such measures shall include, but are not limited to, limitations on the scope of the claims and stipulations regarding licensing arrangements for third parties engaged in research or development related to that substance. The Controller may require the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating the non-infringing nature of the claimed process with respect to existing pharmaceutical formulations as provided herein. Failure to comply shall render the patent liable to revocation under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a certify goods trade mark shall furnish with the application a detailed specification of the goods or services in relation to which certification is proposed, and such specification shall be deemed to define the scope of certification under this Act. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding the standards of quality, characteristics, or other attributes that the certified goods must possess, provided that these criteria are objectively verifiable and do not relate to trade marks themselves. Any person claiming rights in relation to a registered certify goods trade mark may apply to the Registrar for rectification if it is used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial competition. The registrar shall consider any opposition filed against registration of such marks based on likelihood of confusion with existing marks.

For the purposes of this Act, a layout design is deemed to have been “entered register disclosed” when particulars relating to such layout design, including but not limited to its title, name and address of the claimant, and a copy of the relevant documentation as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, are published in the Official Gazette. The chairperson shall ensure that such publication occurs within thirty days of the registration being completed. Further, any person may inspect the register entry so disclosed at the office of the Registrar. This disclosure does not prejudice any right to confidentiality otherwise enjoyed by the claimant as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of a patent, or the rectification of a specification claim, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall have power to entertain appeals under this Act and shall pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable by way of fine. Further, any party seeking enforcement of a patent granted under this Act may apply to the relevant High Court for appropriate remedies in cases of infringement, provided that such application is made within three years from the date of the order appealed against.

For the purposes of this Act, “basic registration” shall mean the initial entry of a mark onto the Register of Trade Marks, signifying its protection under this Act. A basic registration confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior conflicting rights as provided herein. An application for basic registration must include a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may refuse a basic registration if the mark lacks distinctiveness or is otherwise objectionable under this Act.

Any person who, knowing that any information relating to the invention has been obtained in pursuance of this Act, communicates such information to any other person without authorization shall be liable for damages as determined by the High Court. An applicant seeking patent protection under this Act may elect to file an application patent cooperation request, provided that such election is made within the time limits prescribed herein and subject to compliance with all applicable international regulations. Failure to adhere to these timelines will render the cooperative request void ab initio. The Controller shall have power to impose a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees but not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees on any party found in violation of this provision, without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act.

A registered trade mark owner shall have recourse under this Act where another party intentionally utilizes a sign in commerce that creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Such utilization constitutes falsify trade mark if the infringing sign incorporates elements substantially identical to the distinctive characters of the registered mark, or combines those elements with other signs in a manner which produces such confusion. Provided that, where the use is solely for descriptive purposes relating to the characteristics of the goods or services and does not suggest any trade connection with the proprietor, it shall not be deemed an act of falsify trade mark as provided herein. Further, this provision applies irrespective of whether the infringing party had knowledge of the existence of the registered trade mark.

The term "publication," for the purposes of this Act, shall mean the reproduction of a work in tangible form and its dissemination to the public, whether through sale, distribution, rental, lending, or any other means that makes it accessible to members of the public beyond a limited circle of individuals present at the time of communication. A work shall be deemed published when such copies have been made available for use or enjoyment by the public. Any person claiming copyright in a work prior to its publication may register their claim with the designated office, submitting prescribed particulars and supporting documentation as provided herein. Such registration shall not, however, confer any additional rights beyond those already vested under this Act. The Registrar of Copyrights may require further evidence to substantiate the claim and may reject the application if it finds that the work has already been published or that the claimant lacks sufficient title.

Where any person without leave of the Controller makes, uses, sells, or offers to sell, or imports for sale, any patented article, or attempts so to do, knowing it to be an infringement patent, such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence. This determination is subject to the proviso that use solely for purposes directly related to research and development, conducted without commercial exploitation, does not constitute infringement. Further provided that a party demonstrating prior use of the patented invention in India before the date of application for the patent may petition the Controller for equitable relief, but shall remain liable for any subsequent infringing activity. Any individual convicted under this provision may be subject to a punishable imprisonment term extending up to three years and a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an interest in a patent, or who is desirous of obtaining a license to exercise a right conferred by a patent, may apply to the Controller for registration of an assignment or a license. Such application shall specify the details of the assignor and assignee, or licensor and licensee, as the case may be, including their addresses for communication. The Act 1970 extends to cover situations where such assignments or licenses are granted outside India, provided that the patent itself relates to an invention applicable in India. Further, any assignment shall include a description of the right assigned, whether it is sole or partial and for specific territories. Consideration paid for the grant of a license shall be disclosed in the application, and may be subject to review by the Controller to ensure fairness and transparency under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall contain, as petition particulars contained therein, a detailed description of the layout-design, including its intended function and any relevant manufacturing processes employed. Such particulars must specify the name and address of the applicant claiming ownership of the design, along with proof of such claim, subject to verification by the Controller. The application shall also include copies of the layout-design in a format prescribed as rules made under this Act. Provided that where the integrated circuit incorporates elements previously registered or claimed elsewhere, these prior registrations must be explicitly disclosed within the petition particulars contained. Failure to provide complete and accurate information may result in rejection of the application.

Applications for the registration of offices trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Every application shall contain a clear representation of the mark distinguishing it from any other mark registered under this Act or applied for, and shall state the goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the mark. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to determine whether an application is complete and complies with the provisions herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a filing date. Objections to the acceptance of any trade mark for registration may be raised by any person claiming an interest in a similar mark already registered or applied for under this Act within the time specified. The Registrar shall consider such objections and issue a decision as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "International Bureau" means the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization, and references to the International Bureau shall be construed as references to that body acting in its capacity under the Madrid Protocol. Any communication required or permitted to be sent to the Trade Marks Registry may, subject to any rules made by the Registrar, be transmitted electronically to the International Bureau for onward transmission. The Registrar shall cooperate with the International Bureau in matters relating to international registration of trade marks as provided herein and shall furnish such information as it deems necessary for the proper functioning of the system under the Madrid Protocol.

Any aggrieved party claiming to have suffered damages as a result of an infringement of copyright under this Act may institute proceedings before the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall, upon hearing all parties involved, determine the extent and nature of such damages, taking into consideration factors including the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing acts occurred with the owner’s consent, any profits realized by the infringer as a consequence of the infringement, and the flagrancy of the violation. Provided that, in assessing damages, the Tribunal shall not award sums exceeding an amount equivalent to three times the actual damage sustained or, where such damage cannot be readily ascertained, an amount deemed just and equitable under the circumstances. The decision of the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to appeal to a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the infringement occurred.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses permitting the use of their trade mark for purposes identifying goods, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the trade mark and the specific classes of goods covered by the license. A license granted under this Act shall be assignable along with the underlying trade mark registration, provided that notice of such assignment is filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the transfer. Any subsequent use of the trade mark by the assignee shall be deemed to be authorized by the original proprietor until such time as the assignment is formally registered. The Registrar may require proof of consent from the original proprietor before registering an assignment involving a license agreement.

For the purposes of defining “breeder’s exemption” as provided herein, a farmer shall be deemed to have exercised breeder's exemption if, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act, they are engaged in activities relating to the propagation and sale of plant variety material derived from seeds obtained by them. Such activities include multiplication of seeds for self-consumption or distribution amongst other farmers, and may extend to commercial sales where the farmer has not entered into a legally binding agreement restricting such actions. The term "derived" shall mean originating from a protected variety through subsequent generations, retaining substantially similar characteristics as defined under section 41 clause (b).

An application for rectification of a trade mark shall be entertained against an internationally registered trade mark where India has been designated only if the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the existence of such registration within Indian territory. The proprietor of the internationally registered trade mark shall, upon receipt of notice of any such application, have thirty days to file a counter-statement denying the allegations and presenting relevant evidence in support of their rights. Failure to do so may result in the Registrar proceeding ex parte. Subject to this, rectification proceedings concerning an international registration referred shall be conducted according to procedures applicable to domestic trade mark applications, provided that any claim of prior use must be substantiated with documentary proof admissible under Indian law. The Registrar may order the cancellation or limitation of rights in respect of the internationally registered mark if satisfied that it is contrary to public interest or infringes upon existing Indian trade mark rights.

Subject to any agreement entered into prior to the filing of an application trade mark, the registered proprietor may grant a license to use the trademark for specific goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement and subject to conditions stipulated therein relating to quality control and permitted geographical territories. An assignment of the entire undertaking or a substantial part thereof shall include an automatic transfer of all pending applications trade mark related thereto, provided that the assignor provides written notification to the Registrar within thirty days of such assignment. The assignee may elect to continue the application as their own, or request its cancellation; failing either action, the application lapses after sixty days. Any sub-license granted under a primary license shall be subject to the terms and conditions of that initial agreement, as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, engages in any act restricted under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for damages. Such acts include, but are not limited to, reproduction, adaptation, or direct or indirect commercial exploitation of a protected layout-design. The registered patentee may pursue civil remedies including injunctions preventing further infringing activity and recovery of lost profits attributable to the unauthorized use. Further, where the infringement is proven to be willful, enhanced damages up to three times the actual loss suffered by the patentee may be awarded. Any employee or agent acting on behalf of an infringer shall also be held accountable for their contribution towards the violation, subject to mitigation based on demonstrable lack of knowledge.

Where a trade mark is ordered to be erased under this Act following a rectification action, the aggrieved party may appeal such erasure order to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of service of the order. Provided that, during the pendency of such an appeal, the appellate tribunal may, subject to just cause shown, grant an interim injunction restraining the respondent from utilizing or adopting the trade mark in question. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate tribunal concerning a refusal of an erasure order injunction may further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified under this Act. The court shall consider whether the balance of convenience warrants such restraint pending final determination.

Any person aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider only such grounds of appeal as are specifically pleaded and substantiated with relevant evidence; failure to do so will render the appeal inadmissible. Where a party fails to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal or any supporting documentation, the Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Furthermore, wilful suppression of material facts during appellate proceedings shall be deemed a cognizable offence and subject to prosecution under relevant penal laws as provided herein. The Controller’s decision on procedural matters relating to appeals is final.

Where a patentee elects to assign or license rights arising from an invention disclosed in a patent granted following a convention application shall, upon execution of such assignment or licensing agreement, provide written notification to the Controller within thirty days detailing the assignee’s name and address, or the terms governing the licensed use. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the initial convention application was filed prior to or subsequent to the commencement of this Act. The Controller may request further clarification regarding the scope of such assignment or license; failure to provide satisfactory information shall be deemed a breach of procedural requirements under this Act. Furthermore, any assignment or license granted in contravention of these provisions relating to convention applications shall be voidable at the option of the Controller, particularly where it impacts recognition of a well known trade mark associated with the invention.

The Register of Patents shall maintain a record of all patents granted and related documentation, including particulars of the inventor, assignee, and claims as detailed in the patent specification. Any modification to the registered details concerning a patent, such as a change in ownership or address for correspondence, must be formally notified to the Controller and duly recorded within thirty days of the occurrence of the alteration. The Register shall be open to public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any restrictions imposed under this Act relating to trade secrets or confidential information. An application may be made to the Controller seeking rectification of entries in respect patent granted if they contain errors or omissions. Such applications must specify the nature of the error and provide supporting evidence.

A denomination variety shall be eligible for registration subject to compliance with the requirements as provided herein. An application for registration may be filed by any breeder, being either an individual, institution or other legal entity and shall include a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical classification, origin, method of production, and expression of essential characteristics. The Authority shall assess whether the denomination proposed is distinct from existing denominations under this Act and does not comprise deceptive or misleading terms. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that the denomination has been consistently used for at least three years prior to the date of application. Any alteration to a registered denomination variety requires prior approval by the Authority, subject to guidelines issued as per rules made thereunder.

Where a broadcasting organisation provides a service incorporating distinctive signs or images used to identify its programmes or broadcasts, such signs and images shall be deemed capable of constituting a registrable trademark under this Act. The right to use and exclusively represent such a trademark shall extend to preventing the unauthorized use thereof in connection with identical or similar services offered by another entity, provided that the broadcasting organisation demonstrates genuine use of the mark within the territory for which registration is sought. Any person infringing upon these rights may be subject to remedies including injunctions restraining further infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the broadcasting organisation. A broadcasting organisation shall also have standing to pursue actions against those who falsely represent their services as affiliated with or endorsed by the organization, utilizing similar marks in a misleading manner.

Where an infringement action is brought before a competent court, and it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the court that the alleged infringer has knowingly exploited a patent without authorization, the court shall order damages equivalent to a percentage of the profits derived by the infringer from such exploitation. This percentage shall be determined based on factors including but not limited to the extent of the infringement, the willfulness thereof, and any attempts made by the infringer to mitigate harm following notification of the infringement. Further, where an attempt to negotiate a license has occurred, failure to reach agreement within a reasonable period shall be considered as evidence of unwillingness to engage in good faith, impacting the assessment of damages. The court may also order the destruction of infringing goods or materials.

For the purposes of this Act, a layout design consisting of three-dimensional features, topographical arrangements and spatial relationships of elements within an integrated circuit shall be deemed to include any variations thereof arising from alterations in size or ratio, provided that such variations do not substantially alter its overall appearance. This definition shall apply geographically to all territories within the jurisdiction of India, irrespective of where the original layout design was first conceived or manufactured. Further, a layout design incorporating elements derived from prior art shall be eligible for protection under this Act only if it demonstrates sufficient originality and inventive step as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending, and prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark exists, demonstrating continuous use in India before the date of such pending application, the applicant’s entitlement to registration shall be assessed with due consideration given to that pre-existing use. Provided that if the proprietor of the earlier mark subsequently applies for registration under this Act, and their application is accepted and registered, any amendment antedating registration by the later applicant shall not prejudice the rights established through such prior continuous use. Further, the Registrar may require evidence substantiating the extent and nature of said pre-existing use before making a determination as provided herein. The burden of proving such prior use rests upon the proprietor of the earlier mark.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act concerning the alleged improper geographical indication use relating to ‘Kashmir Apples’, direct the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive linkage between the goods and the specified territory. Such evidence shall include verifiable data on agricultural practices, unique environmental factors, and historical production records. The objector shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rebut such evidence through expert testimony; for this purpose, the Registrar may appoint independent scientific bodies possessing expertise in pomology and soil science. Any dispute arising from the assessment of said evidence may be referred to an appellate authority constituted as provided herein, whose decision shall be final subject to judicial review on limited grounds.

Where an appeal arises from an order passed by a civil court exercising original jurisdiction under this Act concerning allegations of unauthorized reproduction or distribution of cinematograph films, such appeal may be made to the High Court within one year from the date of the said order. Provided that, if the appellant is able to satisfy the appellate court that they were prevented by accident or some other exceptional circumstance from preferring the appeal within the aforementioned period, the High Court may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision of an instituted district court concerning the quantum of damages awarded for copyright infringement shall have the right to petition the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of that decision.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication, duly registered under this Act, may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the use of their registered indication for goods conforming to the standards established in the registration certificate. Such licenses shall specify the territory and duration of the permitted usage, as well as any restrictions on quality or presentation of the licensed goods. The proprietor retains full authority to assign such licenses, subject to prior written consent from the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses sufficient resources to uphold the integrity of the geographical indication. Any sublicense granted by a licensee shall be void unless expressly authorized in writing by the original proprietor and registered with the Registrar. Further, any use of the geographical indication without authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act, regardless of whether such use is intended to deceive or mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods bearing that indication.

For the purposes of this Act, "cosmetic" means any article intended for application to the human body or any part thereof for cleansing, beautifying, promoting growth, preventing or correcting defects, or otherwise altering its appearance; and includes articles used for manicuring or pedicuring. Such articles shall be deemed cosmetics irrespective of whether they are manufactured or imported. The term "cosmetic" excludes products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (23 of 1940), where such products primarily claim to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, prevent, or heal any disease or condition. Any substance added to a cosmetic as a preservative shall be deemed part of the cosmetic for the purposes of this definition.

The Controller may, upon receipt of a request from an applicant who has filed a patent application in India and subsequently deposited biological material under this Act, register such deposit as part of the subject matter of the invention. Such registration shall be conclusive evidence of the date of deposition for the purposes of determining priority under this Act. An applicant seeking registration under this provision shall furnish to the Controller a certified copy of the international search report, if available, and details regarding the designated institution where the biological material is deposited. The Controller may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary before proceeding with the registration. This process is subject to compliance with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure, as adapted by Indian law.

An applicant seeking registration of a service mark shall furnish detailed particulars regarding the nature of services rendered under the proposed mark. Such application must include representations of the mark, specifying whether it is word-based, figurative, or a combination thereof, along with a clear statement of the goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may require further clarification concerning any aspect of the application and shall provide an opportunity for the applicant to respond in writing. Regulations governing the use of the mark by authorized users must be submitted alongside the application; these regulations are crucial for ensuring consistent brand representation and preventing dilution under this Act. Any alteration to these mark regulations requires prior notification to, and approval from, the Registrar.

Where an applicant has filed an international application claiming priority from an Indian patent application, and a request for preliminary examination is received under this Act, the Controller shall proceed with the examination as if the international application were a domestic application. However, any communication relating to maintainability or novelty raised during the preliminary examination stage of the international application shall be deemed to be in response to the said application only, and not to the underlying Indian patent application. The applicant may appeal against such communications before a Bench constituted under sub-section (1) of section 105. Provided that any decision rendered by the Bench concerning an international application shall not prejudice the rights or remedies available to any party in relation to the corresponding Indian patent application, should it proceed independently.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Commercial Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Where a design is copied and reproduced for commercial purposes without authorization, constituting infringement of copyright design rights as provided herein, the proprietor of the registered design shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of reproduction or exploitation. Furthermore, damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty that could have been charged for the use of the design, or in cases of willful infringement, three times the amount of proven damage, may be awarded. The Court may also order the destruction of infringing articles and materials used in their production. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender liable to further penalties as determined by the Court.

Where a patent relating to a pharmaceutical process is granted under this Act, the Controller may, upon application by any person demonstrating substantial investment in research and development related to the patented invention, authorize the compulsory licensing of that process. Such authorization shall be subject to conditions ensuring fair remuneration to the patentee, determined based on prevailing market rates and accounting for the costs incurred in establishing and maintaining the patent process. The license may be granted for a period not exceeding five years, renewable only upon demonstration of continued need and adherence to stipulated royalty payments. Assignment of such compulsory licenses shall require prior approval from the Controller, who will consider the licensee’s capacity to manufacture and distribute the pharmaceutical product effectively and equitably across India.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of patent rights under this Act, they shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. Such injunctions may be granted by the relevant High Court, subject to just terms and conditions determined at its discretion, considering the balance between protecting the patentee’s exclusive privileges and ensuring reasonable access for others. The court may also order compensation for past infringements, calculated based on the loss suffered by the patent holder or a reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. Further, any act of inducement to infringe shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, rendering those who actively encourage such acts liable for remedies as provided herein. This includes providing technical assistance with knowledge that it will facilitate infringement; however, a mere suggestion does not constitute an act reference provision triggering liability.

Where an objection is raised by any person against the grant of registration for a particular plant variety, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the objector with an opportunity to present their respective arguments in writing and be heard, subject to such reasonable time limits as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The decision regarding whether or not to proceed with the application for registration variety shall be based on a careful consideration of all evidence presented, including any expert testimony relating to the distinctness, uniformity, and stability of the plant variety in question. Further, if the objection pertains to the provision of services related to the propagation or marketing of the registered variety, the Registrar may require both parties to submit detailed accounts of such activities for verification.

For the purposes of this Act, "permitted use" with respect to a registered trademark signifies the application of the mark upon goods or services as authorized under this Act. Such authorization may be granted through registration as a registered user, subject to conditions stipulated therein. A permitted use shall not extend beyond the scope of goods or services specified in the registered user’s certificate; any deviation from such specification constitutes unauthorized exploitation and is actionable accordingly. Further, a permitted use does not confer upon the registered user any right to challenge the validity of the trademark itself, as provided herein.

Where an applicant seeks rectification of a registered trade mark based on acquired distinctiveness, and the Registrar deems such evidence sufficient for preliminary consideration, notice of the application shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any party claiming an interest in the registered trade mark may, within sixty days from the date of publication, file with the Registrar a written counter-statement opposing the rectification. The applicant shall then have fourteen days to respond to the counter-statement filed. If the Registrar finds that the applicant has demonstrated acquired distinctiveness through extensive advertising and consumer recognition, he or she may proceed to consider the application further. An advertised acceptance of this finding by the respondent shall be deemed conclusive for purposes of procedural finality, subject to appeal under this Act.

An applicant seeking patent protection for an invention relating to a novel type of agricultural implement shall ensure that the date filing application accurately reflects the earliest possible priority claim. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical or substantially similar application in another jurisdiction, the date filing application under this Act shall be deemed to be the later of either the date of the initial foreign filing or the actual date of submission within India. Provided that, if the invention incorporates improvements relating to specific goods, such as enhanced harvesting efficiency for rice paddies, and these modifications were not disclosed in the prior foreign application, a subsequent examination may be undertaken to assess novelty. The Controller shall have discretion to reject the application should inconsistencies arise between the claimed priority date and the documented details of the invention’s development.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product containing a copied creators layout designs without the authorization of the owner shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalty fees as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Further, where an infringement is established, the court may order the destruction of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The owner of a creators layout designs shall have the right to apply to the civil court for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success. Penalties under this Act are without prejudice to any other action that may be brought against the infringer.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its genetic composition, lineage, and distinctive characteristics as determined through rigorous testing procedures prescribed under this Act. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may initiate an examination process involving expert assessors to ascertain whether the plant variety meets the criteria for novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. If, following such assessment, the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has fulfilled all requirements, a registration issued act shall be executed, granting exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization of the registered plant variety for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of application. Provided that any challenge to this registration may be brought before the Appellate Board within six months of publication in the Official Gazette.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a representation of the integrated circuit layout design and a statement specifying the name and address of the applicant. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars as are necessary for the proper examination of the application, including details regarding the date on which the layout design was first commercially exploited anywhere in the world. Where an objection is taken by the Controller under this Act concerning the novelty or originality of a layout design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in support of their claim. The determination of whether a layout design constitutes a novel and original *layout design commercially* is subject to the provisions regarding prior publication and use as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "office patent office" means the designated governmental body responsible for receiving, examining, and processing applications for patents, and for granting or rejecting such patents as provided herein. The functions of the office patent office shall include maintaining records pertaining to patent applications and granted patents, conducting searches relevant to novelty and inventive step assessments, and communicating with applicants regarding deficiencies in their submissions. An applicant whose invention is found to infringe upon an existing patent may be deemed to have committed an accused offence under this Act, subject to appeal before the appropriate appellate authority as prescribed.

Where an aggrieved party disputes the validity of a registered layout design and seeks revocation through appeal before the Intellectual Property Tribunal, the Tribunal may, subject to due process and affording the registrant opportunity for hearing, issue a register effect order. Such an order shall temporarily suspend the legal protections afforded by registration pending final determination of the appeal. The applicant seeking such relief must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood of success in establishing invalidity based on prior publication or other grounds as provided herein. Layout design vested rights of the registrant remain unaffected during this interim period, and the Tribunal may impose conditions to safeguard against irreparable harm should the appeal ultimately fail.

Any person who, having knowledge of the registration of a Plant Variety, commercially exploits such variety without authorization from the Registrar, or in contravention of the terms and conditions stipulated during registration, shall be liable to pay compensation determined by the Central Government. Such compensation may include damages sustained by the registered plant breeder, reasonable costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies, and an additional penalty not exceeding five times the value of the infringing exploitation. Further, any entity found guilty of repeated violations under this Act relating to crop sciences indian practices shall face suspension of their registration for a period as determined by the Registrar. The Central Government may issue directives regarding enforcement actions against those engaging in unauthorized propagation or marketing of protected plant varieties.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licensee is defined as a person to whom copyright in respect of a work has been exclusively assigned under a written agreement, or who is party to a license which confers upon them all rights normally enjoyed by the owner of copyright in that work, subject to any conditions specified therein. Such exclusivity shall extend to all acts permitted under this Act which are not expressly reserved for the assignor or licensor. An exclusive licensee shall be deemed to possess such title and interest as would accrue to an assignee had the copyright been formally assigned. Provided that nothing herein shall prevent the assignor from exercising rights not explicitly excluded by the license agreement.

Any person found to have reproduced or exploited a protected integrated circuit layout design without authorization shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five per cent of the plaintiff’s reasonable royalty losses, or one million rupees, whichever is greater. Furthermore, where such reproduction or exploitation demonstrably jeopardizes the interest of the security of India, as determined by the Central Government, the infringing party may also face prosecution under relevant penal provisions. The government shall have the power to grant patent protection for innovations incorporated within layout designs deemed critical to national technological advancement, provided that such grants do not conflict with existing obligations under this Act and are subject to rigorous review.

The Controller shall maintain a national register pertaining to all applications for patent concerning agricultural inventions, subject to compliance with subsection (2). An application shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to respond to any official communication within six months of its dispatch, or such extended period as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The register means register maintained in electronic form and accessible through the Controller’s designated online portal, where all relevant details concerning patent applications, including inventor information, claims, and examination reports, shall be publicly available. Any alteration to entries within the register must be authenticated by a duly authorized officer of the Patents Office and recorded with appropriate justification. The applicant shall ensure that all data submitted is accurate and complete; failure to do so may result in rejection under this Act.

The Registering Officer shall maintain an entry register pertaining to all applications filed under this Act seeking notification of intended use. Such entry register shall record, for each application, the date upon which the application was received, the particulars of goods or services in relation to which the mark is sought to be registered, and a statement confirming compliance with the requirements of section 9 regarding descriptiveness. The Registrar may, at any time, inspect the entry register maintained by the Registering Officer to verify adherence to prescribed procedures. Any alteration made to an entry within the entry register shall be authenticated by both the Registering Officer and a designated supervisory official, ensuring transparency in record-keeping as provided herein. Failure to maintain such a register accurately may result in penalties under this Act.

An international application patent, once granted, shall remain subject to assignment and licensing agreements executed prior to or subsequent to its registration, provided that any such agreement explicitly addresses the scope of rights transferred and royalties payable. The Controller may, upon receiving a formal request accompanied by requisite documentation demonstrating due diligence in identifying all assignees and licensees, issue certificates confirming the validity of these assignments and licenses for evidentiary purposes in legal proceedings. Furthermore, where an international application patent incorporates subject matter derived from pre-existing intellectual property held by third parties, the applicant shall ensure that appropriate license agreements are secured to facilitate commercial exploitation, failing which, remedies available under this Act pertaining to infringement may be invoked against the licensee. Any transfer of rights relating to an international application patent requires notification to the Controller within thirty days.
