Applications for patents relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs shall be made in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The Controller General, upon receipt of an application, shall furnish a date accorded patent to the applicant, which date shall serve as the initial point for determining priority under this Act. Where an application incorporates by reference any other document, the manner applications clause dictates that such incorporation must clearly identify and describe the referenced material within the application itself. Failure to adhere to this requirement may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment at the Controller General’s discretion. The prescribed form shall include a detailed description of the layout design, including its functionality and intended use. Any alteration to the described features after the date accorded patent requires notification and approval from the Controller General.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a proposed trade mark based upon its similarity to an earlier registered *name*, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for registration and to the proprietor of the prior registration. The applicant may, within such time as prescribed, file a counter-statement rebutting the grounds of objection. Upon receiving the counter-statement, the Registrar shall afford the proprietor of the prior registration an opportunity to submit a reply. Subject to any directions issued by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Registrar shall consider all submissions and determine whether the proposed trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion as regards the identity of goods or services. The decision of the Registrar may be appealed against under this Act.

Where two or more signs are applied for by an applicant for registration as trade marks, and it is established that such signs, though distinct, function to identify goods or services offered under a common enterprise or brand identity, the Registrar may, subject to due consideration of consumer perception and potential confusion, register them as separate trade marks. This power shall not be exercised if such registration would unfairly prejudice existing proprietors of similar marks. Any proprietor aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar registering signs as separate trade marks may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of that decision. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the distinctiveness of each mark is adequately protected and whether consumer confusion is reasonably likely to arise, taking into account all relevant circumstances presented during the appeal proceedings.

An applicant seeking protection through an application patent period exceeding twenty years from the date of filing shall furnish a declaration to the Controller affirming that the invention does not infringe any existing intellectual property rights. Failure to submit this declaration within three months of the application’s publication, as provided herein, renders the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any person demonstrating demonstrable prejudice due to an applicant's non-compliance may petition the relevant authority seeking redress and imposition of a monetary penalty, recoverable from the defaulting applicant. The Controller shall have discretion to waive this requirement in cases involving compelling circumstances, subject to recording reasons thereof.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall include a representation of the mark, which may be in the form of words only, or accompanied by a device or depiction. The Registrar shall examine each such application and, if satisfied that the mark is distinctive in its class and does not conflict with any existing registered trade marks or pending applications, unconditionally registrar shall proceed to accept the same for publication in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, where the applicant seeks registration of a colour as a trademark, they must furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. Any opposition filed under this Act against an accepted mark shall be heard by the relevant intellectual property tribunal, and the Registrar’s decision is subject to appeal.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall, as part of the prescribed application process, submit detailed schematics illustrating the physical arrangement of elements constituting the board use layout. These schematics must clearly delineate all layers and interconnects within the design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may require the submission of additional documentation or clarifications deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to originality and non-infringement under this Act. A relevant entry register shall be maintained by the Registrar, documenting each application received, including dates of filing, applicant details, and any correspondence pertaining thereto. The Controller shall provide a reasoned order for any rejection or modification proposed, which may be appealed before the Intellectual Property Tribunal as provided herein.

An applicant seeking to avail themselves of the Madrid Protocol system shall file an international application form within six months from the date of publication of their Indian trademark in the Trade Marks Journal, provided that such filing is made in respect of goods or services identical to those for which registration exists under this Act. Failure to adhere to this timeframe will render the international registration ineffective as against third parties who have acquired rights prior to notification under Article 34 of the Protocol. Any alteration to the list of goods and services specified in the international application form after its initial submission shall be deemed a material change, requiring fresh publication and potentially impacting priority claims. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the international registration or to demonstrate continued use of the mark internationally.

Where a trade mark is registered following an international application form filed under the Madrid Protocol, and opposition proceedings are initiated based on prior conflicting rights existing in India, the registration shall not be deemed invalid solely due to the absence of earlier use within Indian territory. Justified registration, in such circumstances, requires demonstration by the applicant that the adoption of the mark, despite lack of prior use, does not create confusion amongst consumers or otherwise unfairly prejudice the interests of those possessing pre-existing rights. The Registrar may require submission of evidence substantiating this justification, including market surveys and consumer perception studies. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall render the registration vulnerable to revocation under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding justified registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any person claiming title to the invention has suffered damage by reason of acts done during the term of the patent which but for the existence of the patent would have infringed a right vested in that person, such person may sue for damages against the patentee. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the benefit accruing to the claimant from the use of the invention as if the patent had never been granted. It is provided that an objection to the validity of the specification claimed claim may be raised by any interested party in proceedings before the Controller, and such objection shall be deemed to be a ground for revocation. The burden of proving the existence of such damage rests upon the claimant, subject to provisions regarding estoppel as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly furnishes false particulars for inclusion in the register, or who obstructs an officer authorised under this Act in the performance of his duties relating to the maintenance of the register, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. The Controller, upon receiving credible information regarding such false particulars or obstruction, may initiate suo moto proceedings against the offending party. Failure to comply with directions issued by the Controller in connection with rectification of erroneous entries within the prescribed timeframe shall attract daily penalties as determined under this Act. Furthermore, any deliberate misrepresentation affecting the rights of other patent holders will render the perpetrator liable for damages recoverable through civil action. The particulars comprising register are deemed sacrosanct and subject to rigorous verification procedures.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "design registry central" refers to the designated authority responsible for maintaining records pertaining to registered designs and related applications. The design registry central shall maintain a publicly accessible electronic database containing details of all registered designs, including but not limited to the name and address of the claimant, the date of registration, and a graphical representation of the design. Applications for registration shall be processed by officers appointed by the Central Government, subject to appeals being heard before an appellate tribunal as provided herein. The design registry central may issue certificates of registration in the prescribed form.

Any person seeking to register a certification trade mark shall furnish evidence demonstrating adherence to prescribed quality standards and operational procedures as determined by the relevant regulatory authority. Failure to maintain such standards or demonstrate compliance may result in suspension of registration and imposition of penalties not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. The Registrar, upon receiving a rectification register notice alleging misrepresentation or deceptive practices associated with a certification trade mark, shall issue a hearing notice to the proprietor. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding rectification may appeal under this Act within sixty days; wilful violation of conditions relating to a certification trade mark constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and fines as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “breeder complied provisions” shall mean the conditions stipulated within a Plant Variety Registration Certificate pertaining to the sharing of breeder’s material and derived varieties. These stipulations are binding upon any person conducting activities involving the registered variety, including but not limited to commercialization, propagation, or research. Failure to adhere to these breeder complied provisions, as determined by the Board under this Act, constitutes an infringement of the rights granted to the plant breeder. Such infringements may result in penalties and injunctive relief, provided that farmers’ rights relating to saved seed are unaffected.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar receives an objection under this Act within the prescribed period following publication of the acceptance thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, any person intending to oppose may file such notice electronically or in physical form at the designated office, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by regulations. The applicant for registration shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to respond to the objection and submit counterarguments or evidence in support of their application. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to the filing of an application registration notice may render it invalid. Further, any alteration to the proposed trade mark after acceptance requires notification to the Registrar and may necessitate re-examination.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an applicant seeking protection for a layout-design relating to alphabetical index goods shall provide detailed schematics and descriptions sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the design. The Registrar may require submission of physical samples where deemed necessary to ascertain conformity with submitted documentation. Disputes concerning the validity of a registered layout-design or the scope of its protection shall be referred to a Bench constituted under this Act, comprising not less than three persons possessing expertise in semiconductor technology and intellectual property law. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to such Bench. The decision of the Bench shall be final and binding, subject to further appeals as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication alleging that entry is erroneous or obtained through misrepresentation shall file an application before the Registrar. The Registrar may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, direct amendment or cancellation of the register as provided herein. An appeal from any order made by the Registrar under this Act lies to the Appellate Board. Where a geographical indication is used in contravention of this Act, the proprietor of the registration may institute suit for damages recoverable subject to such limitations as are prescribed. The functions registrar act includes the power to issue interim injunctions restraining such use pending final determination of the matter before the court or the Appellate Board.

The distribution of royalties collected by a copyright society shall be determined according to the terms of its constitution, provided that any dispute arising from the interpretation or application of those terms may be referred for resolution to an adjudicating authority constituted under this Act. Such adjudication shall consider representations made by both right owners and users whose interests are affected by the royalty distribution scheme. The copyright society shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all collections and distributions, accessible for inspection upon request by any aggrieved party seeking to challenge its actions. Any order passed by the adjudicating authority may be appealed against within a period of ninety days, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to their invention, they shall execute a written instrument detailing the scope of such license, including but not limited to territorial limitations, field of use restrictions, and royalty arrangements. Such instruments must be filed with the Controller within thirty days of execution; failure to do so renders the license unenforceable against third parties. The Controller may, upon application by any interested party, require further clarification regarding the terms of a license agreement. Patents shall entered in the Register detailing all assignments, transmissions, and licenses granted under this Act, along with the date of such actions and the names and addresses of the relevant parties involved. Any subsequent modification or revocation of a license must also be recorded as provided herein to maintain transparency and facilitate public access to patent information.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout design shall furnish with the application, a detailed technical description elucidating the functionality and intended purpose of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Where an application incorporates elements previously disclosed in publicly accessible publications, the applicant must provide evidence demonstrating substantial originality and inventive step beyond such prior disclosures. The layout design government shall be considered to have been infringed if any person without authorisation reproduces the registered layout-design for commercial purposes. Any alteration or adaptation of a registered layout design which substantially replicates its essential features constitutes infringement as provided herein.

Where an invention far claimed extends to a process for producing a substance intended for use or employed in the manufacture, preparation, or processing of a pharmaceutical product, the patentee shall be obliged to grant licenses under this Act upon such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Such terms shall include provisions ensuring non-discriminatory access and pricing within India, subject to reasonable compensation being paid to the patentee reflecting their research and development expenditure. Assignment of rights relating to such processes requires prior notification to the Controller, detailing the assignee’s commitment to upholding these licensing obligations. Further, any subsequent assignment must also be notified. The Controller may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, impose conditions on licenses granted under this Act to safeguard public health and welfare, provided that such conditions do not unreasonably prejudice the patentee's commercial interests.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any copyrighted work for transmission via radio or television signals shall obtain a license from the copyright holder or their designated agent. Such licenses shall specify the duration of usage, geographical territory covered, and the type of adaptation permitted, if any. The fees payable under these licenses may be determined through negotiation between the parties, provided that they are reasonable and reflect the value conferred by the broadcasting organisation’s transmission. Any assignment of copyright relating to a work previously licensed for broadcast shall require notification to the original licensor, enabling them to exercise rights of pre-emption as provided herein. Further, where a broadcasting organisation incorporates excerpts from multiple works into a single programme, it is deemed to hold a composite license encompassing all such materials, subject to limitations on subsequent commercial exploitation.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours subject to any restrictions deemed necessary by the Registrar to protect confidential commercial information. Applications for registration of index names shall be examined in accordance with established procedures and may be refused if they are deemed deceptive or likely to cause confusion with existing trademarks. The register shall clearly indicate the goods or services associated with each registered index name, along with the date of registration and any subsequent modifications or renewals as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration or rejection of an index name may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “patented process” shall mean any method or series of acts described in a claim of a patent, wherein such method or series of acts are novel and involve an inventive step as provided herein. A patented process includes, but is not limited to, industrial processes for manufacturing substances, compositions, or products; methods for treating materials to alter their properties; and techniques employed in agricultural production. Subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licenses under this Act, the use of a patented process shall be restricted unless authorized by the patentee. Any activity constituting an infringement of a patented process shall be actionable as per the remedies available under this Act.

A person seeking registration of a registered certification mark shall submit an application detailing the specifications for goods or services eligible for certification under the proposed mark. The applicant must demonstrate that they possess the requisite control over the certified characteristics, including but not limited to quality, origin, process, or other features as specified in the application. Such control shall be evidenced by legally binding agreements with producers and certifiers, ensuring adherence to prescribed standards. Certification marks may only be used on goods or services meeting these established criteria, and any deviation from those criteria constitutes a violation under this Act. The Registrar may require periodic audits of certification processes to verify ongoing compliance as provided herein.

A variety shall be deemed to be an essentially derived variety if, in the opinion of the Authority, it is clearly designated as such in the application for registration and meets all conditions stipulated under this Act. Such designation must explicitly state the predecessor variety from which derivation occurred and demonstrate that the subsequent characteristics result solely from techniques like selection, hybridization, or genetic modification, excluding any introduction of genes derived from non-variety sources. Provided that, if the applicant seeks to register a denomination for the essentially derived variety, it shall not be identical or confusingly similar to marks indications used in connection with the predecessor variety, as determined by the relevant intellectual property office. The Authority may require further documentation substantiating derivation claims and genetic analysis confirming absence of extraneous genetic material.

Where an application for a patent has been refused solely on the ground that the claimed invention lacks novelty, and subsequent evidence demonstrates that the prior art disclosure was rendered ineffective due to alterations introduced by an issued breeder who subsequently disseminated those altered materials without knowledge of the pending patent application, the Controller may, subject to just terms and conditions, order the restoration of the application for further consideration. Such terms shall include compensation to the applicant reflecting demonstrable commercial prejudice suffered as a result of the unauthorized dissemination. The determination of “just terms” shall consider the extent of the breeder’s contribution to the loss of novelty and any benefit derived therefrom. Provided that this remedy is only available where the applicant can prove, with reasonable certainty, that the alteration directly impacted the assessment of novelty under this Act.

Registration of a geographical indication for ‘Kashmir Apples’ requires annual maintenance fees to be remitted within thirty days of the anniversary of its registration, as provided herein. Failure to remit said fee shall render the geographical indication liable to removal from the Register of Geographical Indications. Any application for restoration following such removal must include payment of all outstanding fees and a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the original prescribed fee. The Registrar may, subject to due process, waive or reduce these fees in cases where demonstrable hardship is presented by the registered proprietor. Furthermore, any layout design vested in the consortium managing the ‘Kashmir Apples’ geographical indication shall be protected from unauthorized use unless accompanied by timely payment of the requisite fee paid fee.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or the entry of a mark on the Register of Trade Marks, shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against and failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, at any time, require the surrender of a certificate of registration if it is found that the mark was registered in contravention of provisions under this Act or through fraudulent means. Penalties for wilful violation of these provisions include fines up to one million rupees and imprisonment extending to three years. The marks registry established herein shall maintain records accessible only upon due process.

An application for registration as a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall include detailed specifications outlining the production methods employed within the defined territory. These specifications must demonstrate adherence to established practices and techniques traditionally utilized in cultivating, processing, or manufacturing the goods. The applicant shall provide documentary evidence substantiating the distinctiveness of the good’s qualities attributable solely to its origin; such evidence may comprise historical records, expert testimonies, or scientific analyses. Provided that the geographical indication does not denote any ingredient or component introduced outside the defined territory after initial production. Further, the application must confirm that the applicant represents a substantial proportion of producers whose interests are directly linked to the continued protection of this geographical indication.

Any person who, without due authorization from the copyright owner, makes, distributes, imports into India, or offers for sale any article embodying an infringing copy of a work protected under this Act, and such article is demonstrably employed for industrial application, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. The right holder may, subject to the provisions herein, seek injunctive relief against any party engaged in such infringing activity. Further, where the infringement involves commercial reproduction intended for profit, enhanced penalties as determined by the relevant judicial authority shall apply. Damages recoverable shall be assessed based on demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner.

An international registration shall be deemed to be in force as regards India only if, within three months of the date of receipt of a notice by the Trade Marks Registry from the International Bureau, the Registrar receives a certified copy of the request for extension and the particulars of any marks contained therein. The applicant shall pay such fee as may be prescribed under this Act upon submission of said certified copy; failure to do so within the stipulated timeframe will result in the application being deemed abandoned. Any alteration made to the list of goods or services specified in the international registration, following its extension, must comply with the provisions relating to trademark registrability as provided herein and shall not prejudice any existing rights under this Act.

Where a person aggrieved by any order made under this Act concerning the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent has suffered loss or damage as a direct consequence thereof, that person may institute proceedings seeking compensation. Such compensation shall be determined having regard to the prejudice caused and taking into account any undue delay in processing the application for patent. The Registrar General Plant Varieties shall provide all relevant records pertaining to the filing date of an application upon request from parties involved in such proceedings, subject to appropriate confidentiality safeguards as provided herein. Any applicant who knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses material information relating to the patent filed date may be liable to pay damages to any party demonstrably prejudiced by that misrepresentation. The right to seek compensation under this provision shall not prejudice other remedies available under this Act or general law.

An application for the cancellation of registration of a layout-design may be presented to the Controller by any person claiming an interest adversely affected by the said registration. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, and shall include all relevant documents or other evidence relied on in support thereof; provided that the mere existence of prior use of a similar integrated circuit layout-design does not, of itself, constitute sufficient ground for cancellation under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or evidence as deemed necessary. Upon receiving such an application, the Controller shall serve notice upon the registrant and afford them an opportunity to be heard, subject to the provisions regarding timelines as provided herein. Any order made by the Controller relating to cancellation registration is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

A registration issued act, in relation to a plant variety, shall be deemed to occur when an action undertaken by the registered holder directly impacts the rights conferred under this Act and is brought to the attention of the Registrar. Such actions may include, but are not limited to, unauthorized sale for commercial purposes, offering for cultivation without proper authorization, or making representations misleading regarding the genetic composition of the variety. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for the alleged wrongdoer to be heard before determining whether a registration issued act has occurred and what remedial measures, as provided herein, should be implemented.

Where an application for registration of a design is deemed likely to affect national interests, the Controller shall require the applicant to furnish security, the amount thereof being determined based on factors including the potential commercial impact and scope of the design’s claims. Such security shall be considered prejudicial security india if it is found that its forfeiture would compromise the sovereignty or integrity of India, or disrupt relations with a foreign state. The Controller may, at any time, demand further security from an applicant already providing such assurance, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing. Failure to comply with this requirement regarding the provision of adequate security shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

Any proprietor seeking to utilize a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services shall ensure such use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation concerning respect registered trade marks, initiate an inquiry into whether the said usage constitutes unfair competition under this Act. Provided that, any entity claiming infringement must demonstrate actual damage resulting from the unauthorized application of the mark. Further, where the proprietor has demonstrably altered the character or quality of the goods bearing the registered trade mark, such alteration shall be deemed a material change and may invalidate subsequent claims regarding identical usage.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register for each class of goods or services appearing in the Trade Marks Register. This register shall record particulars relating to entries made concerning trade marks, including but not limited to applications filed, advertisements published under this Act, and any alterations or amendments effected to existing registrations. The Registrar may prescribe the form and manner in which such relevant entry registers are maintained, provided that they allow for efficient retrieval of information pertaining to individual trade mark records. Any party seeking access to a relevant entry register shall submit a written request specifying the particulars required, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Registrar shall process requests promptly; however, confidential commercial information contained within the register may be redacted as deemed appropriate by the Registrar.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person aggrieved by a proposed trademark, provide such objector with a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for opposition and affording them opportunity to submit written arguments within sixty days. The applicant may then file a rejoinder addressing these objections, also within sixty days. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall right to determine whether the trademark is deceptively similar to any existing mark or conflicts with section 9, provided that such determination shall be based solely on the documentary evidence presented and without regard to oral testimony. Any party dissatisfied with the Registrar's decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of the order.

A trade mark shall be deemed to enjoy registration respect from the date of publication of acceptance under this Act. Such respect extends to any identical or confusingly similar signs used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, provided that such use is undertaken by a person who had knowledge of the prior registration. Where a proprietor utilizes a reference use mark—that is, a sign adopted solely for the purpose of indicating the source or intended purpose of goods—such utilization shall not constitute an infringement of the registered trade mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed and without prejudice to the rights of the registered proprietor to seek remedies under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "invention" means a new and useful art, process, manufacture or composition of matter; provided that it is patentable under this Act. An invention shall not include discoveries of scientific principles, merely the properties of living things, nor any method for treating diseases in human beings or animals unless such methods are formulated using novel techniques and compositions. The term "application" means a request made to the Controller for the grant of a patent, containing all particulars as may be prescribed; subject to which the applicant seeks to obtain exclusive rights under this Patents Act 1970.

Where any person, being aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the rectification of the Register, or by any other action taken by the Registrar affecting his rights as a registered proprietor trade, alleges that such order or action is without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider the alleged offence reason presented and may, after affording the parties an opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

An opposition to registration under this Act is deemed to exist when a registered proprietor or any other person interested in the reputation of a trade mark applied for, or of a similar mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, notifies the Registrar that they oppose the application. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use and acquired distinctiveness. The Registrar may require further particulars supporting the opposition within a prescribed timeframe. Failure to provide such particulars as provided herein may result in the rejection of the opposition. Any party affected by an opposition registration may appeal under this Act.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Such direction shall be given only if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s validity, supported by documentary evidence filed prior to commencement of trial. The Court shall provide the registered proprietor with an opportunity to file its response within thirty days from the date of such direction. Any determination made regarding the validity of the trade mark registration shall be final and binding only for the purposes of that particular prosecution. Further, this determination shall not prejudice any other proceedings concerning the same or similar matters under this Act or otherwise. The Court may, at any stage, set aside its earlier direction if it finds that the challenge to registration is frivolous or vexatious.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design, or concerning infringement proceedings, appeals to the Appellate Board, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. In determining whether infringement has occurred, the Board shall consider not only the literal similarity between the allegedly infringing layout-design and the registered design but also any substantial resemblance that creates confusion as to the origin of the goods or services. The Chairperson Appellate Board may issue directions for interim relief pending final adjudication. Further, where a denomination variety is involved in a claim of infringement, evidence establishing consumer perception shall be given significant weight.

Where any unauthorized recording means person infringes upon the copyright in a work, such person shall be liable to pay an account of profits derived from the infringing act, together with damages assessed by the Controller. The assessment of damages may take into consideration not only the retail price of copies made without authorization but also any loss suffered by the owner of the copyright as a direct result of the infringement. Further, where such unauthorized recording means person has acted fraudulently or recklessly in making the infringing copy, the Controller may award exemplary damages to deter similar conduct. An application patent shall not be granted for a method of circumventing technological protection measures employed by the copyright holder to prevent unauthorized access to works. Remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedies that may be available to the copyright owner in law or equity.

The Appellate Board shall be constituted by a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court and two other Members to be appointed by the Central Government, one of whom shall be a person having special knowledge and experience in copyright law. The Board may, subject to the provisions under this Act, hear and decide appeals from any order passed by an Adjudicating Officer. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are recorded for such delay. For the purposes of determining whether an invention means new, the Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the parties and apply principles of established jurisprudence. The decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any licensee operating under a license granted prior to such lapse shall be entitled to continue exercising the rights licensed to them for a period not exceeding six months from the date of the lapse. This entitlement is subject to the condition that the licensee files an application with the Controller seeking recognition of their continued right to practice the invention and provides evidence demonstrating substantial reliance on the license during its active term, including documented investments made in manufacturing or commercialization activities. The Controller may grant a temporary extension beyond this six-month period if satisfied that the licensee’s interests would suffer undue hardship due to the abrupt cessation of operations; provided that such extension shall not prejudice any subsequent application for patent restoration by the original patentee.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to copyright in a work, such license shall be deemed a contractual arrangement governed by principles of contract law, notwithstanding any provisions herein. The patentee transferring ownership of underlying technology essential for exercising those licensed rights may not subsequently assert claims that materially impede the exclusive licensee’s ability to exploit said copyright, subject to equitable considerations and bona fide commercial practices. Any dispute arising from actions taken by the patentee which demonstrably frustrate the intended scope of the license shall be referable to arbitration as provided herein, with costs determined at the arbitrator's discretion. The aggrieved party may appeal such an arbitral award to a court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction, demonstrating manifest error or perversity in the decision.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all patent licence agreements entered into concerning inventions protected under this Act. Every such agreement, prior to its implementation, must be submitted for registration within thirty days from the date of execution. The prescribed fee for registration shall be remitted at the time of submission. Registration confers upon the licensee certain rights as provided herein, including the right to enforce the terms and conditions stipulated in the licence patent terms against any infringement by the patentee or third parties. Failure to register a licence agreement does not invalidate it but renders the licensee unable to pursue legal remedies relating to its enforcement under this Act; however, the patentee remains bound by the unregistered agreement.

The Controller may, upon application by the patentee or assignee, grant a license to utilize the invention for which a patent has been registered, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit, provided that the applicant demonstrates compelling reasons justifying the need for such licensing. Any assignment of the patent, including the right to grant licenses under this Act, shall be recorded in the means register maintained by the Patent Office, and such recording shall vest validity upon the assignee’s entitlement to exercise all rights pertaining to the patented invention. Further, where a license is granted involving the use of a registered trade mark associated with the patented process or product, the Controller may stipulate conditions ensuring that the licensee adheres to quality standards equivalent to those maintained by the patentee. The fees for recording assignments and licenses shall be as prescribed.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a specification patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal unless it is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for believing that the decision appealed against is erroneous and has occasioned undue hardship. Failure to comply with the prescribed time limit shall be deemed a ground for dismissing the appeal summarily, subject to considerations of natural justice. The Controller may, upon receiving evidence of infringement of a specification patent, initiate proceedings for recovery of damages as provided herein, including punitive damages not exceeding three times the proven loss or actual harm suffered by the patentee.

Where a proprietor seeks registration of a trade mark incorporating a descriptive term, the Registrar shall require evidence demonstrating that, at the time of application, such term was widely accepted by the relevant consumer base as an indication of origin or quality. This requirement applies particularly when the proposed trade mark incorporates a *trade description manner* relating to the characteristics, properties, or intended use of the goods or services. The proprietor must submit affidavits from industry experts and documented market research confirming this widespread acceptance. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall constitute grounds for refusal under this Act. An appeal against such a decision may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication. The Board's determination shall be final, subject to further judicial review on limited grounds as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "adulterated food" shall mean any food which is not of the nature, substance, quality or purity demanded by its character and name; or which contains an admixture of another substance which impairs its conformity to that standard; or which has been manufactured, prepared, preserved, packaged or transported under unsanitary conditions whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. Food shall be deemed adulterated if it contains any added poisonous or deleterious substance, irrespective of whether such substance is present as a result of the manufacturing process or otherwise. The term "food" includes all articles intended for human consumption and also encompasses edible oils, milk, and processed foodstuffs as defined under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

Any producer failing to remit the prescribed registry fee within thirty days from the date specified on the official demand notice issued under this Act shall be deemed to have committed an offence and is liable, upon conviction, to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated failure to pay such fees, or attempting to evade payment through fraudulent means, will attract further penalties as determined by the Controller. The Controller may, at his discretion, initiate proceedings for recovery of outstanding registry fees as arrears of land revenue. Any person found assisting a producer in circumventing these fee obligations shall also be subject to similar fines and potential prosecution under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “association with goods” in relation to a trade mark means the use of a sign, whether registered or unregistered, in connection with goods or services in such a manner as to indicate, directly or indirectly, sponsorship or approval by the owner of the trade mark. A trade mark relation shall be deemed to exist where there is an intentional representation that the proprietor of the trade mark has approved of, or is connected with, the goods or services; provided that such representation may be inferred from the manner in which the sign is used and the impressions created in the mind of the public. Nothing herein shall prevent the use of a trade mark for descriptive purposes only, as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services connected with parliamentary proceedings, specifically during a house parliament session, and another person uses an identical or confusingly similar mark relating to dissimilar goods or services, the owner of the registered trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. Such relief may include an order restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned mark, and may also encompass damages for losses suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringement. The register shall brought before the relevant court as prima facie evidence of ownership and validity of the trade mark. Provided that, any defence based on honest concurrent use shall be considered only if the infringing party can demonstrate continuous and bona fide usage prior to the date of registration, subject to conditions prescribed herein.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of an invention, the Controller may require such evidence as he deems appropriate to determine said status, including but not limited to declarations from individuals involved in the conception and development of the invention, documentation relating to laboratory notebooks or design records, and testimony regarding the circumstances surrounding the initial disclosure of the inventive concept. The burden of establishing entitlement to be regarded as the true and first inventor shall rest upon the applicant for a patent. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller's determination on such matters is final. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision made concerning inventorship may petition the Controller within ninety days from the date of communication of that decision. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, revise any prior order if it appears necessary in the interests of justice or to ensure proper application of this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical substance” shall mean any novel chemical entity or biological product intended for use in diagnosis, mitigation, or cure of disease, or for improvement of health conditions in human beings or animals. Such a pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to include salts, esters, ethers, and other derivatives thereof, provided that such derivative possesses substantially the same pharmacological activity as the parent compound. The determination of novelty under this Act shall consider prior public knowledge relating to the chemical structure, method of manufacture, or intended therapeutic application of the pharmaceutical substance. Any process for producing a pharmaceutical substance may be patented subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall utilize a registered trade mark except with the consent of the proprietor, provided that such utilization complies fully with established guidelines regarding fair competition. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating actual damage resulting from unauthorized uses registered trade marks, issue an order restraining further use where the infringing activity creates confusion amongst consumers concerning the origin or quality of goods or services. Such orders shall specify the precise nature of the prohibited activities and may include requirements for corrective advertising to mitigate any existing consumer deception. Any subsequent violation of a restraint order issued under this Act will be deemed a continuing offence, subject to penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a breeder shall retain exclusive rights over a breeder registered variety for a period commencing from the date filing application, unless such rights are expressly assigned or licensed. Any assignment or license of rights in a breeder registered variety shall be recorded with the Authority within thirty days of execution, and shall specify the scope of such assignment or license, including geographical limitations and permitted uses. The assignee or licensee may, subject to conditions prescribed by the Authority, exercise the rights granted under the assignment or license as if they were the original breeder. Further, a registered breeder may grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the commercialization of the breeder registered variety; however, such licenses shall not impair the breeder’s right to continue propagating and selling the variety.

The Register of Registered Trade Marks maintained by the Registrar shall contain particulars as prescribed under this Act relating to each trademark’s registration date, proprietor details, goods or services for which it is registered, and any licensed users. Any alteration to a registered trade mark's specifications, including changes in ownership or the description of associated goods, shall be recorded promptly upon verification by the Registrar. The safeguards prescribed register shall be open to public inspection during specified hours, subject to applicable regulations regarding confidentiality of sensitive commercial information. Applications for rectification of entries on the Register may be filed with the Registrar, and such applications shall be processed according to procedures as provided herein. Any appeal against a decision concerning an entry on the safeguards prescribed register lies before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any entity seeking registration as a proprietor of an indication certification trade mark must demonstrate exclusive control over the characteristics defining the goods or services it certifies. Such demonstration requires submission of detailed operational protocols outlining quality assurance measures and adherence standards applicable to all certified producers. The Registrar may, after due consideration, require further clarification regarding these protocols if they are deemed insufficiently specific to ensure consumer confidence. Certification marks shall not be used in relation to goods or services that do not conform to the prescribed regulations as provided herein; any deviation from those regulations constitutes a violation under this Act and is subject to penalties. The Registrar may revoke registration where it appears that the entity no longer maintains such control.

Where an india patent is infringed, the patentee may institute a suit for relief including injunction and damages. Subject to appeal under this Act, a court shall grant such remedy as appears equitable in respect of the infringement, considering the extent of damage sustained by the patentee and the benefit derived by the infringer. Damages awarded shall be assessed on the basis of lost profits, reasonable royalties, or other measures deemed appropriate by the court; provided that in cases where the infringing act was committed unknowingly, the court may reduce the amount of damages accordingly. The patentee shall be entitled to recover costs incidental to the suit, as determined under this Act. Further, any person found guilty of wilful infringement of an india patent shall be liable for enhanced penalties and may face criminal prosecution.

An applicant seeking to obtain a patent under this Act may submit an application for amendment of the patent application at any time before the grant of the patent or during pending opposition proceedings. Such application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, as determined by notification issued by the Central Government. The Controller shall consider such applications, subject to the condition that the proposed amendments do not substantially alter the scope of protection initially sought. Any amendment requested must relate only to matters of clarification or detail and cannot introduce new matter which was not disclosed in the original specification. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or explanations supporting the request for an application amend, and shall provide a reasoned order detailing any decision regarding acceptance or rejection.

Where proceedings are instituted under this Act relating to infringement of a patent, the Controller may, upon application by the patentee or any interested party, direct the Registrar to issue notice to any person who is shown to be in possession or control of an article patented and alleged to have been infringed. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the patent, the nature of the alleged infringement, and require such person to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified in the notice to show cause why they should not be restrained from dealing with the said article. The Controller may, after hearing all parties concerned, make such order as it deems fit, including an order for the destruction or disposal of the includes article patented found in possession or control of the person failing to satisfy the Controller. This power shall extend to articles manufactured outside India and imported into India.

Where an application for a patent relates to any invention already described or claimed in a prior document, the Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, require the applicant to amend the specification so as to clearly define the scope of protection sought and distinguish it from that disclosed in the said prior document. The date application patent shall be construed strictly in accordance with the amended claims, notwithstanding any reference made within the original application to the name or names of inventors. Any party aggrieved by such a requirement may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of communication of the order. It is provided that the Controller’s determination regarding the relevance of prior art and its impact on the date application patent shall be final, unless demonstrable prejudice arises from an error apparent on the face of the record.

An application for registration of a registered trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated. Where an objection is raised under this Act, the applicant may submit evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use in commerce prior to the date of the application. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider such evidence and may require a consumer survey to ascertain public perception of the mark. Further, any person claiming ownership of a similar registered trade mark may file a caveat opposing registration, provided that they demonstrate likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed mark’s use. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both parties to present arguments and documentary proof before rendering a decision as provided herein.

Where infringement of layout-design rights has occurred, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. Such remedies include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further manufacture, import, sale, offer for sale, or hire of the infringing integrated circuit layout-design. Damages recoverable shall be assessed at a rate not exceeding three times the actual cost incurred by the proprietor in establishing and protecting their rights under this Act, or where such costs cannot be ascertained, an amount determined to be just and reasonable considering factors such as lost profits and the infringer’s gain. The Central Government may, upon application of any party, appoint a judicial member technical to assist the relevant court in determining complex issues relating to semiconductor technology involved in infringement proceedings.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a reasoned response within the prescribed period, or where such response demonstrably does not address all material aspects of the objection, the Registrar shall appear before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and present arguments substantiating the initial refusal. Failure by the Registrar to diligently pursue enforcement actions as provided herein regarding trade mark infringement will render them liable for penalties determined by the Board, proportionate to the demonstrable harm suffered by the aggrieved party. Any order issued by the Board concerning such appearances or penalties shall be final, subject only to appeal to the High Court on grounds of legal error. The Registrar’s appearance is deemed essential for ensuring procedural fairness and upholding the integrity of the register.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without due cause, and another person, having no connection with the proprietor, applies for registration thereof, the Registrar shall consider whether such application is likely to deceive or cause confusion as to the origin of the goods or services. In determining this likelihood, regard shall be had to all relevant circumstances including, but not limited to, the similarity of the marks and the corresponding wares. The register shall construed liberally in favour of protecting the distinctiveness of registered trade marks against unauthorized use by others. Any proprietor demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from such deceptive use may apply to a court for an injunction restraining the infringing application or subsequent registration. Further, damages may be awarded as provided herein to compensate for losses incurred due to the misleading nature of the competing mark.
